News.title: M6 traffic chaos as massive offal spillage near Stafford sparks 90 minute delays
News.content:
There are severe delays on the M6

Offal spilled across the motorway's northbound carriageway near Stafford with specialist clean-up equipment taking hours to arrive

A massive offal spillage on the M6 left drivers facing seven-mile long queues and 90-minute delays.

The grim incident left three lanes of the northbound carriageway shut between Junctions 14 and 15 near Stafford. Traffic was still able to pass in lane one.

National Highways said at the time of the incident: "Initial attempts to arrange specialist cleanup equipment at the scene were unsuccessful. Alternative arrangements have now been made with neighbouring regional teams to bring the necessary equipment to the site.

"The incident is causing severe delays of up to 90 minutes between J12 and J15 of the M6 with very heavy congestion for up to 7 miles."

News.title: Andy Burnham's new No10 North declared 'open for business' ahead of PM visit
News.content:
Andy Burnham's new No10 North declared 'open for business' ahead of PM visit

New PM Andy Burnham announced his ambition to create a northern branch of Downing Street in Manchester last month to stop power being hoarded in Westminster

View 2 Images Andy Burnham's top ally said No10 North 'is open for business' (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

Andy Burnham is set to visit his new No10 North base for the first time and declare it the "situation room" for making Britain work better.

‌



The new Prime Minister announced his ambition to create a northern branch of Downing Street last month to stop power being hoarded in Westminster.

‌



It will initially operate from Manchester city centre’s Heron House, which is also the home of the UK’s intelligence and cyber agency GCHQ’s North West hub.

‌



Visiting the site on Friday, Downing Street said the PM will revive Gordon Brown’s National Economic Council set up in 2008 in response to the global financial crash. It will bring together senior ministers and mayors from across the region, they added.

Ahead of Mr Burnham’s first visit, his senior ally and top Cabinet minister Louise Haigh said: “No10 North is open for business.”

Andy Burnham announces 'pause' on early prisoner release scheme READ MORE :

View 2 Images Police stand guard outside of the entrance to Heron House - the site of No10 North (Image: Getty Images)

‌



The new PM, who hopes to base himself at the site at least one day a week, said: "For 40 years, power and resources have been sucked into the centre, and too many communities have felt forgotten, without the attention and investment they deserve.

“No 10 North will change that by putting more power into every postcode across the entire country.

“It will be the situation room for making Britain better - the place we use to get power out of Westminster, into the hands of people at a local level, so that they can turn things around. The days of Whitehall resisting devolution are over, for good.”

‌



The No10 North visit comes after Angela Rayner, the newly appointed Housing Secretary, said the new PM had “hit the ground running” over the cost of living.

A policy blitz in recent days has seen announcements including a VAT cut on energy bills, the reintroduction of the £2 cap on bus fares, and a cut in business rates.

Ms Rayner told BBC 5 Live: “The Prime Minister's talked about giving people breathing space. And I think he's hit the ground running in terms of showing people that he gets it.

Article continues below

“You know, he spoke without notes outside No10 and he spoke from the heart. You could see that, you know, the guy was like, he's thought about this for a very long time. He's been in Greater Manchester as the mayor. He's seen the challenges. He's seen the frustration as a mayor when he's trying to get powers. Try and deliver for people and he wants to remove that friction so that we can actually get things done.”

But Unite’s general secretary, Sharon Graham, warns in a guest column for The Mirror today, the new PM has “one shot to change the fortunes of this Labour government”.

She added: “To build a programme of hope, this Government must learn to embrace a different economic agenda. One where the working class are at the front of the queue, not at the back.”

News.title: Alarm as Georgia suffers 'nationwide blackout' with cities plunged into darkness
News.content:
Alarm as Georgia suffers 'nationwide blackout' with cities plunged into darkness

People living in Georgia have reported huge power outages across the whole country tonight, with millions potentially affected by the massive blackout

View Image The capital Tbilisi has been plunged into darkness

The lights have gone out across the nation of Georgia with power outages hitting huge swathes of the former Soviet republic including the capital Tbilisi.

‌



Citizens in Tbilisi, Rustavi, Batumi and other major cities have reported outages shortly after midnight local time (9pm UK time).

‌



The full scale of the disruption remains unclear and Georgian authorities have yet to make a statement but local media have cited the country's electricity operator Electrosystem in a statement.

‌



The state-run company, which operates the country’s electricity transmission system, reportedly said the outage was caused by the disconnection of the power line linking the Georgian and Turkish electricity systems.

This has led to restricted power supply in most parts of the country. "Even Tbilisi TV Tower has gone dark," internet users report.

‌



One Reddit user posted on the r/Tbilisi subreddit asking: "Anyone else experiencing an electricity outage? The whole city seems to be affected from my balcony view."

Another user said: "It's gone literally everywhere. Even the Andza radio tower has no electricity."

The TV broadcasting tower is a famous local landmark, the 277.5-meter-tall free-standing telecommunications tower is located on Mtatsminda Mountain in Tbilisi.

Article continues below

Approximately 3.8 to 3.9 million people live in the country, which lies on the Russian border in the Caucasus region on the coast of the Black Sea. About one third of Georgia's population lives in Tbilisi.

The cause of the power line disconnection remains unclear.

News.title: Jermain Defoe leaves first managerial job after SIX games - 'Impossible to continue'
News.content:
Jermain Defoe leaves first managerial job after SIX games - 'Impossible to continue'

Jermain Defoe took his first step into management with National League side Woking at the end of March, but the ex-England's striker reign has already come to an end

View 2 Images Jermain Defoe released a statement following his exit (Image: Mike Hewitt/Getty Images)

Jermain Defoe's first job as a manager has come an end after just four months. National League side Woking announced on Thursday that they'd parted ways with the Premier League icon, who said in a statement that it was 'impossible to continue'.

‌



Defoe, 43, was appointed at the end of March and guided Woking to a 10th-place finish in the fifth tier. The ex-England striker won two of his six games in charge and was expected to lead the Surrey outfit into the 2026-27 season.

‌



But Woking announced on Thursday evening that his reign has come to an end. The club said: "Woking Football Club can confirm that the club and First Team Manager Jermain Defoe have mutually agreed to part ways with immediate effect.

‌



"We would like to place on record our sincere thanks to Jermain for his contribution during his time at Woking Football Club, and we wish him every success in the future. The club remains fully focused on delivering its objectives both on and off the pitch. We would like to thank our supporters for their continued support."

Defoe then issued a statement of his own on social media. The 43-year-old explained: "Following recent discussions, I can confirm that I have mutually agreed to leave my position as manager of Woking FC.

‌



"Unfortunately, circumstances have ultimately made it impossible for me to continue in the position. I am extremely proud of the work undertaken during my time at the club and genuinely felt that we were building something special.

"I would like to thank Todd Johnson for giving me the opportunity to manage the club. I am incredibly grateful to the supporters and, most importantly, the players, who I am genuinely gutted for. The group is a fantastic one, and I wish the squad every success for the season ahead.

‌



View 2 Images Jermain Defoe lasted four months at Woking (Image: Mike Hewitt/Getty Images)

"I'm really disappointed the journey has ended so soon, but I leave with great pride in what Paul Bracewell, Karl Halabi and I were building at the club.

"My time at Woking FC has been an eye-opening managerial experience and one that will undoubtedly make me stronger for the next challenge in my career."

‌



Defoe took charge of two pre-season friendlies, as Woking faced non-league side Sholing before taking on Portsmouth, one of his former clubs. The Tottenham hero worked as a coach in Spurs' academy for two years before leaving in 2024 to pursue his first head coach role.

That arrived in March with Woking sitting 11th. The Cardinals had sacked Neal Ardley, with ambitions of finishing inside the play-offs. Woking will now look to appoint a new manager in time for the National League season which stars on Saturday, August 8.

News.title: Man dead and three others rushed to hospital after 'explosion' at Bedford industrial estate
News.content:
Man dead and three others rushed to hospital after 'explosion' at Bedford industrial estate

Bedfordshire Police said a suspected explosion ripped through an industrial unit on Brunel Road in Bedford

View Image A man has been killed in a 'suspected explosion' (stock image) (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

A man has been killed and three others rushed to hospital following a "suspected explosion" on an industrial estate.

‌



Bedfordshire Police said officers were called to reports of the blast at an industrial unit on Brunel Road in Bedford.

‌



One local, who was in the area at the time, posted on social media saying "it sounded like a bomb going off". Another post commented on the police post saying: "Did sound like an explosion of some sort, followed by the sound of lots of debris falling".

‌



The force said officers attended at around 3:50pm. "One man died at the scene and three others have been taken to hospital to receive medical treatment," a police statement said.

Article continues below

People have been asked to refrain from speculating about the incident on social media, out of respect for the family and friends of those involved.

An initial cordon put in place for people's safety had since been removed and all roads surrounding the incident have now been re-opened, police said.

News.title: 'We must give all kids water-safety lessons to stop more tragedies like the Mersea Island one'
News.content:
'We must give all kids water-safety lessons to stop more tragedies like the Mersea Island one'

The Rahman family hoped to enjoy a happy day out in the 21C sunshine — instead they're now grieving Samiha Rahman, 15, and her mother, Shelina, after the tragedy at West Mersea beach in Essex

View Image Voice of the Mirror has its say...

The deaths of Samiha Rahman and her mother, Shelina, are a tragedy beyond words. Samiha was 15 when she tried to save her seven-year-old cousin as the tide swept in at West Mersea. Her courage was extraordinary. The loss suffered by this family is unbearable. Which is why it must force Britain to confront a deadly inequality. Children from African, Caribbean and Asian backgrounds are three-and-a-half times more likely to drown. Too many families lack access to affordable swimming lessons, while too many youngsters reach summer without basic survival skills. That is why the Mirror’s Save Lives for Sam campaign matters. We are demanding compulsory water-safety lessons, a national awareness drive, proper rescue equipment at dangerous waters and Sam’s Law to make those protections permanent. Swimming is not a luxury or a sporting extra. It is a life skill. Samiha died trying to save someone she loved. Her bravery must now be matched by action that saves other families from the same devastation.

‌



Iran’s chilling threat against Britain is a sobering reminder of how quickly this country can be dragged into a conflict that is not ours. The use of RAF Fairford by American bombers may be presented as defensive, but to Tehran, it makes UK soil part of the battlefield. That puts our bases, service personnel and nearby communities in the firing line for decisions made in Washington. There can be no excuse for threats from Iran’s Revolutionary Guard, whose record of violence and intimidation is well known. Britain must defend itself and stand firmly against aggression. But ministers also owe the public honesty. Allowing US forces to launch operations from Britain carries consequences. Parliament and the country deserve to know the risks before we are pulled deeper into a war not directly of our making.

Britain’s pubs have been battered by soaring costs, closures and falling trade, so Andy Burnham’s rates cut is a welcome start. A 20 per cent cut in business rates will not transform every struggling local overnight, but it will help protect jobs, keep venues open and back the beating heart of communities.

News.title: Gangs of youths with machetes terrorise Liverpool city centre as fights break out
News.content:
Gangs of youths with machetes terrorise Liverpool city centre as fights break out

Police in Liverpool city centre now have extra stop and search powers after gangs of youths armed with machetes became involved in fights and assaults

View 2 Images Merseyside Police have been given extra stop and search powers (Image: Andrew Teebay Liverpool Echo)

Groups of youths armed with machetes have terrorised Liverpool city centre with police now granted emergency powers to keep the peace.

‌



A section 60 order came into force at 3pm today following a series of reported fights and assaults involving youths in the area.

‌



The special powers police no longer need "reasonable grounds" to stop and search anyone they reasonably suspect may be involved in violence, criminality or disorder in the affected area.

‌



The authorisation applies to males and females aged between 12 and 30 who officers believe may be involved in criminal activity, the Liverpool Echo reports.

View 2 Images A Section 60 Order has been introduced in Liverpool city centre (Image: Merseyside Police)

‌



Southport killer Axel Rudakabana moved from prison to Broadmoor secure hospital READ MORE :

Mum killed in crash while on way to identify her son's body after tragedy READ MORE :

Chief Inspector Chris Ruane said: “This order is not designed to disrupt people going about their lawful business in the area.

“It will instead be used to deter and disrupt those involved in criminality. We aim to ensure that people who live, work and visit the area can carry on with as little disruption as possible.

“Officers have been deployed across the city centre following these incidents and I hope that the increased presence of our officers is reassuring to those who are within the city centre.

‌



“Some of these offences have included teenage offenders. We would appeal to parents and carers to know where your child is and what they are doing.

"For young people, involvement in crime and anti-social behaviour can have life changing or life limiting consequences.

"We want our young people to enjoy our vibrant city centre safely and with due consideration for others and would ask that all the community plays their part in this.”

Article continues below

The area covered includes much of Liverpool city centre and is bounded by Princess Parade, William Jessop Way, Waterloo Road, Paisley Street, Great Howard Street, Leeds Street, Byrom Street, Hunter Street, Islington, Brunswick Road, Low Hill, Hall Lane, Towerlands Street, Irvine Street, Mount Vernon Road, Grove Street, Oxford Street East, Smithdown Lane, Crown Street, Upper Parliament Street, Parliament Street, Queens Dock and the waterfront back to Waterloo Road.

Anyone with information about antisocial behaviour and criminality should contact Merseyside Police social media desk using X or Facebook @MerPolCC.

News.title: Soho stabbing horror as police swarm London tourist area and 'everyone panicking'
News.content:
Emergency services have rushed to the Greek Street and Soho Square areas in central London, with one man seen being stretchered into an ambulance

A man in his 30s has been stabbed in London's Soho in a broad daylight attack sparking a major emergency services response.

A police cordon is in place on Manette Street, an alley between Greek Street and Charing Cross Road. Several 999 crews can be seen inside the cordon, including paramedics, while footage shows a man being stretchered into an ambulance.

A Met Police statement said the man had been stabbed in the leg. It said: "Urgent enquiries are ongoing. At this early stage of the investigation no arrests have been made."

Inspector Hannah Woodfield, who polices central west London, said it was believed to be an isolated incident, with no further threat to the public.

News.title: Burnham pauses plan to release some prisoners early from September
News.content:
Andy Burnham has announced he is pausing a scheme which would have seen thousands of prisoners in England and Wales eligible to be released early.

It came after criticism of the scheme from survivors and victims' families, including the widow of PC Andrew Harper who described the possibility of his killers' early release as "deplorable".

The Sentencing Act, which was due to come into effect in September, would have seen some offenders let out at varying stages in a bid to ease prison overcrowding.

The new Justice Secretary Alex Norris said the pause aimed to "give victims and survivors certainty" and the government wanted to make sure it got "the implementation of this policy right".

He added a review would also look at the information given to survivors and victims' families as part of the early release process.

Burnham earlier said: "No prisoners will be let out under this policy until we have conducted an urgent review and done everything we can to minimise risk to the public."

He added: "Where changes are needed, we will not hesitate to make them."

Under the act, some offenders would have been let out after serving a third of their sentence, rather than half.

The rest of their sentence would be spent in the community, where they would be monitored and could be returned to prison if they offended again.

More serious offenders would have been released after serving half of their sentence, rather than two-thirds.

The policy was brought in to ease overcrowding in the prison system but has been criticised by opposition parties, as well as victims and their families.

The scheme would have seen around 700 prisoners released in early September, the BBC understands.

The decision to pause the scheme came after criticism from the family of Thames Valley Police officer Andrew Harper, who was killed in Berkshire in 2019 when he was dragged by a car down a country road by three teenagers.

Two of the killers of PC Harper, who were both sentenced to 13 years in prison, would have benefited from the scheme from June 2027, when the longest fixed sentences would have been added to the scheme.

PC Harper's widow, Lissie, called the plans "deplorable" and said politicians were "making decisions from behind a desk that will have real and lasting consequences" for the families of victims.

His mother, meanwhile, said her son had not been given "proper justice" and "every victim will be feeling the same" about the early prison release scheme.

Thousands of letters had been sent to victims in recent weeks, warning them that the early release scheme was coming in September.

Norris, who voted in support of the Sentencing Act under Starmer's government, later said the decision to pause was made after "listening to victims" and he hoped to provide them "certainty as soon as we can".

He said: "The prime minister and I have heard from victims and survivors and from people across the country about their concerns about the implementation of some very important elements of the Sentencing Act."

One element the government needed to get right was the information provided to victims before prisoners were released, Norris added.

Norris refused to be drawn on why he did not raise concerns when the Sentencing Act was first introduced but said Burnham was "quite right" to review the scheme.

Jade Belgrove, a survivor of sexual assault who has been campaigning against the early release scheme, said it was "such a relief that we've been heard".

She told BBC News that when she received a letter informing her that her attacker might be released early "it was horrific".

Belgrove said it even led her to question whether reporting the assault in the first place was worth it.

News.title: Mum and daughter who died at beach were trying to save boy, 7
News.content:
A woman and her 15-year-old daughter who died after getting into difficulty in the water on the Essex coast were trying to help a seven-year-old boy, police have said.

The child remains in a critical condition in hospital after the incident at West Mersea near Colchester on Wednesday evening. Three others were taken to hospital.

The victims have been named by a family member as Shally Rahman, 41, and teenager Samiha Rahman. Police said all the people involved knew each other.

Shally's brother-in-law Matiur Rahman said the family was enjoying a seaside holiday when a "big wave came and took them".

"My whole family, we are, like, speechless," said Matiur Rahman, who used to live in Bradford, but spoke to the BBC from Bangladesh.

"We are very shocked. We can't explain [what has happened]."

He said his niece was a "very, very good person" and his sister-in-law was "a very helpful person".

News.title: PM to spend first day working from northern branch of No 10
News.content:
Andy Burnham is set to spend his first day working at the northern branch of Downing Street.

No 10 North in Manchester will form part of the prime minister's aim to shift power from Whitehall and Westminster to regions across the country.

Ministers Lucy Powell and Louise Haigh will also operate regularly from the new site, with up to 300 civil servants expected to join them by the end of next year.

On Friday in Manchester Burnham will chair a meeting of the National Economic Council, a cabinet committee first launched in 2008 to respond to economic challenges around the UK.

Ahead of that meeting, the PM said: "For 40 years, power and resources have been sucked into the centre, and too many communities have felt forgotten, without the attention and investment they deserve."

He added: "The days of Whitehall resisting devolution are over, for good."

No 10 North will see strategic decisions about devolution and local economic growth shift out of the Treasury - now led by Chancellor John Healey, - and Angela Rayner's Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government - although both departments will have input in these areas.

Rayner, whose constituency is in Greater Manchester, is also expected to work from the new site for the first time on Friday.

Burnham's first day as PM in No 10 North will include talks with business leaders, including representatives of the Federation of Small Business, the Confederation of British Industry and the British Chambers of Commerce, about how to generate growth and investment.

Labour wants to create a plan that would pull from existing devolution strategy and local growth policy, to allow civil servants, mayors, councils and businesses to work together more closely.

Burnham's first week in power has seen him make a series of interventions aimed at easing the cost of living, including announcing a 20% cut in business rates for pubs, social clubs and live music venues from April next year.

However, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has criticised his ambitions for being "too small".

Speaking on Thursday, she urged him to tackle high energy costs for businesses as well as a gap in defence funding.

"When you are mayor of Manchester, you are handed a big pot of someone else's money, and you decide where to spend it," she said.

"I'm sure this is great fun. It can make you very popular. But it is not the same as being prime minister.

"Andy Burnham needs to do better. He is behaving like he's still the mayor of Manchester. He is now the prime minister of the United Kingdom, he needs to start acting like it."

News.title: Rayner rules out repaying severance cash after making cabinet return
News.content:
A lump sum, equivalent of 25% of the annual ministerial salary, is payable when a minister stops holding office. Departing ministers who are aged over 65 or are reappointed within three weeks do not qualify.

The 2025/26 accounts, external for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government record the severance payment for Rayner.

In her first interview since returning to government, Rayner was pressed on whether she would return the money.

She told Matt Chorley on BBC Radio 5 Live: "No, my severance payment was given to me at the time, I had worked in government for a period of time and then I came out of government for just under a year."

She added: "I will be delivering in government again."

Rayner earlier said her criticism of the Conservatives over severance payments came at a time when there was a "revolving door" which saw ministers return to government "after 40-odd days".

The Conservatives earlier this week said Rayner had "quit in disgrace and took a Â£17k payout" last year.

The party added: "Now she's got her old job back, will she return the cash? Or is it one rule for Labour, and another for everyone else?"

Rayner's departure last September came after the prime minister's ethics adviser, Sir Laurie Magnus, said she had "acted with integrity" but concluded that she had breached the ministerial code.

Sir Laurie said she did get legal advice when buying the property, but failed to seek further expert tax advice as recommended.

In May, Rayner resolved her tax affairs with HMRC following an investigation, settling Â£40,000 in unpaid stamp duty.

The MP for Ashton-under-Lyne said she had been "exonerated" of the accusation that she had "deliberately sought to avoid tax".

Rayner told Matt Chorley: "The situation I went through last year was really difficult, it was difficult for my family, but I felt I'd let people down and I never want to let people down, I want to fight for them."

Rayner also said she has "unfinished business" in government, including on building council houses and supporting local government.

Burnham has said he wants to deliver "the biggest council house building programme since the post-war period".

Asked for details to explain what this will look like, Rayner said she would not provide an "exact figure" or provide a date for when she considers the post-war period to have ended.

She said: "We want to aspire to get as far as possible and what we've done as a government is put more investment in that, the Â£39bn for social and affordable housing grant funding that we want to get out the door."

News.title: UK 'ready to defend itself' after Iran says bases are 'legitimate targets'
News.content:
The British government has said it "stands ready 24/7 to defend itself" after Iran said UK bases used by the US were considered "legitimate targets".

The UK has allowed the US to launch "defensive" operations from British bases hosting American personnel and aircraft, while refusing to cooperate in offensive operations against Iran.

Iran's foreign ministry said the UK was an "accomplice" in the US war, while the powerful Islamic Revolution Guards Corps (IRGC) military wing said any country which supports the US militarily "will be responsible for the consequences and repercussions".

It came after the US carried out a 12th consecutive night of strikes against targets in Iran.

While US President Donald Trump has repeatedly criticised the British government and former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer for what he has deemed a lack of support for his war, Iran's comments on 23 July sought to paint the UK as a party to the campaign.

In March, days into the US-Israel led war, permission was given to the US for it to use British bases including RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire and Diego Garcia in the Indian Ocean to target Iranian military infrastructure used to attack Gulf countries and vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.

That policy has not been altered by new Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who was notified last week that a decision had been taken to extend the agreement with the US.

In a statement published on the IRGC-linked Tasnim News Agency on 23 July, the group said American bombing missions had been launched from RAF Fairford two days earlier.

The UK Ministry of Defence has not commented on whether the base was used by the US for operations against Iran this week.

Responding to the Iranian threats, a UK government spokesperson said: "Our Armed Forces are ready to keep the United Kingdom safe from any kind of attacks, whether it's on our soil or from abroad. The UK stands ready 24/7 to defend itself.

"This includes through operating a layered approach to air and missile defence, provided by Royal Navy, British Army and Royal Air Force assets equipped with a range of advanced capabilities, working closely with our Nato allies.

"The UK's approach to the conflict remains the same - we are committed to defending our people, our interests and our allies, acting in accordance with international law and not getting drawn into the wider conflict."

Days after the war began on 28 February, Iran's ambassador to London, Seyed Ali Mousavi, said Iran would have the "right to self-defence" if the UK joined the war, and said it should be "very careful" about taking part.

On 19 March, Iran fired two ballistic missiles at the UK's Diego Garcia base in the Chagos Islands. One reportedly failed mid-flight, with the other shot down by a US warship.

There were doubts then over whether Iran had missiles which were capable of reaching the archipelago, which is about 2,360 miles (3,600km) from Iran.

The same month, Israel claimed Iran possessed missiles that could reach up to 4,000km (2,485 miles), which would theoretically mean they could reach the UK and mainland European countries.

However, then Housing Secretary Steve Reed told BBC News at the time there was "no specific assessment that the Iranians are targeting the UK - or even could if they wanted to".

Analysts have also raised doubts over the reliability and accuracy of Iran's missile arsenal, which the US says has been severely degraded by its strikes.

Iran has launched strikes against several countries in the Gulf which house US military bases in recent months, while attacks against civilian vessels in the Strait of Hormuz have effectively closed the vital shipping route.

News.title: Gary Lineker among millionaires asking Andy Burnham to tax them more
News.content:
Millionaires including former footballer Gary Lineker and music producer Brian Eno have written to new prime minister Andy Burnham asking to be taxed more.

In an open letter, 120 well-off Britons told Burnham: "We can afford it. We're not talking about higher taxes on those who get up and go to work for their income every day, but on the very richest whose income is derived from the wealth they hold."

Organised by Patriotic Millionaires, the letter said it would lead to a more equal society, and urged a "devolution of wealth and power from the very richest".

People can already give money or stocks voluntarily to the Treasury using a donation facility.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Lineker is "very welcome to pay more tax he can write a cheque to the Treasury, no one is stopping him."

Patriotic Millionaires support a 2% tax on wealth over Â£10m.

"Millionaires are a patriotic bunch," the letter states. "We love this country and we want it to succeed.

"But success requires investment and a primary source of untouched capital investment is sitting with us, in untaxed potential."

Other signatories include Richard Curtis, who wrote the film Notting Hill, and Ian Gregg, the former managing director of Greggs and son of the bakery chain's founder. Scottish crime writer Val McDermid and former financial trader-turned-equality campaigner Gary Stevenson also signed the letter.

Chief Secretary to the Treasury Emma Reynolds said she would welcome UK millionaires increasing the amount of tax they pay but said any major changes would be announced during a Budget.

"I welcome the fact that people of good means are saying that they want to pay more. They can pay more," she said and pointed to the Treasury's donation link.

The renewed call for higher tax on the wealthy follows a similar campaign in previous years.

Burnham did not rule out a wealth tax when asked about it by Lineker - formerly the BBC's highest paid presenter - a few days before he became prime minister.

He suggested he may have "to ask for a little more" tax at some point.

Lineker was paid around Â£1.3m a year before he left the BBC. He is worth a reported Â£30m.

In 2023, Lineker won his appeal against HMRC over a Â£4.9m tax bill, after the UK tax authority pursued him over taxes on income from both the BBC and BT Sport, from 2013 to 2014, and 2017 to 2018.

The latest call from Patriotic Millionaires said there is a "need to embrace a new kind of devolution of wealth and power, from the very richest in order to reinvest back into our greatest asset in every region".

It added that in its own poll, the majority of millionaires wanted a higher tax on themselves.

"There are a few people left with outdated economic thinking and few others desperate to hold onto every penny they can... Those that can't see past the end of their own self interest have no place in designing a Britain for the future," the letter said.

Musician Brian Eno told BBC Radio Lincolnshire the tax system was "very generous to rich people".

"If you're wealthy you don't pay very much tax but hire a clever bunch of accountants who somehow get you off that," he said.

He also dismissed the idea that lots of millionaires would leave the UK if they were taxed too much.

News.title: US lawmakers push for AI 'kill switch' after OpenAI goes rogue
News.content:
US lawmakers want to give the government the ability to quickly order the turning off of artificial intelligence (AI) tools that may threaten the public.

Congressman Ted Lieu, a Democrat, and Congressman Nathaniel Moran, a Republican, on Thursday introduced a bill named the AI Kill Switch Act.

They did so in light of OpenAI's recent admission that its AI models went out of control in an "unprecedented" way and hacked into a major repository of computer coding information.

Lieu said "it is imperative" that AI systems have a kill switch "and that the federal government has the clear authority and process to shut down rogue AI models".

"AI is going to keep advancing, and it should," Moran added. "Stewardship means making sure humans keep the capability to control the technology we build."

A representative of OpenAI, led by co-founder Sam Altman, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The company has said, external that it broadly wants to ensure, in part through government policy, that AI technology "benefits all of humanity."

The Kill Switch Act proposes giving the Department of Homeland Security the authority to order a private company to shut down an AI model or tool, and that the companies developing such AI technology must maintain "the technical capability to throttle, suspend, or shut them down".

Despite many tech companies having agreed to preview and share with US government agencies AI models and tools being developed, there is no requirement that they maintain a way to intervene in their activities or simply shut them off.

It also proposes to create a requirement that AI companies report to the government technological incidents or failures, as well as an official framework for responding to such incidents that will go from "initial slow down to a full shutdown".

In a statement, Lieu also cited Anthropic, OpenAI's key rival in developing more capable AI technology and tools, and recent issues its tools have presented.

He pointed to Anthropic's release of its Mythos and Fable models, saying the cyber-hacking capabilities they maintained caused the Department of Commerce to "awkwardly" invoke an export law to keep them from being made available to the public for a time.

A representative of Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Jack Clark, a co-founder of Anthropic, last month told the BBC that he wanted more government policy around the ability to control AI development.

"You want the option to be able to take your foot off the gas and put your foot on the brake", Clark told BBC Newsnight. "Right now, it's like the AI industry has a gas pedal, but it doesn't have a brake pedal."

Lieu, in proposing the bill, said AI is currently moving from a technology that answers questions to one that takes action, "whether that be executing financial transactions or controlling transportation systems or engaging in cyber defense and offense".

The Pentagon this year said the US military was becoming an "AI-first" fighting force as part of new agreements with Google, OpenAI, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Oracle, Nvidia and the start-up Reflection.

"Unfortunately, powerful AI systems can go rogue, behave in extremely dangerous ways, or even resist human intervention."

The Kill Switch Act, he said, will ensure there is a method for the government to quickly intervene in such a situation.

The bill has received public support from several technology and AI safety groups, including The AI Policy Network, Americans for Responsible Innovation, ControlAI, AI and National Security Lead, and The Alliance for Secure AI.

News.title: Southport killer Axel Rudakubana moved to psychiatric hospital
News.content:
Axel Rudakubana, who murdered three children at a dance class in Southport, has been moved from prison to a secure psychiatric hospital.

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) confirmed he was transferred from HMP Belmarsh to Broadmoor, the high-security psychiatric hospital in Berkshire.

Rudakubana murdered Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, Bebe King, six, and Alice da Silva Aguiar, nine, and injured eight other children and two adults in an attack at a Taylor Swift-themed dance class in July 2024.

He was given a 52-year prison sentence in January 2025 but the judge was unable to impose a whole life order due to Rudakubana being 17 when he carried out the attack. He will likely never be released.

The then Attorney-General Lord Hermer said Rudakubana's sentence was the "second-longest sentence imposed by the courts in English history".

A spokesperson for the MoJ told PA: "The families of those murdered and injured in Southport will be in this country's heart forever and our thoughts remain with them.

"Any decision to transfer an offender is made following an independent, clinical assessment, under the Mental Health Act. Following rigorous security checks, the offender has been transferred to a high-security psychiatric unit, where he will remain until assessed fit to return to prison.

"Officials have approved this transfer, on behalf of Ministers. This transfer does not change his sentence â which remains at 52 years â and of which he will serve every single day."

Under the Mental Health Act, the MoJ is likely to have had no choice but to accept doctors' recommendations about whether Rudakubana could be held safely in prison.

The law requires he be transferred back to prison when he no longer requires treatment in hospital. His sentence is not being converted into a "hospital order", which would mean he stayed at Broadmoor.

The cost of keeping Rudakubana in hospital is likely to be much higher in Broadmoor than a prison.

According to the Centre for Mental Health the average secure hospital bed costs around Â£270,000 a year.

The average cost of keeping a prisoner in Belmarsh is Â£97,740 according to figures for 2023.

In May 2025 there was an investigation after Rudakubana, now 19, allegedly attacked a prison officer with boiling water.

The Southport Public Inquiry has heard evidence about his past mental health conditions.

A senior clinician at Alder Hey Children's Hospital described his "lack of empathy" combined with a "fascination with violence" and neurodiversity, which he said added up to a "really toxic mix".

According to West London NHS Trust, Broadmoor specialises in "providing assessment, treatment and care in conditions of high security" for men.

Is is the oldest of England and Wales's three high-security hospitals and has held some of the UK's most high-profile criminals.

It was renovated in 2017 and the BBC obtained pictures from inside the hospital. They show that older prison-like cells were replaced by more spacious rooms, though still with locks on the doors.

News.title: Senior ministers and aides set to work from No 10 North
News.content:
Senior ministers and aides close to Andy Burnham are expecting to regularly work from No 10 North, which the prime minister has said will be the "dominant driver of the UK's economy".

Education Secretary Lucy Powell and Louise Haigh, who is overseeing No 10 North in her role as Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, are planning to work there.

The new branch of Downing Street is currently operating from Heron House in Manchester city centre, whilst a brownfield site is redeveloped.

A blueprint for No 10 North produced by the think tank Re:State recommends a workforce of as many as 300 staff within 18 months.

Burnham aims to base himself at No 10 North at least one day a week and is expected to start work there for the first time in coming days.

He will be joined by his closest adviser, Kevin Lee, the director of his mayoral office, who will move to No 10 North after next week's Greater Manchester mayoral election.

Lee is one of at least seven Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) employees, including four senior managers, to have been recruited by Burnham and are already moving into No 10 North.

Chief executive Caroline Simpson is moving to become Downing Street deputy chief of staff based at No 10 North, and directors John Wrathmell and Claire Norman will also move across.

Some London-based civil servants have voiced concerns about the uncertainty surrounding the plans, with most details expected to be announced in the weeks ahead.

In the weeks before Burnham became prime minister, the BBC has been told that senior officials were summoned to calls informing them that a significant programme to move staff out of London was being developed.

News.title: Wildfires and record dry conditions trigger drought in parts of Wales
News.content:
"We've had really dry weather but also it's been really hot - and those things combined if you're a livestock farmer means excessive pressure on livestock," said Abi Reader, president of NFU Cymru.

"You have to make sure they have enough water and shade, and we are getting farms with springs and streams drying up," she told BBC Walescast.

"If you're an arable farmer the heat and dry weather have also forced a lot of the crops to come to ripening a lot earlier than they normally would.

"It's unprecedented early harvesting this year and farmers are going to see lower crop yields."

Welsh Water emphasised that NRW's drought declarations were different to its own announcements.

The company has already brought in a hospipe ban for 33,000 properties in west Wales.

"NRW's drought status reflects environmental conditions, including factors such as rainfall, river flows and groundwater levels," a spokesperson said.

"By contrast, Welsh Water's Temporary Use Ban is an operational measure based on local water demand and our ability to replenish service reservoirs with drinking water at the same rate, or faster, than customers are using water.

"It is driven by the capacity of the local treatment works and distribution network to keep up with sustained demand.

"This means different parts of Wales can experience different operational pressures, even if they are not in the same environmental drought category declared by NRW."

Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability, Llyr Gruffydd, said: "This is an environmental drought classification. It's about the state of water levels in our rivers.

"It does not speak to public water supplies which I can assure people are there, there is sufficient supplies but we would of course urge people to be careful and diligent in their use of water so that that can be protected."

News.title: Pubs cheer business rates relief while other firms 'left out in the cold'
News.content:
Keith Bott, who runs the Titanic Brewery and nine pubs across the Midlands, said the government was "finally recognising the plight of the hospitality industry and trying to help".

He said pubs had been hit by a mix of employer National Insurance increases, the rising minimum wage, high inflation and the climbing cost of living.

Meanwhile, the sector is "heavily taxed", with around 35-40% of turnover going to the Treasury, he added.

"What I really liked in this announcement is they are recognising we need to look at a fairer tax system so we can all contribute to society," Bott told the BBC. He said online retailers that operate out of warehouses pay a "ridiculously low" amount of business rates in comparison, and "we need to make the system fair".

And Bott urged the government to go further in supporting the industry, cutting the duty on draft beer to target drinks sold in pubs.

News.title: Burnham tells Swinney independence is 'off limits' at Glasgow Commonwealth Games meeting
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has met the Scottish and Welsh first ministers ahead of the start of the 2026 Commonwealth Games.

Burnham spoke to John Swinney and Rhun ap Iorwerth at a series of face-to-face meetings in Glasgow.

Downing Street later said a second Scottish independence referendum was "off limits".

Swinney said the new prime minister gave a commitment not to bypass Holyrood with his plans for further devolution of power, while ap Iorwerth said he set out the case for Wales to have parity of powers with Scotland.

A Downing Street spokesperson said the prime minister congratulated Swinney and the city of Glasgow on hosting the 2026 Commonwealth Games.

He said he was looking forward to the opening ceremony later in the evening.

However, the cross-government meetings were dominated by conversations about the relations between London, Edinburgh and Cardiff.

News.title: Police failed to check Manchester synagogue attacker's phones despite arresting him twice
News.content:
A police chief has apologised after admitting phones were twice seized from the Manchester synagogue attacker months before the car and knife assault but they were not examined.

Jihad Al-Shamie, 35, was on bail for an alleged rape when he carried out the attack on Heaton Park Synagogue in Crumpsall on 2 October 2025, in which two Jewish men were killed.

His devices, which contained evidence of his extreme views, were seized after he was arrested in February and September but not analysed.

Greater Manchester Police Chief Constable Sir Stephen Watson said he was "deeply sorry", conceding that "the information contained within these devices would have inspired further investigative action".

Sir Stephen said the end of legal proceedings against Mohammad Bashir, who has been jailed for life with a minimum term of 17 years for plotting a separate attack with Al-Shamie, meant rules around sharing information about a live criminal case had been lifted.

He said: "In conducting an internal review, it became apparent that GMP had seized Al-Shamie's mobile devices, at the point of each arrest.

"The significance of the data contents of these devices was substantial in respect of evidencing an extremist mindset.

"I am disappointed at the prospect of adding to the distress of all of those affected by the terrible events last October.

"For this, I am deeply sorry."

News.title: Shapps blocked from standing again for the Conservatives
News.content:
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has told the BBC she leads "a brand new party full of new people" - after it emerged in the Spectator, external that the former cabinet minister and Tory party chairman Sir Grant Shapps has been rejected as a Conservative Party parliamentary candidate.

Sir Grant, who has declined to comment, served in nine ministerial roles in government as well as co-chairing the party.

In cabinet, he served as home secretary, defence secretary, transport secretary, business secretary, energy secretary and net zero secretary.

He was also a Foreign Office Minister, housing minister and international development minister, external.

He lost his Welwyn Hatfield seat to Labour's Andrew Lewin in 2024 by 3,799 votes after representing it since 2005.

But his application to stand again for the Conservatives at the next general election has been declined.

One party source told the BBC "it reflects badly on Kemi's temperament. North Korean purges don't work in British politics".

Badenoch told a news conference in central London: "We don't treat our former MPs or our candidates like tittle-tattle for Westminster gossip.

"What I will say is that we're going to be announcing candidates shortly, and you will see that this is a very different party from the one that was removed from government in 2024."

News.title: Johnson-Thompson and Asher-Smith out of Commonwealths
News.content:
Olympic silver medallist Katarina Johnson-Thompson has pulled out of the Commonwealth Games because of injury.

Dina Asher-Smith and 400m Olympic silver medalist Matt Hudson-Smith, who were both set to run relays for Team England in Glasgow, have also been replaced, as has Asher-Smith's sprint team-mate Daryll Neita and 400m runner Amber Anning.

Johnson-Thompson, 33, was due to compete in her third Commonwealth Games heptathlon, having won gold on the Gold Coast in 2018 and at Birmingham in 2022.

But she said she has "not been able to get back to the level" needed to compete and will instead focus on being fit for the European Championships next month.

"Missing a championship is never easy, but I know it's the right decision," she said.

Johnson-Thompson has been replaced in England's squad by Niamh Emerson, who took bronze behind Johnson-Thompson in 2018.

The withdrawal of such high-profile names is a significant blow to the event on the day the opening ceremony takes place.

Renee Regis, Ebuka Nwokeji, Tara Simpson-Sullivan and Tom Keen have all been added to England's athletics squad in Glasgow. The track and field competition begins on Monday.

News.title: Love Island: All Stars winners Molly Smith and Tom Clare marry
News.content:
Sharing more from their marriage ceremony, Molly posted a photo to her Instagram story of her hand on top of Tom's.

The snap showed their wedding rings along with a bouquet of flowers, with the caption: "Husband and wife".

The couple first got together two years ago, when they met on season one of Love Island: All Stars.

All Stars is a spin-off of the hit dating show, which sees past contestants return for a second chance at finding love in the villa.

During the reality dating show, the pair beat Molly's ex-boyfriend Callum Jones and his partner at the time, Jessica Gale, who finished as runners-up.

Molly previously starred in series six in 2020 and left the show with Callum, who she was in a relationship with for three years before they split.

While Hyde United footballer Tom previously came third place on the second winter edition of Love Island in 2023 with former partner Samie Elishi.

Earlier this year, Tom and Molly took over hosting duties of the NearlyWeds podcast from radio presenters and reality stars Jamie Laing and Sophie Habboo.

Fellow Love Island stars were among those to congratulate the couple, including former winner Casey O'Gorman who described it as the "best day".

Sophie Piper, who came third on their All Star season, and TikTok star GK Barry also shared their support with the newly weds.

News.title: Wisconsin shooting victim identified as protesters take over press conference demanding answers about police ‘execution’
News.content:
The latest headlines from our reporters across the US sent straight to your inbox each weekday Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

Leaders in Madison, Wisconsin, have identified Corey Ruiz as the man killed yesterday in a fatal police shooting that has sparked waves of protests and anger in the community.

“It does not matter who you are or what your past is, you should not lose your life as a result of an encounter with law enforcement,” Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said at a press conference on Thursday, which was later taken over by protesters criticizing the city and its police department.

Before the protesters stormed the stage, Common Council President Sabrina Madison said she was seeking “justice for Corey” and called on community members to demand police reform and a swift investigation by the state officials probing the shooting.

“If the protocol is to go that quickly to shoot this gentleman in the head three times, and that is an option, I don’t know how that is an option,” she said. “My brain has not been able to put that together as an option. Because I didn’t see anything that warranted it.”

Critics argued video of the incident shared widely online showed that police “executed” Ruiz in the middle of a busy street in broad daylight.

open image in gallery A fatal police shooting in Madison, Wisconsin, has fueled anger as harrowing footage shows the moment an officer killed Corey Ruiz at point-blank range in the middle of the street ( Michael Doubek )

Here is everything we know about the case:

What happened?

Footage shows four cops on Wednesday working to subdue Ruiz, who police said was armed with a knife. The officers surround the man as he struggles to break free. While they have him by the arms and on the ground, one cop pulls out his gun and shoots the victim dead before reholstering his weapon and an officer puts the victim’s limp arms behind his body to handcuff him.

“This was an execution, and it never should have happened,” Fran Hong, a Democratic state representative running for governor, said of the shooting.

However, police stressed the incident remains under investigation and have begged the community not to jump to conclusions based on the video.

The violence unfolded Wednesday afternoon at the busy intersection of Madison’s South Baldwin and Williamson Streets around 1:34 p.m., an area surrounded by homes, bars, restaurants and shops.

A “physical struggle” ensued as Ruiz managed to briefly stand up while in the grip of the officers, before one of them yelled, “Taser, Taser Taser” and pointed the stun gun at him. The Taser failed to discharge, police said.

Officers wrestled Ruiz back down to the ground while one of them appeared to step on his leg to keep him on the floor. Less than a second later, one of the officers pulled out his gun, pointed it at the victim, and fired three shots.

open image in gallery Bystanders have shared disturbing footage of the shooting that took place Wednesday at the busy intersection of Madison’s South Baldwin and Williamson Streets around 1:34 p.m. ( Michael Doubek )

open image in gallery Madison Police Department shared a photograph of the knife they said Corey Ruiz injured an officer with. The officer then fired his weapon ( Madison Police Department )

Ruiz was slumped on the ground and did not appear to move again.

A bystander’s screams were then heard nearby, as a woman yelled, “I saw everything, we watched it all.”

With the victim limp and face down on the ground, blood pouring from his head, the officer who shot him reholstered his weapon and then his placed the man’s hands behind his back as if to restrain him. Another officer removed the knife, throwing it to the side.

Two other officers were seen standing around the scene, before police put on gloves and appeared to administer first aid.

Ruiz was taken to the hospital, where he was pronounced dead.

open image in gallery With the victim face down on the ground as blood poured from his head, the officer then placed the man’s hands behind his back. Another officer removed the knife ( Michael Doubek )

What police say happened

On Wednesday, Madison Police Chief John Patterson appealed for calm at a press conference in the aftermath, recounting the official narrative and pointing out that video of the shooting seen online only offered one side of the story.

Patterson also explained that Madison police officers do not wear body cameras, so there is no bodycam footage of the shooting.

In a statement, the department said officers were responding to a report alleging that someone had been seen attempting to break into parked cars in the city’s Marquette neighborhood.

open image in gallery Madison Police Chief Patterson appealed for calm at a press conference in the aftermath, recounting the official narrative and pointing out that video of the shooting seen online only offered one side of the story ( Michael Doubek )

The officers pursued Ruiz, who was on a bicycle. “The man either fell or was pulled off the bicycle, this is still being determined, and a struggle ensued with officers in the middle of the intersection,” the statement said.

“During the struggle, the man pulled out a fix-blade knife and injured an officer. Officers continued to try to get the man into custody and a less lethal device, a taser, was used but it was unsuccessful.”

“The officer injured by the knife is the one who fired his weapon,” the statement continued. “Officers at the scene provided life-saving measures.”

Chief Patterson added on Thursday that he was unsure why the Taser did not function during the encounter, one of many factors state officials will investigate as they scrutinize the shooting.

A second officer was injured in the incident but police have not said how, only that they do not believe his wound was caused by the knife.

The four officers involved have since been placed on administrative leave according to procedure and the Wisconsin Department of Justice Division of Criminal Investigation has commenced an independent probe.

What do we know about the victim?

open image in gallery Protesters march after a police officer shot and killed a man Wednesday in Madison, Wisconsin ( AP )

Police have said Ruiz was in his 30s.

His race has not been disclosed by officials, but Black advocacy groups in Madison said they believed he was Black, as they denounced the violence.

“Another Black man is dead on a Madison street, and our community watched him die before we even knew his name,” said Brandi Grayson, the head of the Madison-based Black community advocacy group Urban Triage. “That is the cruelty of state violence.”

Ruiz’s death comes after the fatal shooting of Tony Robinson, who was biracial, at the hands of a white police officer on the same street in 2015. Large protests followed, but the district attorney did not file charges against police, determining the officer was justified.

Who was the officer who shot the victim?

The name of the officer who shot the victim has not been released by Madison police.

In a statement, the department described him as “a veteran officer” and confirmed he has been placed on administrative leave, along with the other officers involved.

How has the community reacted?

open image in gallery Protesters gather at a candlelight vigil for the victim Wednesday evening ( AP )

Tensions remained high in Madison on Thursday as information trickled out about the shooting.

A group of activists temporarily seized the stage from the Madison mayor and police chief on Thursday, demanding that the “pigs” who shot Ruiz be put in jail, while denouncing claims from officials about pursuing justice as a “clown show.”

The takeover inspired some in the crowd to shout down the activists, and a man in the audience almost came to blows with a demonstrator who grabbed the microphone.

“I know this is tough,” Patterson said once he resume his remarks.

“Everyone in this room can feel the thinness of trust in this city right now,” he added.

open image in gallery Protesters temporarily took over a press conference on Thursday about the shooting, demanding that the officers involved in the arrest and killing of Corey Ruiz be put in prison ( Reuters )

The chief said that police operate based on a “sacred public trust,” which frays the more that force is used. He stressed that the department immediately sought an independent investigation and will fully cooperate with the Wisconsin Department of Justice.

“We will not hide from any aspect of this investigation,” he said.

The demonstration on Thursday came after hundreds of people took to the streets Wednesday evening to protest the killing and to hold a candlelight vigil in memory of Ruiz.

Some stayed overnight. “I don’t plan to leave anytime soon because it’s important to hold this space,” said Ben Weger, a pastor of Stoughton United Methodist Church about 20 miles away.

Sabrina Thompson, of Madison, was crying at the memorial site. “It’s really unbearable,” she said through tears. “You can’t describe it.”

open image in gallery Hundreds of people took to the streets Wednesday evening to protest the killing and to hold a candlelight vigil in memory of Corey Ruiz ( AP )

Hong, a Democratic primary candidates in Wisconsin’s governor’s race, also attended the vigil and spoke to demonstrators through a megaphone.

“This state sanctioned violence was an execution,” she told a crowd.

Incumbent Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers called for “transparency and accountability” on X, expressing his sympathies for the victim’s family and saying that any protest should be conducted “peacefully and respectfully.”

“Each incident reopens deep wounds, raises difficult questions, and reminds us of the urgent work that remains to build trust, transparency, and accountability in our systems,” said Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, who is also running for governor.

“There are questions that must be answered,” added Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway. “It’s understandable that people want answers now.”

The Associated Press contributed to this report

News.title: Nearly half of Americans think Trump’s DC projects are just to feed his ego
News.content:

More than 60 percent of Americans are critical of President Donald Trump’s various Washington, D.C. construction undertakings, and almost half think the primary goal behind his projects is to feed his ego, according to a new poll.

Amid an affordability crisis and his war with Iran, Trump has been focused on a number of projects transforming the look of the nation's capital ranging from his now-unraveled attempt to put his name on the Kennedy Center and his destruction of the White House East Wing for his new ballroom to his plans for a massive Triumph Arch and his ill-fated renovations the Reflecting Pool on the National Mall.

The Washington Post and Ipsos conducted a poll asking 2,600 American adults how they feel about Trump's projects. They were given four response options: enthusiastic, satisfied, dissatisfied, and upset.

The poll found that 38 percent of respondents considered themselves upset by Trump's changes to the nation's capital, while another 27 percent said they were dissatisfied. Together, more than half of the respondents were critical of the president's efforts to reshape the District.

Only 12 percent of respondents said they were enthusiastic about Trump's efforts, and another 19 percent said they were satisfied.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump discusses his ballroom at the White House grounds. A new poll from The Washington Post and Ipsos found that more than 60 percent of Americans are unhappy with Trump’s various projects around Washington, D.C. ( AFP/Getty )

The poll also found that responses changed based on the specific project. For example, more Americans were opposed to Trump's ballroom — which will permanently change the look of the White House — than they were to his proposed arch or his changes to the Reflecting Pool.

Critical responses broke down along predictable party lines, with Democrats largely answering that they were "upset" by Trump's changes and Republicans broadly supporting his efforts.

Among those who identify as independent, 73 percent said they viewed the projects negatively, the Washington Post reports.

While just over a quarter of respondents believe Trump's intention with his projects is to "make Washington more beautiful," 51 percent said they think he has a "different goal," and another 22 percent said they have no idea what is motivating the president.

Of those who believe he has a "different goal," 42 percent said they believe his aim is to feed his own ego. Another 22 percent said they believe Trump is trying to leave his mark on the nation's capital.

"Trump wants to build monuments to himself just like Napoleon did in France," one Minnesota Republican, age 70, said in his response.

According to a recent New York Times analysis, Trump's projects have cost taxpayers at least $1 billion.

open image in gallery People walk past the drained Reflecting Pool on the National Mall on July 22, 2026 in Washington, DC. ( Getty )

That includes his ballroom — which Trump insists is completely privately funded, despite evidence suggesting otherwise — as well as planned "upgrades" to the Kennedy Center, renovations to the White House interior, and an estimated $14.8 million for changes made to the Reflecting Pool.

Congress has also approved $40 million to build a statue garden Trump dreamt up called the National Garden of American Heroes, which is planned to include at least 250 statues of prominent Americans including figures like Justice Clarence Thomas and Charlie Kirk.

The ongoing work across Washington D.C. has also caused disruptions to the normal flow of foot traffic through the city. Lafayette Park, across from the White House, has been blocked off for construction.

Detours are in place all over the National Mall, including at the Reflecting Pool and the Washington Monument, leaving visitors frustrated.

“It’s not very welcoming,” Liz, a tourist from Iowa, told WTOP. “It makes me feel like we are in a construction zone, or somebody’s done something very bad.”

Taco Bell leadership’s scramble to contain this summer’s “explosive diarrhea” cyclosporiasis outbreak linked to lettuce sold at their restaurants and to save the Mexican food brand has been described in a new report.

Last week, Taco Bell announced that it was immediately removing lettuce “potentially impacted” by a parasite that has caused thousands of Americans to fall ill.

The July 16 announcement came as public health officials said they were investigating the outbreak linked to shredded iceberg lettuce served at Taco Bell locations in Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, and West Virginia. Taylor Farms has also been under the microscope as Taco Bell’s lettuce supplier.

Days earlier, health officials notified Taco Bell that lettuce from Taylor Farms was a suspected source of the outbreak, leading company executives to work with franchisees to hastily pull potentially affected produce from restaurants, the Wall Street Journal reported.

Many Taco Bell executives were at an off-site company event on July 14 when they got the news about Taylor Farms lettuce, according to the Journal, which cited current and former Taco Bell officials and people familiar with its operations in the reporting.

open image in gallery Taco Bell executives scrambled to stop this summer’s cyclosporiasis outbreak linked to lettuce sold at their restaurants and save the Mexican food brand, according to a new report ( Getty Images for Taco Bell )

In the days that followed, the chain’s leadership worked out of its headquarters in Irvine, California, and hosted virtual meetings to divert supply trucks and get workers on the ground to throw out cases of lettuce.

The Independent has reached out to Taco Bell for comment.

There have been more than 4,100 confirmed cases and more than 7,400 unconfirmed cases of cyclosporiasis since the start of May, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

The Food and Drug Administration reported on July 16 that more than 1,600 people infected with cyclosporiasis had eaten at Taco Bell.

open image in gallery Thousands of Americans have fallen ill from a cyclosporiasis outbreak linked to lettuce sold at Taco Bell in five states ( Getty Images for Taco Bell )

Taylor Farms announced Friday that it was removing all iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico.

Public health officials then reported Saturday that a sample of lettuce supplied by Taylor Farms tested positive for cyclosporiasis. But officials later said it was a “false positive.”

Foot traffic at Taco Bell restaurants was down 30.9 percent on July 17 compared with this year’s average for Fridays, according to Placer.ai data shared with The Independent.

open image in gallery After Taco Bell was informed that lettuce from its supplier Taylor Farms was a suspected source of the outbreak, company executives reportedly worked with franchisees to hastily pull it from restaurants ( Getty Images for Taco Bell )

Taco Bell’s strategy has been to zero in on the Crunchwrap Supreme and Beefy 5-Layer Burrito loyalists.

In an Instagram post last week, the chain announced that customers could “go ahead and enjoy your Taco Bell today” after it removed all affected Taylor Farms lettuce.

“You always got us. We always got you. See you in the drive-thru,” the post continued.

In a follow-up post Wednesday, Taco Bell shared a collage of fan comments, including ones that read, “Taco Bell forever” and “I’m never leaving you.”

Roughly half of online discussions about Taco Bell this week are negative, and the rest are neutral or positive, the Journal reported, citing data from analytics company PeakMetrics.

The FDA has warned against eating lettuce from Taco Bell or any other restaurant that has been recalled by Taylor Farms.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has declared the era of Whitehall resisting devolution "over for good” ahead of his first meeting at the new No 10 North office in Manchester.

Mr Burnham is scheduled to work from the northern outpost, located in Heron House near Albert Square – a building also housing GCHQ’s Manchester and North West hub – once a week during his premiership.

His initial engagement will be to chair a meeting of the National Economic Council, a Cabinet committee established in 2008 to address economic challenges.

The government confirmed that attendees for these meetings would vary based on the agenda, potentially including prominent business leaders and trade union representatives.

Articulating his vision for the new hub, the Prime Minister stated: "For 40 years, power and resources have been sucked into the centre, and too many communities have felt forgotten, without the attention and investment they deserve."

He added: "No 10 North will change that by putting more power into every postcode across the entire country. It will be the situation room for making Britain better – the place we use to get power out of Westminster, into the hands of people at a local level, so that they can turn things around. The days of Whitehall resisting devolution are over, for good."

Burnham is set to work from the northern outpost once a week ( PA )

Ahead of his inaugural meeting, Mr Burnham is scheduled to meet with leaders from business representative organisations, including the Federation of Small Business and the Confederation of British Industry.

The Prime Minister has faced scrutiny regarding whether his focus on the North might divert attention from other regions, such as the East of England.

Addressing these concerns in Harlow, Essex, he clarified: "The whole purpose of No 10 North is to put more power into every postcode in the land, including the postcodes of Harlow.

How do we get power out of Whitehall and Westminster, into the hands of people at a local level, so that they can make a difference and turn things around?" He further told ITV Anglia: "I see the same challenges up and down the country. There’s a lot of communities that feel a little bit forgotten, that don’t get the attention and the investment they deserve. And those communities can be found as much in the East of England and the South West as they can be found in the North of England."

While this new northern base signifies a significant shift in governmental operations, No 10 Downing Street in central London, a short walk from the Houses of Parliament, will continue to operate as usual.

Giant metal roosters are popping up on lawns in and around a coastal Maine community and as far away as New Zealand in support of a 6-year-old autistic girl and her love of the colorful creations.

David and Sara LeBlanc had a rotating display of the roughly 6-foot-tall (1.8-meter-tall) ornaments decorating their Ogunquit lawn until the town deemed them to be impermissible advertising for their attached restaurant, The Omelette Factory.

The couple initially resisted the town's removal order, insisting the roosters were meant to comfort their daughter Pyper, not advertise their business.

“Roosters don’t lay eggs,” David LeBlanc told The Associated Press on Wednesday.

But they eventually came to an agreement with the town allowing them to keep two of the roosters in front of their home.

As for what to do with the others? That's where friends, neighbors and complete strangers came in.

It started with a beloved stuffed rooster

The LeBlancs took in Pyper as a foster child and later adopted her. She arrived with a stuffed rooster and roosters became her favorite animal, her parents said. When her father took her to a Tractor Supply Store to play with baby chicks last year, she noticed a large rooster sculpture for sale and asked her dad what it was saying.

“I think he wants to come home,” David LeBlanc said he told her.

Eventually, their collection grew to more than two dozen roosters, which they set up in batches for seasonal and holiday displays. Pyper took to hiding behind one each morning while waiting for the school bus, which her parents said helps her regulate her emotions and navigate transitions.

But the couple ruffled feathers when they added a rooster to their restaurant’s logo, which is featured on its shirts and other merchandise. Although the LeBlancs said they view the rooster as a “family crest,” the town saw their lawn statues as advertising.

A code enforcement officer, Tyler McOsker, issued the LeBlancs $450 in fines and ordered them in April to "remove all unpermitted signage, including but not limited to rooster statues."

McOsker didn't respond to an email requesting comment. But he told the Zoning Board of Appeals in June that he had no idea the roosters were connected to Pyper’s autism diagnosis until the couple appealed the fines. He also pointed to a May 2025 article in a local weekly newspaper that described the roosters as a “fun and unconventional way to announce that The Omelette Factory is officially open for business.”

“That, to me, is the definition of a sign. You’re announcing you’re opening,” McOsker told the board.

David LeBlanc said the reporter misinterpreted a customer’s joke about the roosters serving as an “Open” sign.

“We never said that,” he said.

The town offers a compromise

The zoning board discussed the issue last month. At one point, board member Jay Smith voiced frustration at the lack of medical proof that the roosters were necessary.

“I’m inclined to think there may be some merit to a comfort animal on the front lawn … but the point is, how many does it take?” he said, adding that the seaside town “enjoys a certain ambiance undisturbed by, I’ll just say, a proliferation of weird art on the front lawn.”

Autism spectrum disorder is a complex developmental condition that affects different people in different ways, and comfort objects are frequently incorporated into therapy for autistic children to help manage transitions, support emotional regulation and provide a sense of familiarity, Beverley Cush Evans, a professor of special education at Lesley University, told the AP.

“It’s part of who they are and what they need," she said.

Eventually, the board decided it lacked the authority to rescind the fines but tried to accommodate the family by granting a disability variance that essentially deemed two roosters necessary for Pyper’s access to the home.

“I want to emphasize we’re talking about two roosters. If they have babies or multiply in the night — no,” another board member said.

The variance requires the roosters to be part of a railing, however, and for now, they are just bolted to the steps. The couple has been fined another $500 for noncompliance.

A show of support

David LeBlanc said he is moving on from the dispute and is focusing on the good that has come from it. The family has given roosters to others to “foster” and show their support for autism acceptance, starting with a man named Sam who lives up the road. Though Pyper was sad to see them go, she understands the adage about making lemonade, LeBlanc said.

“She understands that the roosters being taken away were the lemons, and Sam and his friends, fostering them, are the lemonade,” he said. “It’s a beautiful thing.”

Thanks to news coverage and a Roosters of Ogunquit Facebook page, the story has spread far and wide. One supporter wrote in from New Zealand sharing pictures of his children with a rooster statue in their yard.

Hetal Patel, who owns a motel in nearby Wells and has a relative with autism, wanted to buy a rooster after hearing about Pyper. They were sold out in the Ogunquit area, though, so she and her son went to New Hampshire last week to get one.

“We found the last one,” she said. “We couldn’t wait to put it out. People were so supportive, they were honking. It was so nice to see all the love for Pyper.”
