World.title: Nevada GOP nominee Carrie Buck says she’s ‘coming to retire Dina Titus’
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

After flipping a Democrat-leaning state senate district in 2020, Carrie Buck is setting her sights on a bigger target this election cycle: Nevada's first congressional district, an urban Las-Vegas based district stretching east to the Arizona border.

But it will not be easy to oust Congresswoman Dina Titus, an 8-term veteran, with strong ties to organized labor, the tourism industry, and the business community.

MINIVAN MOM PUTS DEM INCUMBENT ON NOTICE IN TOP GOP TARGET DISTRICT: 'SHE HAS DONE NOTHING FOR US'

Recently, Buck sat down with Fox News Digital at Freedom Fest in Las Vegas, to discuss her swing district appeal, her background as a teacher and principal, and why she believes her take on kitchen table economics will enable her to pull off an upset come election day.

First and foremost, Buck is no stranger to challenging Democrats on their own turf:

"Well, in 2020, I flipped a blue district to Republican, and it represents 20% of this [NV-1] district. So, I know I can flip the entire district. People are just tired of my Democrat opponent, and they're ready for change."

Buck cites her three decades of experience in the Nevada education system as critical to understanding the electorate:

"Well, the past 30 years, I've served in the school system here in Nevada. I was a teacher…I taught adult ESL, I taught children for years. Then I became a principal of one of the lowest performing schools in the state and moved it to a national Title I school. I won the Milken Award in that time.

"And so I've been breathing life into children and families for years. When I knock on doors, when I'm out in the community, people are like, ‘Dr. Buck, you were my principal.’ And so, I think a lot of people know that I'm going to really deliver for Nevadans in DC."

Housing affordability is a signature issue for Buck.

She pledges to "ensure that Nevadans have access to lower-cost housing" while also "driving down interest rates so that people can buy whatever house that they want to."

TOP GOP TARGET DINA TITUS FENDS OFF HOUSE PRIMARY CHALLENGERS

Buck also argues that the immigration crisis during the Biden administration was a key driver on the housing affordability issue:

"I think also what impacted housing is the immigration policies of the Biden years, where they allowed all these people into our country and that drove up [the cost of] all of our low-income housing.

"It depleted it. And so now that we're seeing people end up getting deported and going back to their original country, I know that it's definitely driving down prices here."

Buck promises that taking a hard line on the national debt will be a top priority:

"Spending is definitely out of control when we look at the waste of taxpayer dollars, waste, fraud and abuse. When we've seen some of these cases from across the nation, it really is a red alert. We need to make sure that we root that out.

"I just actually saw the vice president is heading up this task force, and they're finding lots of fraud…We can't just release taxpayer dollars. So reining in the waste, fraud and abuse and making sure that [government spending] goes to the seniors and the children and the veterans who need it."

Buck is a strong supporter of pathways to citizenship for immigrants, but also maintains a hard line on issues of border security and illegal immigration:

"There is a pathway to citizenship, and I think we need to get people signed up. I've been part of a movement to ensure that people have access to get citizenship. And that's the way, the legal way.

"But coming here illegally, you are breaking laws. Those people need to be deported. We've seen so many victims of crimes by illegal immigrants, and that has to stop. We need to make sure that we have safe communities. I'm a wife of a law enforcement officer and know how important our safe communities and our men and women are working out there in law enforcement."

Water issues remain an enormous concern west of the Mississippi, and particularly in Nevada. Buck argues that California could and should play a large role in ensuring Nevadans access to water:

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"For too long, Nevada has been the conservationist…Our citizens conserve so much water…All it would take is California to build a basin and hold their rainwater and not release it into the Pacific.

"But they're very selfish neighbors…We need to make sure that our federal government can maybe step in and build these reservoirs to hold water."

World.title: Read the list: 44 lawmakers swept into Jack Smith text sweep as his legal reckoning grows
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Former special counsel Jack Smith’s team obtained and reviewed the contents of text messages exchanged between Trump White House officials and 44 current and former members of Congress, according to Justice Department records released by two Republican-led Senate committees.

The messages were contained in White House records subpoenaed from the National Archives covering Oct. 1, 2020, through Jan. 20, 2021. The Justice Department said Smith’s investigative team "apparently bypassed" a filter team established to screen potentially privileged material before investigators accessed it.

House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, on Wednesday issued a criminal referral for Smith, arguing that he misled Congress when he stated that he did not obtain or review lawmakers' text messages while carrying out his probes into President Donald Trump. The referral functions as an invitation for the Justice Department to launch an investigation into Smith's conduct.

JACK SMITH THRUST BACK INTO SPOTLIGHT AT BLANCHE HEARING OVER EXPOSED SENATORS’ MESSAGES

Read the list of 44 lawmakers:

Among the senators targeted in the probe were: Sens. Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa; Ron Johnson, R-Wis.; John Cornyn, R-Texas; Lindsey Graham, R-S.C.; Josh Hawley, R-Mo.; Mike Lee, R-Utah; Cory Booker, D-N.J.; Cindy Hyde-Smith, R-Miss.; Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska; David Perdue, R-Ga.; Lamar Alexander, R-Tenn.; Martha McSally, R-Ariz.; Rand Paul, R-Ky.; Rick Scott, R-Fla.; Rob Portman, R-Ohio; Roy Blunt, R-Mo.; Susan Collins, R-Maine; Tim Scott, R-S.C.; Tom Cotton, R-Ark.; and Cory Gardner, R-Colo.

On the House side, the investigation targeted: Reps. Kevin McCarthy, R-Calif.; Steve Scalise, R-La.; Jim Jordan, R-Ohio; Devin Nunes, R-Calif.; Adam Smith, D-Wash.; Andy Biggs, R-Ariz.; Mark Walker, R-N.C.; Bryan Steil, R-Wis.; Dan Newhouse, R-Wash.; Doug Collins, R-Ga.; Dusty Johnson, R-S.D.; Elise Stefanik, R-N.Y.; John Katko, R-N.Y.; Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J.; Karen Bass, D-Calif.; Ken Buck, R-Colo.; Lee Zeldin, R-N.Y.; Mario Diaz-Balart, R-Fla.; Mo Brooks, R-Ala.; Morgan Griffith, R-Va.; Rodney Davis, R-Ill.; Russ Fulcher, R-Idaho; Scott Perry, R-Pa.; and Thomas Massie, R-Ky.

Fox News Digital reached out to every current lawmaker named on the list.

Grassley and Johnson, through their senior committee positions, were responsible for the release of the new documents.

Several lawmakers on the list had publicly documented roles in efforts surrounding the 2020 election, including those who have since condemned Smith’s review of their communications.

Sen. Chuck Grassley

As president pro tempore of the Senate, Grassley played a procedural role on Jan. 6, 2021, as Congress moved to certify the results of the 2020 presidential election. The senator, for instance, called the Senate into session before senators moved to the House's chamber to participate in a joint session where the results of each state would be certified.

Prior to Jan. 6, Grassley suggested that he may preside over the Senate’s debate surrounding disputes over the 2020 election if Vice President Mike Pence didn’t show up.

"Jack Smith’s criminal investigation of President Trump was a runaway train that had no brakes," Grassley said of his messages being collected. "Based on the information that’s been produced to me and Senator Johnson, Biden DOJ and FBI investigators apparently ignored their own routine investigative protocols to obtain and review work-related messages from me and dozens of my Republican and Democrat colleagues who were outside the scope of the government’s investigation."

Sen. Ron Johnson

In the lead-up to Jan. 6, Johnson joined a group of Republican senators calling for an emergency 10-day audit of disputed election results and saying they would vote against certifying electors from contested states unless such a review occurred.

Documents released by the House Jan. 6 committee in early 2023 reported that Johnson was communicating with former chairman of the Wisconsin Republican Party about a plan to have the state’s GOP-controlled legislature choose its presidential electors. The senator responded that he had no recollection of the conversation and accused the committee of trying to smear him.

Republicans were intensely critical of the House Jan. 6 committee, arguing that it lacked a meaningful voice for the opposition seeing as then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., selected every member while rejecting the nominations put forward by McCarthy. They also argued that the committee focused too little on security and intelligence failures ahead of the breach of the Capitol.

"This is yet another grotesque example of the Biden administration’s weaponization of the Justice Department," Johnson said of the seized text messages. "Jack Smith’s team acted with impunity as they disregarded their own protocols to obtain and access White House text messages, including messages to and from 44 Members of Congress. This is precisely why Chairman Grassley and I have worked to uncover the truth, bring transparency to the American people, and hold accountable those who weaponized federal law enforcement."

BIDEN SPECIAL COUNSEL’S 'RUNAWAY TRAIN’ SCOOPED UP SENSITIVE LAWMAKER INFO: 'ABUSE OF POWER'

Sen. Lindsey Graham

In the days after the 2020 election, Graham urged Trump not to concede. He later donated to Trump’s legal defense fund and, as chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee, opened inquiries into election procedures in several battleground states and contacted state election officials.

The late South Carolina senator grew frustrated with Trump and his followers as their objections continued to fail in court and fully broke with the movement following the riot on Jan. 6.

"Count me out," he said at the time. "Enough is enough."

Sen. Josh Hawley

Hawley is notable in that he, on Dec. 30, 2020, became the first senator to announce his intention to formally object to Electoral College votes during the certification process. His decision was consequential as federal law required objections from both a representative and a senator to force a debate on the election.

WATCH: HAWLEY FUMES AFTER 4 GOP SENATORS HELP SINK TRUMP-BACKED VOTER ID LAW

Trump attempted to call Hawley six times ahead of the Jan. 6 breach, according to White House call logs obtained by the House Jan. 6 select committee, showing that there was a line of communication between the two.

Though some senators abandoned their objections to the 2020 election after the Capitol was breached, Hawley maintained his objections and voted against certifying the results from Arizona and Pennsylvania.

Hawley called the documents released by Grassley and Johnson "more evidence of Biden corruption" adding that, "Jack Smith illegally scooped up the text messages of Senators — including mine."

Sen. Mike Lee

Text messages turned over by former White House chief of staff Mark Meadows to the House Jan. 6 committee show that Lee discussed possible legal and constitutional avenues for challenging the 2020 election results.

Lee initially told Meadows that he supported exhausting every available legal and constitutional remedy to address concerns about the election. By Jan. 3, 2021, however, he warned that the effort "could all backfire badly," according to text messages Meadows turned over to the House Jan. 6 committee.

The senator ultimately voted against sustaining objections to Arizona’s and Pennsylvania's election results.

Mike Lee slammed Smith's collection of text messages this month as "un-American" and argued that it came "uncomfortably close to spying on a coequal, coordinate branch."

Rep. Steve Scalise

Scalise, as House Republican whip, was responsible for convincing representatives to vote in line with the party’s interests, providing a straightforward reason as to why White House staff may have been in contact with him.

Further, a publicly released deposition shows that a Scalise aide communicated with Pence’s legislative-affairs director regarding a Jan. 3 call organized by Jordan involving Trump, Meadows and members pressing certification objections.

SCALISE URGES PRITZKER TO 'LOOK AT THE MAN IN THE MIRROR' AFTER HE BLAMES TRUMP FOR POLITICAL VIOLENCE

The Louisiana congressman called congressional action the "only remaining recourse" for addressing what he described as improper changes to election laws in several states.

While he condemned rioting, Scalise, like Hawley, ultimately voted to reject Biden’s electoral votes from both Arizona and Pennsylvania.

Rep. Jim Jordan

Jordan participated in efforts to challenge the 2020 election results, including discussions about delaying congressional certification and objecting to electoral votes.

On Jan. 2, the Ohio congressman led a conference call with Trump and other members of Congress to discuss strategies for delaying the Jan. 6 joint session, according to the House Jan. 6 committee’s final report.

Jordan also reportedly had a 10-minute-long call with Trump on the morning of Jan. 6, according to publicly released phone records. After the breach of the Capitol, Jordan condemned the violence but voted to sustain objections to the electoral results in Arizona and Pennsylvania.

"You can’t do that. As Senator Hawley just said, this is a separation of powers issue," Jordan told Fox News host Sean Hannity earlier this month. "There’s a speech or debate clause. It was supposed to be filtered and screened. It wasn’t. It was just given from the National Archives to Jack Smith’s team."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Smith’s attorneys called the criminal referral "meritless" Thursday in a letter previously obtained by Fox News Digital.

"The House Judiciary Committee’s referral to the Department of Justice of our client Jack Smith is based on a spurious claim that Mr. Smith provided false testimony during his eight-hour deposition on December 17, 2025. The referral is made not because Mr. Smith made a false statement—the letter concedes he did not—but because he did not proactively disclose information that was not responsive to a question asked," the lawyer wrote.

"During his testimony, Mr. Smith provided truthful, responsive answers and candidly discussed his work as Special Counsel. This referral reflects a chilling eagerness to weaponize the justice system by attacking a career, nonpartisan public servant who faithfully and fearlessly performed his duties by following the facts and the law."

Fox News Digital's Elizabeth Elkind contributed to this report.

The Mets came into this season overhauling a roster that choked away the best record in the league last summer, which turned in a league—high $329 million payroll.

I don't want to mention teams, because I know all the owners are old friends of mine, I get myself in trouble, but they're always rebuilding. This guy never rebuilds. He just stays at the top. He's amazing," Trump said. "And then he loses the best player. He loses a great first baseman (Freddie Freeman), I would say great first baseman, and they keep going along and they get things for the first baseman. And he was really good, Dodgers got him. But I watched the Braves for years and they've done such a great job."

YANKEES PLAYER'S PITCH CLOCK ANTICS PROMPT WILD HOT-MIC MOMENT, BACKLASH: 'YOU'RE PICKING ON ME'

World.title: House votes to end Iran war, but Senate Republicans vote to let Trump continue waging it
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The House on Thursday approved a Democratic-led proposal to end the Iran war, directing President Donald Trump to remove armed forces from hostilities.

Subscribe to read this story ad-free Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.

The resolution is nonbinding, however. The House voted 214-208, with four Republicans joining all Democrats to cast decisive votes for the measure: Reps. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, Tom Barrett of Michigan, Warren Davidson of Ohio and Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania.

Later in the day, the Senate voted 47-49 to reject a “joint resolution” to end the Iran war that would have the force of law, unlike the House version, but would be subject to a presidential veto. One Republican, Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, joined every Democrat except Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania in voting to advance the measure.

Four Republicans didn’t vote: Sens. Katie Britt of Alabama, Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky.

The votes in both chambers were pushed by Democrats eager to get Republicans on the record about an unpopular war ahead of the midterm elections and to reassert Congress’ role as the branch of government responsible for declaring war.

Multiple Senate Republicans have said the war should not go on for more than 60 days without congressional approval in order to comply with federal law. They include Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Curtis of Utah. But both men on Thursday voted against the measure to end the Iran war.

Asked why, Tillis said the 60-day clock started this month, not back in February when Trump and Israel first launched strikes on Iran. “July 10, to my knowledge, is the first time I heard anyone in the administration refer to it as a war,” Tillis said, adding that it would be important for Congress to authorize the war once 60 days are up.

“The clock is ticking. We got to get serious about that,” Tillis said. “I think politically, we can help the president with an unpopular war right now if we provide some legitimacy to it.”

House Republicans have also indicated their willingness to give Trump breathing room on the 60-day deadline. Still, four GOP members voted with Democrats to pass the nonbinding resolution rejecting the war through the Republican-controlled House, reflecting the unpopularity of the conflict.

“The vote today shows that Congress is starting to join the 70% of American people who are against this war, which is clearly a war of choice, and Congress has to step up to our constitutional responsibility and demand it,” Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, told NBC News.

Meeks added that Democrats have more tools to force Trump to end the war, such as the “power of the purse” ahead of a Sept. 30 deadline for Congress to fund the government, including the military. He added that he’s introducing a resolution “to sue the administration,” accusing it of defying Congress on the Iran war, which he plans to force a vote on when the House returns from its summer recess in five weeks.

Public opposition to the Iran war has put Republicans in competitive areas in a difficult position.

Rep. Rob Bresnahan, R-Pa., who represents a swing district and is a top target of Democrats in November, voted against the resolution. He said he recognizes the war’s economic impact but emphasized that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon.

“I think people see the prices of fuel and they immediately correlate one and the other. But I think we’re all in agreement that this needs to come to a resolution expeditiously. Under no circumstances should Iran have nuclear weapons,” Bresnahan said Thursday. “Iran is not a friend to the United States, but there needs to be a definitive solution there quickly.”

He said he’d like the Strait of Hormuz to open as soon as possible so the prices of gas and fertilizer can come back down. “The sooner, the better,” he said. “But at the same time, you can’t allow a foreign adversary to run rogue and hold hostage American supply chains because ... they are just acting radically.”

Seven Republicans and two Democrats didn’t cast a vote on the House’s Iran measure Thursday.

It is not the first time that Congress has formally disapproved of the war. The House approved a similar war powers resolution in early June on a 215-208 vote, with the same Republicans supporting it who voted for the measure Thursday. The Senate later passed the same nonbinding measure.

Democrats have continued to force these votes to get Republicans on the record about a war that a majority of Americans oppose. The failed Senate measure was led by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md.

“Not only are the vast majority of Americans opposed to this war; it’s the most unpopular war that we’ve had in a very, very, very long time,” Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., said, noting that even self-identified “MAGA” voters are skeptical of the war.

“These are folks who deeply support Donald Trump, but they actually liked when he was talking about ending forever wars instead of getting into them,” she said.

World.title: Member of Vance’s Secret Service detail removed amid probe into alleged compromise of security info
World.content:
A member of JD Vance’s protective detail has been removed pending an investigation into allegations of compromising the vice president’s security, a Secret Service spokesman said Thursday.

Subscribe to read this story ad-free Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.

The development was first reported by CNN, citing sources familiar with the matter who told the outlet that the agent was suspected of leaking information used in an MS NOW report detailing alleged Secret Service complaints about Vance’s travel habits.

Confirming the agent’s removal, Secret Service spokesman Anthony Guglielmi said in a statement shared with NBC News: “A member of the Vice Presidential Protective Division is the subject of an administrative investigation, and potential criminal inquiry, involving allegations of compromising operational and information security.”

“While we will not comment on the specifics of this matter, one principle is unequivocal: any conduct that potentially threatens the safety of a protectee will not be tolerated,” Guglielmi added.

Vance’s office declined to comment to NBC News about the agent’s removal.

Secret Service agents complained among themselves about Vance’s plan for them to join him on Marine Two as he flew with his son to the child’s golf lesson at nearby Joint Base Andrews, a flight canceled at the last-minute because of severe weather, MS NOW reported, citing two people with knowledge of the flight plans, two administration officials with knowledge of his schedule, and a person familiar with the agents’ frustration.

Secret Service agents have also shared concerns internally about being asked to embark on trips and assignments that some believed were inappropriate for government resources, several of those sources told the news outlet.

NBC News has not independently confirmed the details in the MS NOW or CNN reports on the alleged Secret Service members’ complaints or the details surrounding the agent’s removal from Vance’s security detail.

An administration official said Vance’s travel duties can often shift unexpectedly because of important meetings and events, which override previous plans, causing strain on the Secret Service. The official also noted that unlike recent vice presidents, Vance has young children, and he tries to spend as much time with them as he can, presenting his Secret Service with a new aspect of their protective mandate.

Separately, the official said the Marine Two helicopter trip from the vice president’s official residence to Joint Base Andrews is the most common route for the vice president’s helicopter and requires a smaller pull on local law enforcement and other resources than a motorcade.

The Trump administration has taken a hard-line position against leaks to journalists, most recently issuing subpoenas to New York Times reporters who covered security concerns related to the new Air Force One.

On Thursday, a judge will hold a hearing on the Times’ challenge to the subpoenas. The Justice Department has said that people “leaking classified information” are the target of the investigation, not the reporters.

Last month, the Trump administration tried to compel four journalists to testify before a federal grand jury, but reversed after The Wall Street Journal and The Washington Post pushed back, NBC News reported.

World.title: Departures of Senate-confirmed Trump officials are surpassing his first term, new report finds
World.content:
The Trump administration is facing a spike in departures of powerful Cabinet department officials compared with his first term, according to the nonprofit Partnership for Public Service.

Subscribe to read this story ad-free Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.

More than two dozen Senate-confirmed officials have left their Cabinet department positions so far during President Donald Trump’s second term, the nonprofit’s analysis found.

The departure of 27 officials in high-ranking positions far outpaces the total numbers in recent prior administrations, including Trump’s first term, when 11 Senate-confirmed officials in Cabinet department positions left their roles over the course of the four years.

The data analyzed by the Partnership for Public Service did not include departures of Senate-confirmed Cabinet department officials who were nominated under different administrations, nor did it include U.S. attorneys, U.S. marshals or ambassadors. Using the same parameters, only one Senate-confirmed Cabinet department official left during the Biden administration, as well as seven during President Barack Obama’s second term and five during President George W. Bush’s second term, according to the nonprofit.

Senate-confirmed officials depart their roles for a variety of reasons, including moving to other government positions and jobs that also require Senate confirmation.

Billy Long, for example, had served as IRS commissioner, a Cabinet department position that required Senate confirmation. Trump removed him last year, and he was confirmed this year as ambassador to Iceland.

Billy Long at his nomination hearing to become IRS commissioner in 2025. Andrew Harnik / Getty Images

Others have been fired or pushed out.

Navy Secretary John Phelan was fired in April amid internal Defense Department tensions between top officials. Other Senate-confirmed officials in the Defense Department have been fired, too, including Air Force Lt. Gen. Jeffrey Kruse, who was ousted as head of the Defense Intelligence Agency; Navy Vice Adm. Shoshana Chatfield, the U.S. military representative to NATO’s military committee; and Joint Chiefs Chairman CQ Brown Jr. Those three officials were not included in the Partnership for Public Service’s count because they were nominated before Trump’s second term began.

Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Director Susan Monarez was fired by the Trump administration after she refused to resign under pressure after she alleged that Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. wanted her removal for political reasons.

Some officials have resigned, sometimes due to unclear circumstances.

Gail Slater, who served as the head of the Justice Department’s antitrust unit, stepped down in February, writing in her announcement that “it is with great sadness and abiding hope” that she left.

Leslie Beyer, who served in a top role in the Interior Department, left just a few months after she was confirmed by the Senate.

Marty Makary resigned as Food and Drug Administration commissioner in May. NBC News previously reported that a source close to HHS leadership said Makary’s resignation was triggered by the FDA authorizing fruit-flavored vapes for adults, which he opposed.

Then-F.D.A. Commissioner Marty Makary in the Oval Office in 2025. Anna Moneymaker / Getty Images file

“President Trump has the most talented Cabinet in American history who work every day to implement his common sense, America First agenda,” Olivia Wales, a White House spokeswoman, said in response to a request for comment on the number of departures. “In just over one year, the President and his Cabinet have made our country greater than ever before with the most secure border in history, the largest middle-class tax cut ever, and the lowest murder rate since 1900.”

On the top Cabinet leadership level, Trump has seen the departures of Tulsi Gabbard as director of national intelligence, Pam Bondi as attorney general, Kristi Noem as homeland security secretary and Lori Chavez-DeRemer as labor secretary. Gabbard resigned after her husband was diagnosed with cancer, while Bondi and Noem were fired. Chavez-DeRemer resigned as the Labor Department’s inspector general investigated potential misconduct.

At the same time, Trump has seen turnover at a relatively similar rate as prior administrations when considering top officials in the president’s orbit who are not necessarily Senate-confirmed.

An analysis by Brookings, a think tank, found that in the first year of Trump’s second term, 31% of influential decision-makers in the administration experienced turnover, compared with 8% during President Joe Biden’s first year and 9% during Obama’s first year. However, 7% of Trump’s decision-makers saw turnover so far during his second year, compared with 35% during Biden’s second year and 15% during Obama’s second year.

Trump’s first term, too, saw a slew of departures among top White House officials, including positions that required Senate confirmation. The departures included Cabinet officials such as James Mattis, who was defense secretary; Jeff Sessions, who was attorney general; Rex Tillerson, who was secretary of state; and Tom Price, who was health and human services secretary.

Anthony Scaramucci, who did not require Senate confirmation, served just six days on the job as White House communications director during Trump’s first term.

World.title: Man shot and killed by police in Madison, Wisconsin, sparking protests
World.content:
A police officer in Madison, Wisconsin, shot and killed a man who had injured him with a knife while resisting arrest, the city's police chief said Wednesday.

Police have not identified the man who was killed, saying only that he was in his 30s.

The Madison Police Department said in a news release that its officers were responding to calls that someone was stealing bicycles and checking vehicle doors in the city's Marquette neighborhood. The man fled from officers on a bicycle, traveling through backyards to get away, the department said, before officers encountered him again at an intersection.

At the intersection, the man "either fell or was pulled off the bicycle," the department said, noting that how he came off the bicycle "is still being determined." A "struggle ensued" between the man and officers in the intersection, the department said.

"During the struggle, the man pulled out a fix-blade knife and injured an officer," the police department said. The department shared a photo of the knife, which has a black handle. In video reviewed by CBS News, an officer can be heard shouting, "He's got a knife!"

An image of a knife shared by the Madison Police Department. Madison Police Department

An officer deployed a Taser, but it was unsuccessful, Police Chief John Patterson said at a news conference on Wednesday. Then, the injured officer fired his weapon. Video reviewed by CBS News shows police appearing to shoot the man three times about two seconds after the Taser was deployed. Video also shows a knife being thrown to the ground after the shooting. Blood appears to be visible alongside the knife in the photo shared by police.

Lifesaving measures were provided at the scene, Patterson said. The man was transported to an area hospital, where he was pronounced dead, the department said. Patterson said he had "heartfelt sympathies" for the man's family.

In total, four officers were involved or witnessed the shooting. Patterson described the officer who fired his weapon as a veteran officer, but did not reveal any other details about that officer or the others present. The veteran officer was the only one who fired his weapon.

Another officer was injured during the incident, but it's not clear how. The department said it did not believe the officer's injuries were caused by the knife.

Patterson said that "when a knife is produced" during an arrest, "the overall situation is clearly elevated" and "becomes incredibly dangerous."

"It obviously increases risks for everyone there," Patterson said. "For every officer. For the person as well. I think it severely narrows the scope of options and possible outcomes."

Madison Police Chief John Patterson speaks at a news conference after a police officer shot and killed a man in Madison, Wisconsin, July 22, 2026. WKOW via AP

Investigation underway

The Wisconsin Department of Criminal Investigation will investigate the shooting because it involves police officers. All four officers have been placed on administrative leave, Rhodes-Conway said in a statement released Wednesday night. This is standard protocol for the department.

Rhodes-Conway cautioned that the investigation will take time and said that officials will work to resolve the "questions that must be answered."

"It's understandable that people want answers now. I want them too. And in the days and weeks ahead, the Common Council and I, as your representatives, will do our best to get and share information," Rhodes-Conway said, adding that details about a "community listening session" will be shared soon. She added that she was "angered and saddened" by the day's events.

Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers said in a social media post he was "briefed on the officer-involved shooting that occurred in Madison today" and continues "to receive updates as more information is released."

"There must be transparency and accountability in any investigation moving forward," Evers said in the post.

Madison police officers do not currently use body-worn cameras. Patterson has said that securing funding for the devices is a top priority.

Protests held overnight

The shooting happened on a city street in a popular neighborhood lined with restaurants, bars, shops and residential homes less than 2 miles from the state Capitol. Footage of the incident shows numerous cars stopped in the intersection with people watching as it unfolded.

In 2015, a White police officer shot and killed Tony Robinson, who was biracial, on the same street, a shooting that spurred large protests. The district attorney did not file charges against police in that incident, determining the officer was justified. Robinson's family accepted a $3.35 million settlement from the city in 2017.

Attendees gather at a candlelight vigil where a Madison police officer shot and killed a man July 22, 2026, in Madison, Wisconsin. AP Photo/Kayla Wolf

The race of the officer who fired his gun on Wednesday and that of the man were not released by police. But advocates for the Black community in Madison said the man killed was Black.

"Another Black man is dead on a Madison street, and our community watched him die before we even knew his name," said Brandi Grayson, the head of the Madison-based Black community advocacy group Urban Triage. "That is the cruelty of state violence."

A crowd formed near where the shooting occurred on Wednesday, with some people chanting, "Arrest the cops!" Among the protesters who gathered throughout the night was Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong. Some placed flowers and candles where the man was shot and held a vigil. There were no reports of issues related to the protests.

Patterson said the department was reaching out to community leaders to "strike the right balance" and ensure that the city can "support any assembly that might happen."

Gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong speaks alongside protesters near where a Madison police officer shot and killed a man July 22, 2026, in Madison, Wisconsin. AP Photo/Kayla Wolf

The police chief also called for calm as the shooting is investigated. He cautioned that videos shared online show just one perspective of the incident.

"I ask the community to recognize that there is other video that they have not seen, that's not circulating online, that will be reviewed as part of this investigation," he said. "So, to the extent that they can as we all navigate this trauma together, we try to remain calm and remember that not all perspectives are online right now."

World.title: Tampa, Charleston airports to join new TSA privatized security initiative
World.content:
The Tampa, Charleston and Des Moines airports have signed on to a new program to privatize airport security, the Transportation Security Administration told CBS News.

Under the new initiative, called TSA Gold+, TSA would maintain oversight of security standards and operations but would use private contractors for screening instead of federal workers.

Gold+ is an expansion of the Screening Partnership Program (SPP), which similarly allows airports to hire private contractors to conduct security screening under federal oversight. Launched in 2004 by the TSA, the program operates at 20 airports across the U.S., including San Francisco International Airport and Kansas City International Airport.

"The new TSA Gold+ program mostly expands on what those contractors are allowed to manage, including the actual screening technology," said Julian Kheel, founder of travel rewards site Points Path.

In an email seen by CBS News from the TSA to the American Federation of Government Employees (AFGE), a union that represents airport employees, the agency listed January 2027 as the projected launch period for Gold+ at the Des Moines airport, February 2027 for Charleston and May 2027 for Tampa.

The email also mentions briefings the agency held at the participating airports to discuss the Gold+ program and its potential impact on employees at Tampa, Des Moines and Charleston airports.

"TSA Gold+ presents a new way for airports to deliver exceptional service to every traveler, while advancing security, efficiency, and the overall airport experience," a TSA spokesperson said in an email to CBS News. "Throughout the transition of these airports, we remain committed to operational stability and supporting our employees."

TSA did not respond to a request for comment from CBS News about its process for selecting private screening contractors.

On its Gold+ website, the agency claims that introducing new screening technology through the program will expedite screening and enhance security.

"Private investment allows airports to adopt innovative solutions more quickly, improving both safety and the passenger experience," the agency's Gold+ website says.

Security, workforce concerns

The Gold+ program has ignited backlash from AFGE, which represents 47,000 transportation security officers across 400 U.S. airports. In a statement shared with CBS News, the union said that the Gold+ measure would jeopardize public safety by removing TSA workers from the screening process.

The union's national president Everett Kelley called it a "major departure and step backward" from the screening systems that Congress created after the 9/11 attacks.

"Changes of this magnitude should not be made behind closed doors without the input of Congress, the flying public, the local airport authorities and TSA employees themselves," he said.

In November 2001, Congress passed the Aviation and Transportation Security Act, which established the TSA as the agency responsible for overseeing airport security. Prior to its passage, air carriers were responsible for airport screening, a task that most contracted out to private companies, the Government Accountability Office said in a 2005 report.

Kheel said the safety questions surrounding Gold+ aren't just about private versus public security, but are also about the TSA's role in setting and evaluating its own safety standards.

"The TSA has effectively been grading its own homework for the two decades since it both writes the standards and staffs the checkpoints," he said. "That dual role isn't ideal, regardless of whether airports are utilizing government or private screeners."

AFGE also expressed concerns that the Gold+ program will lead to workforce cuts for airport employees. The union pointed to the administration's fiscal 2027 budget for the agency, which includes plans to cut nearly 8,400 workers, including 2,462 transportation security officer (TSO) positions. About half of those would be replaced through the expansion of TSA's privatization efforts, the union said.

"The administration's actions should concern all Americans, and AFGE will continue to speak out against any proposal that threatens our members' jobs and jeopardizes the safety of the flying public," Kelley said.

World.title: Measles outbreak "slowing," but newborn's family still can't meet her
World.content:
Kasey is seven weeks old tomorrow. Her parents keep a running list of the people she hasn't met: great-grandparents in the Midwest, family in Arizona, relatives who are sick and running out of time to fly. Measles is the reason.

The official story in Utah is that the worst has passed. State guidance on the measles shot recently moved back to the usual 12 months, after a stretch of offering it early because spread had slowed. Utah's own weekly case count has fallen sharply since its March peak. The national count hasn't: it passed last year's full-year total this week and is still climbing.

None of that changes the math in Abby Laskey and Liam Hammons' apartment in Mill Creek, just outside Salt Lake City. Kasey is too young for the MMR vaccine. The earliest she can get a dose is six months, and with Utah back to standard guidance, more likely a year. Until then she depends on the one thing measles is built to erase: everyone else's immunity.

So her parents have rearranged their lives around a virus that's supposedly receding. No museums. No indoor public spaces. No flying. They're both vaccinated, both careful, both doing everything the system asks of them. And they still can't introduce their daughter to the people who most want to meet her. "There's not a guarantee," Abby told me, "that by the time she's fully vaccinated they'll be able to meet her at all."

Then came the part I keep thinking about. To justify the caution to older relatives, they caught themselves borrowing authority from others. The pediatricians are really cautioning against travel, they'd say, reaching for the white coat to make the case. It made them uneasy. They were, said Liam, "offloading blame and caution onto systems that are already ... on the ropes … in the public perception." You can hear the grandparent's reply coming: those pediatricians are overreacting; when I was a kid, we all got measles. They didn't love making every pediatrician in Utah the reason a family stayed home.

Vaccination used to spread the cost. Now it doesn't.

Vaccination used to spread the cost of protection across everyone. When enough people are immune, a 6-week-old who can't be is covered anyway, for free, by the wall around her. That wall is what's thinning: national kindergarten MMR coverage has slipped from 95.2% five years ago to 92.5% last year, under the threshold epidemiologists use for herd protection. And when it thins, the cost doesn't disappear. It moves. It settles on the people with the least protection and the least to do with the problem: the immunocompromised, the newborns, and the parents now playing bouncer on their own maternity leave.

Abby kept circling something they couldn't quite name: the scary stories, they said, of kids who "die of related things" years later. They're describing immune amnesia. Measles doesn't only make a child sick in the moment. It infects the immune cells that remember past infections and erases a chunk of that memory. In work led by the immunologist Dr. Michael Mina, the effect lined up with higher deaths from other infections for about 28 months afterward. A child can recover from measles and stay more vulnerable to everything else for two years. Dr. Paul Offit and New York Times writer David Wallace-Wells call the social version "cultural immune amnesia," our forgetting of what these diseases actually did. Both kinds are running at once.

The official reports only tell part of the story

As of July 21, the U.S. had logged 2,295 confirmed measles cases in 2026, according to the Johns Hopkins University's measles tracker, surpassing all of 2025's total of 2,289 and marking the highest count in 35 years, with more than five months still left in the year. (CDC's own weekly count, released separately on Fridays, stood at 2,260 as of July 16. Both trackers are counting the same outbreak. They just close their weeks at different times.)

Even short of that line, 2026 is running about 37% ahead of last year's pace at the same point, and roughly 97% of cases are spreading within U.S. communities. Utah alone has counted 518, spread across 22 of its 29 counties, a share no other state has matched.

Genomic sequencing ties the numbers to one continuous chain: the mutations in Utah's cases trace back to an outbreak that started in West Texas in January 2025, the same signature now confirmed in at least four other states.

The nation's measles elimination status is now on the line

The United States' measles elimination status, held since 2000, requires no continuous domestic transmission for a full year. The Pan American Health Organization is scheduled to make its formal assessment in November, but based on the data, the U.S. has already lost its measles elimination status.

"This didn't have to be," Abby said. They're not that afraid of the virus itself, they told me; they're angry it's forcing the question at all. "If we're losing the plot on this one," Liam said, "what's the next thing we lose the plot on?" He told me that "Trust is going to take a long time to build back up ... a lot of unnecessary suffering and a lot of unnecessary deaths."

Kasey's parents will keep her home. They'll see family at campgrounds and on beaches, outdoors, at a distance, and skip the flights. Her great-grandparents will keep waiting.

This article was originally published in Dr. Céline Gounder's "Underlying Conditions" newsletter on Substack. Read more and subscribe here.

World.title: DOJ to withdraw subpoenas for New York Times reporters over Air Force One story
World.content:
The Justice Department told a judge Thursday it will withdraw its subpoenas for grand jury testimony and phone records from New York Times reporters over an article on security systems in the new Air Force One jet.

During a heated court hearing, U.S. District Judge Arun Subramanian grilled federal prosecutors working for the Justice Department on why it had issued subpoenas before taking further investigative steps, and questioned whether he should issue sanctions over alleged perjury in an application to a judge to secure the subpoenas.

In a brief order following the hearing, Subramanian reiterated that the "government has voluntarily withdrawn the challenged subpoenas, including the subpoenas issued to the journalists as well as the third-party subpoenas. Those subpoenas are null and void."

The New York Times said earlier this month that several of its reporters received grand jury subpoenas soon after it published reporting on President Trump's use of an old presidential aircraft to depart from the NATO summit in Turkey in early July and security limitations on a new plane donated by the Qatari government. The paper said the subpoenas were issued by Jay Clayton, the U.S. attorney in the Southern District of New York who was tapped by Mr. Trump for director of national intelligence.

The news outlet moved to block the subpoenas, calling them "abusive and improper." The newspaper said in a court filing Saturday that prosecutors attempted to gain access to phone records of Times journalists and their family members as part of a Justice Department effort to identity sources who spoke to the reporters about security systems on the new Qatari-donated Air Force One plane.

In one batch of subpoenas, the Justice Department sought grand-jury testimony from several reporters "in regard to an alleged violation of federal criminal law." But subpoenas were also sent to third-party service providers for toll records and data for accounts associated with Times' journalists. Among the information sought by the Trump administration were phone records for the spouses of two reporters and one journalist's mother.

Two of the subpoenas sought phone records dating back to Jan. 1, well before the Times started reporting on the security concerns with the Qatari-donated airplane.

"That timeframe strongly suggests that the Department is using this investigation not to focus on any purported concerns arising from the July 8 and 9 articles, but instead to forage for information about the Journalists' source relationships more broadly," the Times' lawyers said.

They added that the timing of the Justice Department's actions "are deeply troubling" and "raise pressing questions about the conduct of this purported national security investigation."

Ahead of Thursday's hearing, Subramanian halted enforcement of the subpoenas while he considered the Times' request to quash the demands.

World.title: Global oil prices hit $100 a barrel amid attacks in Red Sea
World.content:
Global oil prices topped $100 a barrel on Thursday as the conflict in the Middle East escalated, with Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen targeting shipping in the Red Sea.

Brent crude, the international standard, rose $5.76, or 6.1%, to settle at $100.69 a barrel, according to data from FactSet.

Gas prices are also climbing higher, with the national average hitting $4.09 a gallon on Thursday, up from $3.94 a week earlier, AAA data shows.

Stocks took a hit in the wake of higher oil prices, with the S&P 500 tumbling 91 points, or 1.2%, to close at 7,408 on Thursday, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average slumping 507 points, or 1%, to close at 51,712. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell 2.2%.

Houthi rebels claimed they struck two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea on Wednesday. The attacks threatened shipping in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which carries around 7% of the global oil supply, according to Oxford Economics. The strait, which connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden, is a hub for sea trade.

The surge in oil prices complicates the outlook for the Federal Reserve, which is set to make its next interest rate decision on July 29. Resurgent oil prices threaten to push inflation higher, which could place pressure on the Fed to keep rates steady — or even introduce a hike – to counter rising prices, experts say.

"Rate cuts investors were counting on for later this year look a lot less certain today than they did even a week ago, and then they were on shaky ground," said Nigel Green, the CEO of investment firm deVere Group, in an email.

There's now a 36% probability the Fed could increase its benchmark rate on July 29, according to CME FedWatch, which uses 30-day Fed Funds futures prices to estimate the central bank's interest rate decisions. A week ago, that probability stood at about 11%, its data shows.

The war also showed other signs of intensifying, with the U.S. upping the number of refueling aircraft deployed to Israel. Open-source flight-tracking data also showed American B-1 bombers leaving the U.K. The U.S. has launched 12 consecutive nights of strikes on targets across Iran.

Treasury yields rose amid higher oil prices, with the 10-year Treasury climbing to 4.71%.

The last time global oil prices settled above $100 was on May 22, data from FactSet shows.

World.title: Vance Boelter gets 2 life terms and more in Minnesota lawmaker shootings
World.content:
Vance Boelter, the man who admitted in court to shooting two Minnesota lawmakers and their spouses, was sentenced to two life terms in prison followed by 40 years Thursday morning.

Judge John R. Tunheim said it was "the longest sentence I have imposed after hearing thousands of cases over the years, but it is well deserved."

Boelter, who turns 59 Thursday, pleaded guilty to six federal charges against him in June. As part of his plea, he confessed to killing former House Speaker Melissa Hortman and her husband Mark and wounding Sen. John Hoffman and his wife Yvette in a shooting that also targeted their daughter Hope.

The U.S. Department of Justice announced in June it would not seek the death penalty for Boelter.

In a pre-sentencing filing on Tuesday, prosecutors said, "Justice requires that Boelter never be free again." Thursday's sentence carries no possibility of parole.

Acting U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche issued a statement following the sentencing, saying, "This murderer will spend the rest of his life behind bars for his heinous acts of violence against public servants and their families. ... Our hearts remain with the victims' families, loved ones, and all those whose lives were forever changed by these horrific attacks."

Today, the convicted criminal who stalked and murdered Minnesota House Speaker Emerita Melissa Hortman and her husband, Mark, Minnesota State Senator John Hoffman and his wife, Yvette, and attempted to shoot their daughter—was sentenced to two consecutive life sentences, plus a… — Acting AG Todd Blanche (@DAGToddBlanche) July 23, 2026

The Hennepin County Attorney's Office previously said it plans to move forward with state charges against Boelter: two counts of first-degree premeditated murder, four counts of attempted first-degree murder and one count each of felony cruelty to an animal and impersonating an officer.

The Hoffman family is suing Boelter civilly, accusing him of assault, battery, intentional infliction of emotional distress, negligence and negligence per se, according to the complaint.

The June 14, 2025, shootings in the Twin Cities suburbs of Champlin and Brooklyn Park prompted a manhunt that lasted 43 hours and ended in rural Green Isle, Minnesota. Officials said the attacks were politically motivated.

In the most recent legislative session, Hortman's colleagues approved a number of tributes to her, including a memorial garden for the State Office Building and the renaming of Highway 610 and Minnesota's community solar garden program in her honor. Lawmakers also passed two measures championed by Hortman's son Colin, which aim to ease the burdens on families following traumatic events.

Boelter speaks before sentencing

Boelter gave a brief statement to the court before being sentenced.

"To every person I have caused loss, pain, heartache, confusion, shame or loneliness, I am truly sorry," he said.

Hortman children say they still think of parents' murders daily

Sophie and Colin Hortman, children to Melissa and Mark, told the court the pain they experienced after Boelter killed their parents is unforgettable.

"What I cared about is my entire life had been shattered in 30 seconds," Sophie Hortman said. "My parents were dead. The dog had been shot multiple times. My brother was wrecked."

Colin Hortman said he lives with post-traumatic stress disorder.

"The blood that was spilled is the last thing I see before I fall asleep and the first thing I see as I wake," he said, adding that when he pictures his parents, he sees "bullet holes."

Both admitted no penalty would be fully satisfactory, but Colin Hortman asked for the maximum sentence with no possibility of release.

"Justice can never be served for those who lost," Sophie Hortman said. "I miss my mom. I miss my dad. I miss my best friends. I miss believing in the goodness of humanity."

Hoffmans recount horror of shooting, difficulty of aftermath

John Hoffman said he "returned to the Minnesota Senate because I refuse to allow violence to become the author of my future."

Still, he said, his family lives "with a heightened awareness that enters every room before we do."

"Our home no longer feels like the sanctuary it once was," he said. "We installed solid steel doors and reinforced security. Your honor, those aren't home improvements. They are daily reminders that violence followed us home."

Yvette Hoffman said she "genuinely believed" she was dying after being shot.

"I'll never forget looking down and watching my blood stream down that white washing machine as I felt myself sinking to the floor and fading," she said.

"I came face to face with evil," she later added. "I survived it. I will carry the memory of that day with me for the rest of my life."

Hope Hoffman, whose father said her actions "helped save our lives and many others," said she lives not only with the trauma caused by the attack, but that of the "bias and sensationalism" she endured from the media in the aftermath.

"In all reality, I'd like to just be a victim of gun violence who called 911. I really shouldn't have to be advocating for that, but here we are," she said.

Both Hope and Yvette Hoffman shared ill wishes for their attacker.

"Not only is he a criminal and a loser, he's also the worst kind of father he could possibly be," Hope Hoffman said. "I hope one day he miserably dies with that thought."

"If I had a wish, it is when the defendant's life ends, his body is carried out of federal prison in one of those body bags he intended for my family," Yvette Hoffman said.

Fellow lawmakers say attacks shook, changed them

Before the sentencing, Rep. Kristin Bahner, who said Boelter also visited her home the night he shot the Hortmans and Hoffmans, gave an emotional victim impact statement.

"Nothing could prepare me for an assassin at my door," Bahner said. "I never dreamt that doing the job that I love would put my family in harm's way, forever shattering their innocence."

Bahner told the judge, "I only want one thing. That neither courts nor you can give me, Mr. Boelter. I want Melissa back."

Rep. Zack Stephenson, who took over as House DFL leader after Hortman's killing, said Boelter's actions "sent a message of terror to everyone who serves in public life," but that "our caucus is stronger, more unified and even more dedicated to the values that Melissa and Mark lived their life by."

"Melissa consistently acted the way every Minnesotan, every American, would hope their representative would act," Stephenson said. "There has never been another Melissa Hortman and I doubt there ever will be."
