World.title: Trump allies are poised to weaken protections for historic sites — not just in D.C.
World.content:
Trump allies are poised to weaken protections for historic sites — not just in D.C.

toggle caption Jen Golbeck/AP

The Trump administration is eyeing a workaround for one of the procedural hurdles facing its proposed 250-foot arch: weakening federal oversight of all construction projects affecting historic sites.

Critics say that the move would not only clear a path for President Trump's controversial projects in D.C., but also endanger the preservation of historic and cultural places across the United States.

"Every American who has any place in their heart that is historic or culturally significant to them should be concerned about this attempt to gut historic preservation protections," said Greg Werkheiser, founding partner at the law firm Cultural Heritage Partners.

Sponsor Message

The National Register of Historic Places contains over 100,000 properties, encompassing more than 1.8 million buildings, structures, sites, objects and districts. They take many forms, from a house to a burial ground, a shipwreck to a landscape, a single tree to an entire neighborhood.

"It's the thing that defines America," Werkheiser said. "The places that you go where your family has an attachment over generations … There are millions of these sites in this country, and all of them are made less protected by this effort by the Trump administration."

The White House and the Department of the Interior did not respond to NPR's request for comment.

Part of the National Historic Preservation Act of 1966, known as Section 106, requires federal agencies to evaluate how new construction projects would affect historic places.

Under the Section 106 review process, the federal agency overseeing a project must invite interested parties — like preservation groups and local and tribal governments — to weigh in. Currently, agencies are required to consider whether the project would cause "adverse effects" to a historic property and, if so, explore ways to "avoid, minimize, or mitigate" those harms.

The Advisory Council on Historic Preservation, the federal agency responsible for overseeing the Section 106 review process, is packed with Trump appointees. And now, 60 years after the law took effect, the council wants to water it down drastically.

Sponsor Message

"Because President Trump controls 21 of the 24 members of the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation, it's very likely that they will proceed with doing what the administration wants for them to do," said Sara Bronin, who served as the Senate-confirmed chair of the advisory council under President Biden.

Bronin is the most recent chair of the council, as that position is currently vacant. President Trump has yet to nominate a new one, instead appointing its vice chair, Travis Voyles, to serve in an acting capacity.

Last week, Voyles sent an email to council members asking them to vote on proposed revisions to the wording of Section 106. According to draft language obtained by NPR, those changes include redefining what kinds of properties can be considered historic in the first place, making public comment on new projects optional and removing the requirement to consult with Native American tribes.

"What it means is that the federal government, in its own discretion, can decide whether — if ever — to tell an American community that it's about to do a major project that could harm or destroy a historic resource," Werkheiser said. "The public will be completely cut out of any conversation around the future of places that matter to them in this country."

Council members were given just one week to cast their votes, via email, by the end of Friday. The revision would need to clear several more steps of the federal rulemaking process, including a roughly 30-day public comment period, before it can take effect.

Werkheiser called the vote a "foregone conclusion," but said it sets the stage for a legal fight later.

"As sure as the sun rises and sets over Washington, D.C., there will be litigation in an attempt to stop this absurd gutting of protections of American history," he said.

toggle caption Scott Olson/Getty Images

Why does the Trump administration want these changes?

After World War II, an era of urban renewal and federal highway construction destroyed high-profile buildings like New York City's Penn Station, and devastated many historically Black neighborhoods.

Sponsor Message

The advisory council's memo describes that period as "one of the greatest, yet most destructive building streaks in American history." It prompted public outrage, and resulted in Congress passing the National Historic Preservation Act in 1966.

"Small wonder, then, that Congress enacted a requirement that all Federal agencies take into account historic preservation concerns in future Federal actions," the memo reads. "Consideration, however, was not the same thing as a mandate that historic preservation concerns trump all others."

The memo says the current regulations under Section 106 "create confusion and uncertainty for both the public and regulated entities and contribute to agency delays." It cites a 2019 study that found consultation can take nearly seven years in extreme cases.

And it proposes revisions that it says would help "agencies strike a more appropriate balance between evaluating effects on historic properties and advancing critical federal projects."

The changes would limit the type and number of historic properties that will receive protection, ruling out "significant landscape features" like the Grand Canyon. Bronin says it would also change the type of actions that will be reviewed in the first place, with an "alarming number of exemptions," including for federally funded projects carried out by local authorities.

"Things like state highway widening, which in the past have been highly destructive of historic places, including not only whole neighborhoods but also burial sites … won't [undergo Section 106 review] under the new rules," she said.

The new wording would also narrow what is considered an "adverse effect" to anything that is directly and foreseeably tied to the project (as opposed to indirect or cumulative effects). And it allows agencies to condense much of the process into a written report, which they would then share with third parties for review instead of consulting them along the way.

"This change in consultation will have the effect of not surfacing the location, significance and effects on historic sites, meaning that they could have the potential to be destroyed at scale," she said.

Sponsor Message

The new wording would also remove requirements for public comment, eliminating the phrase: "views of the public are essential to informed Federal decisionmaking."

That stands out to Charles Birnbaum, the founding president and CEO of The Cultural Landscape Foundation, an education and advocacy organization based in D.C. He told NPR over email that he sees similarities between the revised law and the reason it exists in the first place.

"Consent of the governed is being replaced with my way or the highway," he wrote. "This is the same haughty, retrograde, and myopic attitude that resulted in urban renewal, which decimated cities with highways and destroyed countless neighborhoods nationwide, especially underserved communities."

The Cultural Landscape Foundation has already sued over the administration's repainting of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, saying the National Park Service improperly used — by its own words — a "streamlined" Section 106 review. A judge has not yet ruled in the case, as the pool saga continues to unfold.

toggle caption Allison Robbert/AP

What happens next?

Simplifying the Section 106 review process could help to fast-track some of the Trump administration's renovation projects in D.C.

The requirement for third-party consultation — which many historic and cultural preservation groups say is happening too fast or not at all — has been one of the few hurdles in the already fast-moving approval process for Trump's arch.

Bronin says under the proposed new language, near-constant construction noise near Arlington National Cemetery would not be considered an adverse effect, and the 250-foot arch's disruption of historic views would not be considered under the review process.

"Although I would encourage listeners to not simply focus on D.C.'s iconic landmarks, because this proposal would have far-reaching effects, the proposal for the arch in front of Arlington Cemetery is an excellent example of what's at stake with these changes," Bronin said.

The National Trust for Historic Preservation, the National Association of Tribal Historic Preservation Officers and the National Conference of State Historic Preservation Officers have all issued statements opposing the Section 106 changes, taking issue both with the substance and the brief voting timeline. They each have representatives on the advisory council board.

Sponsor Message

Elizabeth Merrit, deputy general counsel for the National Trust for Historic Preservation, wrote in an open letter that she will vote against the proposed changes, calling them "likely to cause

widespread chaos and confusion, and … curtail the consultation process that has led to thousands of win-win outcomes around the country."

Werkheiser agreed that the proposal would be "terrible for developers," who want predictability and information early on to avoid delays and issues down the road. He said that's why the existing Section 106 process generally works so well. Trying to speed it up by even a few days, he said, would be "a losing trade for America in the long-term."

"Folks who complain about the relatively little time it takes to pause in front of a massive development project and say, 'Are we destroying something that can never be replaced?' I think those folks need to ask themselves, what legacy are they handing to their children and their grandchildren?" he said.

Both Werkheiser and Bronin encouraged people who oppose these changes to speak up not only during the public comment period, but to their legislators directly.

"As chair, I saw the topic of historic preservation as a bipartisan issue, and one that unites people who care about their communities, whether they're in red states or blue states," Bronin said. "I think that the public comment on the regulations will really help to send a powerful message that we care about our historic places and we don't want them to be destroyed."

Congress could potentially take action, including passing legislation to strengthen Section 106.

Democrats on the Senate Natural Resources Committee released a statement this week opposing the changes. They urged the council to "go back to the drawing board and work directly with Tribes and states on a new proposal that actually improves the consultation process without undermining the rights and voices of those most directly affected."

World.title: For a 2nd time, House approves resolution to end the war in Iran in a rebuke to Trump
World.content:
For a 2nd time, House approves resolution to end the war in Iran in a rebuke to Trump

toggle caption J. Scott Applewhite/AP

The House on Thursday approved a resolution to remove U.S. forces from hostilities with Iran, in a vote that reflected growing frustration inside Congress over the war and the ability of lawmakers to conduct oversight.

The resolution passed the House by a vote of 214 to 208. And while it is not legally binding, the resolution represents a symbolic rebuke to President Trump over a war that lawmakers never voted to authorize. It was the second such rebuke passed by the House since the start of the war.

Shortly after the House vote, Senate Democrats tried to advance a war powers resolution of their own, but the measure failed 47 to 49.

Sponsor Message

The votes came at a moment when attacks between Iran and the U.S. appear to be intensifying. Eighteen U.S. troops have died since fighting broke out in February, but four have died since July 17. U.S. forces have also suffered nearly 500 injuries, with 100 of those coming in the past two weeks, according to the Pentagon.

Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., who led the effort in the House, said the vote sends President Trump a clear message that Congress will not continue to tolerate what she described as an "illegal war."

"From the beginning, this war has had no clear mission, no strategy, no end goal. Congress has not been consulted," Jayapal said following the vote. "And hostilities have been driven over and over again by a president who won his election by promising to end forever wars."

Four Republicans joined Democrats to approve the measure: Tom Barrett of Michigan, Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, Ohio's Warren Davidson and Thomas Massie of Kentucky.

Republicans who opposed the resolution have defended the war as necessary, given Iran's past attacks on Americans and U.S. interests in the region.

During debate on the House floor on Wednesday, the Republican chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Brian Mast of Florida, held up photos of U.S. service members killed in the war.

Sponsor Message

"To belittle this mission is to belittle and demean the very service these members gave their life for," Mast said. "This operation is bringing reckoning for the hundreds of times Iran has attacked and killed people of the United States of America," he continued.

Last month, the Senate also approved a war powers resolution, only to reverse course on a separate resolution brought the following day after President Trump criticized the initial vote. The president has referred to the war power votes as "meaningless" and a reflection of Democrats "fueled by Trump Derangement Syndrome."

World.title: In a first, Chinese woman wins the prestigious Fields Medal
World.content:
In a first, Chinese woman wins the prestigious Fields Medal

toggle caption Simons Foundation

For the first time, a Chinese woman has been awarded the world's most prestigious mathematics prize, the Fields Medal, bringing the total count of Chinese-born medalists to three, as two mathematicians from the country clinched medals this year.

Often referred to as the Nobel Prize of mathematics, Fields Medals are awarded every four years to between two and four mathematicians under 40, recognizing both achievement and potential.

This year marks only the third time a woman has ever won the coveted award in its 90-year history.

The recipients, whose medals were presented at the opening ceremony of the International Congress of Mathematicians in Philadelphia on Thursday, included Chinese mathematicians Hong Wang and Yu Deng, American John Pardon and Canadian Jacob Tsimerman.

Sponsor Message

"All four mathematicians have made tremendous contributions to their respective fields," Ulrike Tillmann, vice-president and incoming president of the International Mathematical Union (IMU), the institution responsible for organizing the awards, told NPR.

"It's also wonderful to see another woman winning the Medal. We should have the feeling that it has become a normal thing that women contribute to their fields at the highest level, including the Fields Medal," she added.

toggle caption Simons Foundation

First time two Chinese scholars simultaneously won the prize

Originally from China's mountainous Guilin City, Hong Wang is the first Chinese woman to ever receive the medal. In a video released by the IMU she recalls solving her first math problem as a child. "I felt quite happy when I figured out the answer, I feel like I have a clearer understanding of the subject" she said.

Wang, who researches at both NYU and France's Institut des Hautes Études Scientifiques, shot to fame after resolving a century-old problem known as the Kakeya conjecture in three dimensions, together with University of British Columbia's Joshua Zahl.

"Solving this problem has opened the door for a host of theorems and conjectures in harmonic analysis, partial differential equations, geometric measure theory and other fields," the IMU said in a statement.

Sponsor Message

Her victory, alongside Yu Deng, represents the first time two Chinese scholars have simultaneously won the prize.

Yau Shing-Tung was the first ethnic Chinese mathematician to win in 1982, while Australian-born Terence Tao won in 2006.

Originally from China's tech-hub Shenzhen, Deng's research on axiomatizing physics, establishing mathematical rules that could be used to explain branches of the science, drew praise from the IMU. His key paper was co-authored by the University of Michigan's Zaher Hani and Xiao Ma.

The University of Chicago researcher's work is "a leap forward in a centuries-long quest by mathematicians and physicists to derive the basic laws of physics from first principles," the organization said of Deng.

American mathematician John Pardon was cited by the IMU for his contributions in the fields of topology, and geometry, while Canada's Jacob Tsimerman, was praised for extending the scope of logical frameworks from abstract fields of mathematics into algebraic geometry.

toggle caption CARL DE SOUZA/AFP via Getty Images

On Chinese internet, the historic wins spark joy and reflection

This year's Fields Medalists were first revealed prematurely after a vulnerability on the International Congress of Mathematicians website allowed coders to uncover the four winners' names ahead of the official ceremony on Thursday.

On Chinese social media, the news was received by many with joy. "Two Chinese mathematicians!" said one Guangdong-based Chinese social media user. "And one is a Chinese woman!"

"This is what you call truly bringing honor to your country," said another from Henan province.

Although Wang and Deng began their higher education at Beijing's prestigious Peking University, one of China's top universities, their training and subsequent research was done in the United States and Europe.

After two years of studying in Beijing, Deng transferred to MIT before completing a PhD at Princeton University. Graduating from Peking University, Wang continued post-graduate study in France before finishing her mathematics PhD at MIT. Both researchers work outside of China.

For some on China's popular RedNote social media app, this year's award raises questions about how China's research capabilities stack up to the United States'.

Sponsor Message

"Why don't we reflect on why everyone leaves for the United States after completing their undergraduate degree in China?" said a user from Tianjin .

"Breaking up the monopoly of academic cliques is the direction Chinese higher education should take", said one RedNote user from Guangdong .

Despite criticisms of a brain drain from China to the U.S., the awards come at a time when several high-profile Chinese scholars have returned home, some citing an increasingly hostile academic environment in America.

In 2025, Beijing launched a special "K-visa", aimed at attracting foreign tech experts. A project called QiMing, run by China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, also seeks to recruit foreign and overseas Chinese STEM talent.

In addition to the Fields Medal, the IMU also announced winners of other top honors, including Oxford University's Graeme Segal (Chern Medal) and the University of Washington's Shayan Oveis Gharan (Abacus Medal).

Along with massive international prestige, each Fields Medalist receives a gold medal depicting famed ancient Greek mathematician Archimedes and a cash prize of 15,000 Canadian dollars (roughly $11,000 USD).

But for Deng, the real driver isn't fame or prize money—it's raw curiosity.

"Our understanding of the physical universe on the mathematical level is still extremely small," he said in a video provided by the IMU.

"The thing that keeps me in this field is the happiness when your plan works perfectly, [and] you are able to solve the questions you are faced with."

World.title: Republicans urge Justice Department to investigate former prosecutor Jack Smith
World.content:
Republicans urge Justice Department to investigate former prosecutor Jack Smith

toggle caption Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images

House Republicans are urging the Justice Department to launch a criminal investigation into former special counsel Jack Smith, alleging that Smith made false statements last year about his effort to gather phone records of lawmakers.

House Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan, a Republican from Ohio, wrote DOJ late Wednesday to argue that Smith "seemingly made willfully and intentionally false statements" when he answered questions under oath last December.

The criminal referral of Smith marks yet another step in a campaign by the Trump administration and its allies in Congress to pursue people who once investigated Trump. The Justice Department already has attempted to initiate criminal cases against former FBI Director Jim Comey and New York Attorney General Letitia James.

Sponsor Message

Smith has been a frequent target of Trump's ire on social media. "Justice at last???" Trump posted in the early morning hours Thursday amid news of the criminal referral.

Smith, a former head of the Justice Department's public integrity unit, oversaw two criminal probes of Trump. Grand juries indicted Trump for alleged interference in the 2020 election and for allegedly refusing to turn over classified materials he had collected at his Mar-a-Lago resort. Both cases ended before any trial could occur, partly because Trump won the 2024 election and headed back to the White House.

Lawyers for Smith released their own letter to Jordan and the DOJ on Wednesday night, asserting that he provided "truthful, responsive answers" to Congress last year.

"This referral reflects a chilling eagerness to weaponize the justice system by attacking a career, nonpartisan public servant who faithfully and fearlessly performed his duties by following the facts and the law," wrote lawyers Lanny Breuer and Peter Koski.

Rep. Jamie Raskin, a Maryland lawmaker who serves as the top Democrat on the Judiciary Committee, said in a statement that the referral of Smith would be "laughed out of court" if it ever reaches a federal judge.

"This referral deliberately distorts and misstates the facts, including what questions the Republicans actually asked at Mr. Smith's interview," Raskin said. "Jack Smith could not have lied because Republican Members never even asked the question their theory is based on."

Sponsor Message

The testimony at the heart of the dispute concerns subpoenas Smith's prosecution team issued for phone records of lawmakers in contact with top White House officials and allies some six years ago. Smith also gathered text messages from the National Archives from White House phones that included exchanges between White House aides and lawmakers. Republicans in Congress never asked Smith directly about that, Smith's lawyers said in their new letter, and now want to punish him for not "proactively disclosing that."

World.title: Get into med school in the graphic memoir 'See One, Do One, Teach One'
World.content:
Get into med school in the graphic memoir 'See One, Do One, Teach One'

W. W. Norton & Company

For most people, knowledge of what life on the job is like for healthcare workers comes primarily from two limited vantage points: watching television shows and experiencing their own patient care.

The same is true even for many people who eventually become doctors and nurses, as Grace Farris reminds us early on in her sensitive, energetic graphic memoir, See One, Do One, Teach One: The Art of Becoming a Doctor. "Before I started medical school," she writes, "I was completely unprepared." But, as she shows in her new book, once someone has switched over to becoming a professional healthcare worker, a whole new set of issues presents itself. At that point, it can be difficult to toggle from patient to patient — and to remember what it was even like to be the person receiving care.

toggle caption W. W. Norton & Company

In 2012, not too long after Farris completes her residency, she gives birth to her first child at a hospital in Boston where she works. Her years in medical school and after have already acquainted her with all parts of the birthing process, and her labor does not involve serious complications — but she still experiences a state of shock afterwards. She observes: "Becoming a patient made me want to rethink everything and reconsider my medical training. What had just happened?"

Sponsor Message

Farris, whose bio gives equal weight to her impressive accomplishments as both doctor and artist, skillfully guides readers on her long and winding medical school journey. While most people recognize that this process takes years and involves various stages, public knowledge of specifics is often oversimplified, overdramatized, or simply left mysterious. Farris brings readers behind the scenes, to help them develop a better understanding of all aspects of the experience — from anxiety over student loans and persistent bouts of impostor syndrome to friendships forged under stressful circumstances and the impossibility of a work-personal life balance. She takes us with her into her first-year anatomy class, where things go along relatively smoothly until, late in the semester, the bone saw is taken out. One of the students goes down, and the professor, without missing a beat, tells the class this is a "typical reaction." In another scene, Farris describes how medical students end up needing to learn more than 10,000 new words over the course of a year. In a series of illustrated flashcards depicting some of these new words and their meanings ("Necrosis," "Apoptosis"), we get a sense of just how intricate and overwhelming such an endeavor might feel.

toggle caption W. W. Norton & Company

Farris has a knack for breaking down the complexities of the medical school journey to make them accessible and direct, as in a full-page diagram she includes early on, titled, "The Path to Becoming a Doctor." Here, she maps out the assorted typical stages, from preclinical and clinical years to residency, fellowship, and attending. She plays with visual metaphors, too, throughout, in order to give a sense of the texture of certain feelings and experiences. Working in the emergency room for the first time during her internal medicine clerkship feels like encountering a tsunami, as classroom knowledge and limited clinical experiences are suddenly, and forcefully, put to the test. And later, when she's doing her medical internship, she suddenly begins to feel less like an impostor, likening the change to the slow, observable transformation of seasons. This reflective occasion is illustrated in a pair of bright images, a landscape of sturdy trees studded with golden leaves.

Sponsor Message

Farris' depictions — drawn in a loose, minimal style with a bright, colorful palette — offer generalities that seem relatable for those who have attended med school. They also contain peculiarities specific to her own personal history. Throughout her initial years of med school, even well into her clinical years, she does not know what type of medicine she wants to pursue. We act as witness as she comes to recognize the specializations that are definitely not for her (surgery, pediatrics), and those that could be (psychiatry, internal medicine). For Farris, it's a slow, anxiety-provoking, and ultimately fulfilling journey to figuring it all out.

Some of the most charming moments in the book occur when Farris recognizes how her artistic interests and her medical pursuits overlap. It's in dissecting an ear and encountering the tiniest bone in the human body that Farris undergoes a "turning point": "The tiny stapes was a miracle." Her artistic skills and sensitivities come into play at various stages of the learning process, like as a way to help her get better acquainted with human anatomy and also when she realizes that it helps to sketch and diagram the various materials that need to be memorized. The title of the book comes from a phrase one of her surgical rotation supervisors passes along, "a classic expression in medicine." The surgeon asks Farris to watch as the surgical site is sewn up, so she can do this final step of the procedure on her own next time around. "How on earth could I ever teach one?" Farris wonders of the final step in the phrase, after she watches and then attempts the skill on her own.

See One, Do One, Teach One joins a growing body of work often referred to as Graphic Medicine, the community and practice of using comics and illustration to support healthcare workers and patients in their efforts to tell stories that speak to all kinds of experiences. If it's too easy to forget — or too difficult to envision — what it's like to be a medical student, healthcare worker, or even a patient in certain situations, books like Farris' are an effective teaching tool. They offer an important, powerful way to bridge that gap.

World.title: Retaliation being considered if no deal reached by Trump's tariff deadline, Carney says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney says retaliatory measures are being considered if his government can't reach a deal with U.S. President Donald Trump before his new tariffs take effect.

"Everything is on the table depending on the outcome of the negotiations," Carney told reporters following a meeting with the 13 premiers in Charlottetown on Thursday.

Their face-to-face follows a threat from the White House to slap 50 per cent tariffs on billions of dollars' worth of Canadian imports come Aug. 19.

"If these tariffs or other measures come into force, there's a full range of things that we can do," said Carney.

WATCH | Carney on the 'opportunity' of the next few weeks: New tariff deadline 'creates an opportunity' to reach a comprehensive deal with U.S., Carney says | Duration 2:08 Asked whether the Aug. 19 tariff deadline is an opportunity to reach an end-game deal with the U.S. or a pressure tactic, Prime Minister Mark Carney said 'it's both.' Speaking at a press conference after meeting with Canada's premiers on Thursday, Carney said the U.S. has shown a level of engagement this week 'that reflects the seriousness of the trade relationship and the breadth of the issues.'

However, the prime minister wouldn't say what reprisals are in his back pocket, calling it "counterproductive" to talk retaliation with negotiations underway.

The agenda for meetings between the country's leaders this week in P.E.I. was upended on Monday when the White House announced the new tariffs, calling them a response to what it sees as Canadian discrimination against American motor vehicles, dairy and alcohol.

Carney said he sees this latest deadline as a real opportunity to reach a trade deal — while also agreeing it's a classic Trump pressure tactic.

"It's both," he said. But "there's a level of engagement and breadth of engagement that reflects the seriousness of the trade relationship."

WATCH | Carney responds to U.S. tariffs: 'Whatever it takes': Carney on Canada's response to U.S. tariffs | Duration 1:01 Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada isn’t leaving anything off the table when it comes to dealing with the U.S.’s incoming 50 per cent tariffs on goods covered by a North American trade deal. Carney made the remarks at the First Minister’s Meeting in Charlottetown, where Canada’s premiers are gathering to discuss how to respond to U.S. President Donald Trump’s threats.

The question of retribution had been a pressure point during the provincial and territorial leaders' annual summer get-together.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford has been advocating for a more aggressive approach, including withholding Canada's potash and oil to "dismantle" the United States.

"It's very hard to deal with President Trump when he changes his mind every single day," said Ford.

"One day, the prime minister is with him side by side, and the next thing you know, President Trump turns on him like a rabid dog."

Oil as leverage 'a very dumb decision': Smith

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith says she doesn't support retaliatory tariffs, especially when it comes to oil.

"I'm going to try to prevent Canada from making a very dumb decision of putting energy on the table because Line 5 goes through Michigan," she told CBC's Power & Politics, referring to the pipeline that moves around 540,000 barrels per day of oil and natural gas across the Canada-U.S. border.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith crosses her fingers while speaking with Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc, centre, and New Brunswick Premier Susan Holt prior to meeting with Carney. (Darren Calabrese/The Canadian Press)

"If you cut off energy to the United States, they can cut off Line 5 and cut off energy to Ontario and Quebec. So no aviation fuel, no diesel, no gasoline. And we don't want to do that," Smith said.

"I don't think you go into a negotiation promising to punch someone in the nose. You go into negotiation talking about a win-win."

Premiers insist on unity

Despite some disagreement emerging about how to negotiate, the premiers have been emphatic that they are united in a "Team Canada" approach to the trade war.

Carney didn't pass up an opportunity to use Charlottetown's history as the gathering spot for the Fathers of Confederation to make that point, recalling a time when "trade barriers were holding back economic growth, major infrastructure projects increasingly required co-operation across jurisdictions and the threat of American invasion loomed large.

"Plus ça change," he said to the premiers. "What the Fathers of our Confederation suspected then, we know acutely today: that our unity is our greatest strength, and that our destiny is in our hands."

The premiers, in a joint communiqué Wednesday, urged the Carney government "to maintain a clear, timely consultation process with provinces and territories during negotiations."

World.title: Parents in 'unimaginable pain' as search continues for 1 of 2 brothers in Nutimik Lake
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The parents of two young brothers who drowned in the fast-moving currents of eastern Manitoba's Nutimik Lake over the weekend say the only thing sustaining them through the "unimaginable" loss of their children is the outpouring of support from community.

Searchers found the body of Maximo Au Ramirez, 10, near the falls on Nutimik Lake Wednesday night, RCMP Staff Sgt. Cory Meyers said during a Thursday news conference.

"We're going through a terrible, horrible and unimaginable pain for our children," Meyers said, reading out a portion of a statement from the boys' parents, Haidee Ramirez and Roger Au.

"It's hard to understand how a community can be so strong for us and help us so much. The support from everyone is truly what is sustaining our family."

RCMP and volunteer crews continued the search Thursday for Maximo's 13-year-old brother, Aaron Au Ramirez.

The boys are believed to have drowned after Maximo slipped off rocks into the fast-moving water on Saturday, and Aaron went in to try to save him, RCMP previously said.

Meyers said crews found clothing on Monday believed to be Aaron's.

Manitoba RCMP say the body of 10-year-old Maximo Au Ramirez was recovered on Wednesday. The search for his 13-year-old brother, Aaron, continues. (Aaron Au Ramirez and Maximo Au Ramirez/GoFundMe)

He said a bout 20 boats with two to three volunteers per vessel joined an RCMP boat, dive team and drone unit, and the Hutterian Emergency Aquatic Response Team, or HEART, and others on the water as the search continued Thursday.

"We're kind of throwing everything we can ... at it," said Meyers.

The parents' statement said they have "so much gratitude" for people helping look for Aaron.

"This help is so overwhelming," Meyers read from their statement.

'We're not done': lodge owner

Allison Baker-Thiessen, who owns Nutimik Lodge with her husband, Harry Thiessen, said she got a call from one of the volunteer searchers around 7:30 p.m. Wednesday saying they had recovered a body.

"Both of us are definitely struggling," said Baker-Thiessen.

Two locals from Betula Lake, as well as one of the boys' uncles who just travelled from Mexico, were present for the recovery of Maximo, she said.

"It definitely gives a little bit of hope. We are happy that one of the two boys has shown up, but we're not done," she said.

"We want everybody there helping, supporting in different angles, whether it's jumping on boats, whether it's bringing your own boat. We need lots of eyes ... to help the family bring [Aaron] home."

Baker-Thiessen started a fundraiser on the website GoFundMe for the family this week. As of midday Thursday, it had raised nearly $63,000.

Cpl. Ryan Cadotte, program manager for the RCMP drone unit, pilots a drone on Thursday as the search continued for Aaron Au Ramirez. (Submitted by RCMP)

Cpl. Ryan Cadotte, program manager for the RCMP's drone unit, said the vehicles enable police to see a few feet deeper into the water than those searching in boats.

Cadotte is focusing on the area where Maximo was found, as well as shallows near shore in the area on Thursday.

This is the third Nutimik Lake search Cadotte has been part of since joining the RCMP drone unit since 2012.

"Unfortunately, these [drowning] incidents, for this particular falls, is not unique," he said.

Asked about safety concerns at the falls in Nutimik, Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew said the province has "a responsibility around keeping Manitobans safe."

"Our minister is looking at what the next steps are," Kinew said during a media call Thursday from Prince Edward Island, where he is attending the annual premiers' summit.

"What happened is just heartbreaking, and [for] any parent, the mind just races and the heart fills with compassion for these boys and for their family."

World.title: Trump says Saudi nuclear deal hinges on normalizing relations with Israel. Here's what we know
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump said Thursday a new agreement reached with Saudi Arabia for a civilian nuclear program will require the kingdom to normalize relations with Israel through the Abraham Accords , a move Saudi Arabia has long rejected.

Trump's comments come after U.S. and Saudi Arabia announced the agreement Wednesday, letting Riyadh enrich uranium and build nuclear reactors using U.S. technology, without requiring the snap United Nations inspections that Washington has demanded from Iran.

The move has alarmed some U.S. lawmakers and regional states concerned about weapons proliferation. Washington's top regional ally Israel, which has also repeatedly voiced opposition to the idea of a Saudi civil nuclear program, welcomed the prospect of Saudi Arabia joining the Abraham Accords — a series of diplomatic agreements first signed in 2020 t hat normalized relations between Israel and some Arab states.

Here's what we know about the deal, the concerns raised and what it could mean for the region.

What does the deal include?

The White House and Saudi Arabia have not made public the text of the nuclear co-operation agreement, known as a "123 agreement," alongside what the Trump administration described as a "bilateral safeguards agreement."

Under Section 123 of the U.S. Atomic Energy Act of 1954, the U.S. may negotiate agreements to engage in significant civil nuclear co-operation with other nations.

It specifies nine non-proliferation criteria those states must meet to keep them from using the technology to develop nuclear arms or transfer sensitive materials to others.

The announced deal was signed Wednesday by U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Saudi Minister of Energy Abdulaziz bin Salman.

The pact is expected to last 30 years and involve U.S. firms in the program's development — if passed by Congress.

Saudi's Energy Ministry on Wednesday said the agreement bolsters "efforts to diversify energy sources, advance cutting-edge technologies, and expand opportunities for co-operation and investment in ways that serve the mutual interests of the two friendly countries."

Why is uranium enrichment a key concern?

A key issue is whether Washington might agree to build a uranium enrichment facility on Saudi territory, when it might do so, and whether Saudi personnel might have access to it or it would be run solely by U.S. staff in a "black box" arrangement.

In a post on social media, Trump said the deal does not allow for enrichment of uranium.

Non-proliferation experts have raised concerns that the deal fails to include guardrails to prevent enrichment of uranium to weapons-grade levels.

WATCH | Why this nuclear deal is so significant: U.S. and Saudi Arabia sign landmark nuclear deal: Why it matters | Duration 4:05 The United States just struck a landmark nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia, marking a significant milestone in relations between the two countries. CBC’s Willy Lowry breaks down what it means, and why some experts are concerned.

Without rigorous safeguards built into an agreement, Saudi Arabia, which has uranium ore reserves on its territory, could theoretically use an enrichment facility to produce highly enriched uranium, which, if purified enough, can yield fissile material for bombs.

The agreement does not include the International Atomic Energy Agency's "additional protocol," which would allow for more monitoring, inspections and verification, according to a second person familiar with the decision who spoke with The Associated Press.

Deal hinges on Saudi acceptance of Abraham Accords

Trump said the agreement "will be approved, but is totally subject to Saudi Arabia joining the very respected and successful Abraham Accords."

White House ​press ⁠secretary ⁠Karoline ⁠Leavitt ⁠said later Thursday that the U.S. will continue conversations with Saudi Arabia.

The Saudis have made clear that normalizing relations with Israel would first require the establishment of a clear path for Palestinian statehood. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected the idea of Palestinian statehood as being untenable for his country's security.

The Saudi Embassy in Washington declined to comment Thursday on Trump's assertion the deal will require the kingdom to join the accords.

WATCH | From 2020, signing of the Abraham Accords:: Abraham Accords signed at the White House | Duration 2:39 Bahraini Foreign Minister Abdullatif Al Zayani, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, U.S. President Donald Trump and U.A.E. Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan participated in the signing of the Abraham Accords, normalizing relations between Israel and some of its Middle East neighbours.

Netanyahu's office in a statement applauded the prospect of Saudi Arabia joining the Abraham Accords as a "historic leap forward for peace in the Middle East." The statement made no mention of the deal to bolster Saudi's civil nuclear program.

Trump has sought to build on the 2020 agreements, which expanded the number of Arab and Muslim-majority nations with diplomatic ties with Israel. Saudi Arabia is the most important Arab power in the Middle East, and Trump believes the kingdom joining the accords is critical to establishing long-term stability in the region.

The aftermath of Israel's war in Gaza and the nearly five-month-old U.S. and Israel war against Iran have complicated Trump's push to expand the accords.

The agreements have proved unpopular among the public in certain signatory countries such as Morocco and Bahrain, sparking widespread protests.

Still, the Trump administration has made clear it remains optimistic an agreement with Saudi Arabia on joining the accords can be sealed by the end of Trump's second term.

Other countries pursued nuclear deal

Washington and Riyadh have for years been discussing a nuclear co-operation deal that would give Saudi Arabia access to U.S. technology and American companies a chance to win big contracts for Saudi atomic energy facilities.

Should the U.S.-Saudi pact fail, even at this late stage, several countries with established nuclear industries have expressed interest or are seen as potential partners for Saudi Arabia's nuclear program.

State-owned China National Nuclear Corp. reportedly submitted a bid in 2023 to construct a nuclear plant.

WATCH | Trump announces landmark deal with Saudi Arabia Wednesday: Trump approves nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia: report | Duration 7:03 U.S. President Donald Trump is reportedly set to announce a landmark 30-year civilian nuclear co-operation agreement with Saudi Arabia, which may allow the country to start enriching uranium.

Russia's state nuclear firm Rosatom, which built a nuclear plant in Egypt, has also signed preliminary co-operation agreements with Riyadh. Other potential contenders include South Korea, which built reactors in the neighbouring United Arab Emirates and France.

The choice of partner will likely depend on technological offerings, financing and geopolitical alignment, including conditions related to nuclear fuel handling.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters Thursday in Manila that the agreement would make certain that Saudi Arabia works with American companies instead of "competitors" to build its civil nuclear program.

What happens next?

The Trump administration said on Wednesday the deal has been submitted to Congress.

Lawmakers have 90 session days to prevent it from going into force, but only if they get the two-thirds majority to overcome any presidential veto.

United Nations nuclear watchdog, the International Atomic Energy Agency, said it is aware of a U.S.-Saudi plan to ask it to carry out verification work in relation to the nuclear co-operation deal they are discussing, but has yet to receive a request from them.

World.title: New La La Land poster addresses Ryan Gosling's gripe
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The upcoming 10th anniversary of Damien Chazelle's musical romantic-comedy La La Land has people talking. Not about the cinematography, the iconic ending or even that infamous Academy Awards fiasco .

They're talking about Ryan Gosling's wrist.

Ahead of a celebratory re-release that will hit theatres across the U.S. on Aug. 16, Lionsgate Studios unveiled a new La La Land poster addressing a detail that Gosling said "haunts" him.​

In a 2024 interview with the Wall Street Journal, the Canadian actor was asked if there was one role he would like a chance to do over. Gosling admitted he'd like another crack at his Oscar-nominated performance as jazz pianist Sebastian Wilder.

"I didn't know that this would become the poster for the movie," Gosling said, recalling a pivotal dance sequence alongside co-star Emma Stone overlooking a Los Angeles sunset.

"[Stone and I] were supposed to have our hands up, and I thought it would be cool to put my hand like that," he said, flattening an outstretched wrist with pointed fingers to a limper pose the interviewer referred to as "hamburger hands."

"Even though everyone told me it wasn't cool, I was sure that that was cooler than that," he continued, recreating both gestures. However, Gosling went on to say he now thinks the limper pose he struck "just killed the energy."

The new poster, which features an altered version of Gosling's pose that more closely resembles Stone's straight arm and hand, was accompanied by a winking press release where Lionsgate wrote, "Well, Ryan, you have been heard!"

Gosling's first attempt at revisionist history for the poster came earlier this year during the promotion for his sci-fi smash Project Hail Mary.

"This is my Hail Mary attempt to fix my ‘La La Hand,'" Gosling said in a clip posted to TikTok , before striking a straight-armed version of the pose alongside Rocky, his puppeteered alien co-star.

While unveiling the new poster, Justin Manfredi, executive vice-president of worldwide television marketing at Lionsgate, said that Gosling was "happy" when they consulted him about the change.

"We let him know and he approved it," Manfredi said at the promotional screening held at Los Angeles' Griffith Observatory, a key location in the film.

However, not everyone's as thrilled as Gosling.

"I got it tattooed the other way. So, respectfully, don't even," one user commented on Lionsgate's Instagram post announcing the altered poster. Other users on Instagram and TikTok expressed disappointment, arguing the mismatched poses better communicated the film's themes.

World.title: 'Challenging conditions' ahead for wildfires near Boston Bar, as evacuation orders, alerts issued across B.C.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

With hot, dry weather in the forecast and gusty winds expected in the Fraser Canyon, B.C. firefighting crews are gearing up for a difficult day battling the Boston Bar wildfire complex.

B.C. Wildfire Service (BCWS) information officer Morgan Blois said there are still some safe routes to leave the area, but that most communities are essentially "surrounded by wildfire."

Evacuation orders are in place and people have been told to leave immediately, although officials say some residents have chosen to stay.

"We're entering a period of really challenging conditions," Blois said Thursday.

She noted that a layer of smoke that had been moderating fire behaviour has lifted, and said there's potential for "extreme fire behaviour" to happen in the Fraser Canyon in the next 24 to 48 hours.

The three wildfires burning around Boston Bar — the Brunswick Creek, Ainslie Creek and Anderson Creek fires — in total make up about 277.7 square kilometres (27,771 hectares), although Blois noted smoke Wednesday had made it difficult for aviation crews to get an updated look at the size.

Blois said there is a worry that the Anderson Creek and Ainslie Creek fires could join together.

"With the aggressive fire behavior that we're seeing and the rate of spread that we've been seeing in the last few days, it is a big concern."

One of three wildfires burning near Boston Bar, B.C., can be seen in this photo taken by resident Attila Banhegyi on the night of July 21. (Submitted by Attila Banhegyi)

She stressed that people who aren't evacuating in the communities under order impede BCWS operations, as crews then dedicate resources to public safety that should be focused on structure protection and preventing further wildfire spread.

Highway 1 remains closed in both directions between Spuzzum Creek Road and Jackass Summit due to the wildfire, according to DriveBC.

Motorists are recommended to use Highway 5 as an alternate route.

More evacuation orders, alerts around B.C.

Elsewhere in B.C., evacuation orders and alerts are also in place .

B.C.'s Ministry of Emergency Management said approximately 640 properties were under order and about 6,600 were under alert as of 10:50 a.m. PT on Thursday, due to wildfires.

Of those under order, about 420 properties were in the Boston Bar region, and another 180 were in Thompson-Nicola Regional District due to the Fiftynine Creek wildfire, according to the ministry.

The majority of the properties under alert were in the Kimberley area in southeast B.C. due to the Matthew Creek wildfire, the province said. Residents under evacuation alert must be prepared to leave on short notice.

The province noted the numbers are considered approximate as conditions evolve.

Orders and alerts have been issued by the Squamish-Lillooet Regional District, the Thompson-Nicola Regional District, the Cariboo Regional District, the Fraser Valley Regional District and the Regional District of East Kootenay.

Patricia Ross, board chair of the Fraser Valley Regional District, said the Anderson Creek fire "blew up really quickly" Tuesday night, quadrupling in size on Wednesday.

"I've been on council for 32 years now, and I have never seen fires like this in our area before," she said.

She said the majority of residents affected by the orders have left.

"We really appreciate those people; we know how hard it is to leave their home — but you're actually helping the firefighters on the ground when you leave."

EmergencyInfoBC lists current emergencies by last updated date.

There are more than 80 active wildfires burning across the province.

World.title: University of Toronto mathematician Jacob Tsimerman wins Fields Medal
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

University of Toronto math professor Jacob Tsimerman has won a 2026 Fields Medal, the top global honour in mathematics.

He's the first mathematician based at a Canadian institution to win the award and the second Canadian. Manjul Bhargava, who is Canadian but based at Princeton University, won the award in 2014.

Tsimerman accepted the award at the International Mathematical Congress in Philadelphia on Thursday.

"It's a big honour, obviously, getting this award for me and my collaborators, who I'm very happy are being recognized, as well," he said.

Tsimerman stressed the importance of collaboration in mathematics in a video shown at the ceremony that also describes the work for which he's being recognized.

WATCH | Tsimerman and his work:

Tsimerman won for his contribution "in the recasting of o-minimality as a fundamental method of arithmetic and complex algebraic geometry," said organizers, and for his role "in the proof of many central conjectures, including Griffiths' conjecture on the algebraicity of images of the period maps, and the Andre-Oort conjecture for Siegel modular varieties."

Adam Stinchcombe, a colleague and an associate professor of mathematics at the University of Toronto, said in order to come up with those proofs, Tsimerman developed new techniques that "can be used in other areas of math."

The medal and a cash prize are awarded to four mathematicians under 40 every four years by a committee of the International Mathematical Union. This year's other winners were Yu Deng of the University of Chicago, John Pardon of Stony Brook University and Hong Wang of New York University.

The awards are named after Canadian mathematician John Charles Fields and funded by a trust he established at the University of Toronto.

World.title: Mexican authorities probe alleged scam that wiped out Canadian couple’s retirement savings
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Mexican authorities are probing an alleged condo fraud scheme in the tourist hot spot state of Quintana Roo that wiped out a Canadian couple’s retirement savings.

The couple, Cindy Thompson and Glenn Brown of Curve Lake, Ont., sent $280,000 Cdn to a company co-owned by a British and Mexican national who promised big returns on a condo-flip play in Playa del Carmen that never materialized.

Thompson and Brown’s money vanished, along with their retirement plans.

"I’m just overwhelmed by it all," said Thompson, 62.

"We’ll have to work until we die," said Brown, 63.

While the couple hired a local lawyer who filed a criminal complaint, the case seemed to flounder until CBC News raised the issue with Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum during one of her morning press conferences in late June.

"We’ll look at this particular case that’s [been] raised, but we can say that there is legal certainty, and when there is a problem, for sure, we deal with it," said Sheinbaum.

Within hours, Quintana Roo Gov. Mara Lezama’s administration took up the case. The investigation is now led by Rogelio Estrada Heleria, state deputy prosecutor for the central district. Estrada Heleria did not respond to a CBC News request for comment.

Looking for investment opportunity

The case stems from late 2024 when Thompson, searching the internet for possible real estate investments in Mexico, came across the webpage for XMEX Investments, which was run by a British national named Harry Robinson.

Robinson bills himself as "Licensed in Wealth Building & Financial Services, Mortgage Broking [sic] & Real Estate," according to the XMEX website.

Harry Robinson bills himself as 'Licensed in Wealth Building & Financial Services, Mortgage Broking [sic] & Real Estate,' according to the XMEX Investments website. (Harry Robinson/Facebook)

CBC News contacted Robinson, who turned down a request for an interview.

"Unfortunately this matter is ongoing through the legal system here in Mexico and I can not make any comment at this time until we have a resolution in the courts," said Robinson, in a WhatsApp message to CBC News.

Thompson said she noticed that "bank-owned" properties — that is, properties repossessed by banks — on the XMEX site were advertised for 30 per cent or more below market value.

"So when I started to look at the individual properties, I thought, hey, this sounds like a really good opportunity, and I wonder who this guy is," said Thompson.

Thompson said she checked into XMEX Investments, saw it was registered in Florida, and believed Robinson was a legitimate businessman.

She reached out to Robinson, who called her back. They spoke multiple times over the course of a couple of weeks before she travelled to Playa del Carmen in October 2024 for a face-to-face meeting.

Thompson, who travelled with her sister, said Robinson introduced them to his business partner, a Mexican national named Jacqueline Herrera Herrera. The two were co-owners of another company called Xen Investments, which is registered in Mexico, according to records.

"He said that he had partnered with Jackie … and that she’s … a well-known lawyer, a well-respected lawyer, and a realtor," said Thompson.

"We had about an hour, an hour and a half conversation, and got to meet them all."

During the conversation, Herrera pitched a one-bedroom condo for sale in a Playa del Carmen building called Taak Maya. Thompson's plan was to live there for a while but eventually sell it.

The Taak Maya condo building in Playa del Carmen was used as part of an alleged fraud scheme now under investigation by Mexican authorities. (Gustavo Huerta/CBC)

Robinson took Thompson to the building, but she couldn't get in to see the condo unit, because Robinson said they didn't have the key.

Still, Thompson sent two installments — in November and December 2024 — totalling $170,000 Cdn to purchase the condo to an HSBC bank account in Mexico connected to Xen Investments.

The purchase agreement was printed on Xen Investments letterhead and signed by Robinson, according to a copy Thompson provided to CBC News.

"I was told that I’d have the keys within two to three months," Thompson said.

She never saw the keys.

'It hurts all of us'

Mexico loses an estimated $48 million Cdn every year to real estate scams, according to the Mexican Association of Real Estate Professionals.

Wilberth José Gutiérrez Álvarez, president of a separate group called the Mexican Association of the Real Estate Industry, said that the government of Quintana Roo is slowly tightening its regulations around the real estate industry.

Gutiérrez Álvarez said the state government has created a database for licensed real estate agents and firms, along with a registry for realtors who have been sanctioned. However, one can still do real estate business in Quintana Roo without registering for the database.

"There are real estate professionals that know how to do things well, that you can have legal certainty with," he said. "You just have to know who to go to, and sometimes this lack of information is what generates this kind of problem."

Winnipeg native Jason Waller has lived and worked in Mexico for 21 years and is CEO of Christie's International Real Estate Mexico Luxury Properties. He said the safest bet in buying property in Mexico is to go with an established real estate brand. (Tania Miranda Perez/CBC)

Winnipeg native Jason Waller has lived and worked in Mexico for 21 years and is CEO of Christie's International Real Estate Mexico Luxury Properties. He said the safest bet in buying property in Mexico is to go with an established real estate brand.

"You need someone on the ground that you can trust, that can hold your hand and help you through it," said Waller, who lives in Puerto Aventuras, Quintana Roo.

"When you’re a legitimate business and you’re trying to do the right things and then somebody else is giving the area a bad name, it hurts all of us that are trying to do things the right way."

'Lie after lie'

While Thompson waited for her condo keys in late 2024 and early 2025, Robinson suggested she join his sales team. He shared leads and property listings, but nothing came of it, Thompson said.

She decided to return to Playa del Carmen in March 2025 to take possession of the condo, but Robinson and Herrera said they couldn’t hand over the keys because there were still some outstanding parts in the process.

"We should be able to get the keys, Jackie’s hoping, in the next few weeks," Robinson told Thompson in a March 3, 2025, WhatsApp voice message, which she provided to CBC News.

"So all good news other than the fact that, you know, it’s a small delay and you won’t be able to actually stay there this trip, but everything’s good."

Then Robinson told her that Herrera had scored an even better deal. He said Thompson's $170,000 investment could go toward a seven-condo purchase in the Taak Maya building in Playa del Carmen that promised a big payout.

In a WhatsApp voice message, Robinson said that they would be buying the seven units for $100,000 US each and then flipping them for $250,000.

"It’s looking like it’s going to be 100 per cent profit," Robinson said in the message.

Thompson’s partner, Brown, then put $110,000 Cdn from his retirement savings into the pot. Brown had a "share purchase agreement" with Xen Investments signed by Robinson and the money went into an HSBC account in Mexico under the company’s name.

But then Robinson told Thompson that Herrera told him one of the investors had died, and that they needed to find someone else to cover the shortfall.

The deal never materialized and the money vanished.

Jacqueline Herrera Herrera was co-owner of a company called Xen Investments, which is registered in Mexico. Herrera pitched the sale of a condo to Cindy Thompson. (Jacqueline Herrera Herrera/Facebook)

"It was lie after lie after lie," said Thompson.

In a July 26, 2025, WhatsApp message to Thompson, Robinson claimed Herrera "was in control of that money 100 per cent" and that "as soon as it hit Xen's bank account … she took it out" for herself.

CBC News could not reach Herrera for comment.

In late May, Herrera messaged Thompson over WhatsApp saying she was in the United Arab Emirates and was "doing everything to return the money" and that Thompson would have it by "July."

Robinson filed a criminal complaint in Mexico against Herrera in fall 2025, claiming he had also been duped.

Meanwhile, Thompson and Brown’s criminal complaint names both Robinson and Herrera.

"It is devastating. I don’t think of anything else," said Thompson. "I’m angry, I feel foolish, frustrated."
