World.title: Armenian rights lawyer files ECHR complaint over Ruben Vardanyan’s 20-year jail sentence in Baku
World.content:
ECHR complaint over Vardanyan case

Human rights lawyer Siranush Sahakyan has filed a complaint with the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) over the case of Ruben Vardanyan, the former state minister of the former unrecognised Nagorno-Karabakh Republic. She said she would represent Vardanyan before the court. Sahakyan has represented Armenian detainees at the ECHR for many years.

“The application sets out in detail violations of eight articles of the European Convention on Human Rights, supported by comprehensive legal and factual arguments,” Sahakyan said in a statement shared with the media and posted on social media.

Vardanyan is one of 19 Armenians still held in Azerbaijani prisons. In February 2026, a military court in Baku sentenced him to 20 years in prison.

According to Sahakyan, the defence was only recently able to obtain the court’s written judgment, which was required before an application could be submitted to the ECHR. She said Azerbaijan had withheld the ruling until then, which is why the complaint was filed only on 19 July.

The court found Vardanyan guilty of a number of serious offences, including waging war, financing terrorism and deportation.

Armenian rights groups, however, have described the trial in Baku as “political rather than legal”. Vardanyan himself called the proceedings “a farce” and “a mockery of justice”. During the hearings, he instructed his lawyer not to present arguments in his defence.

“It is impossible to protect rights in a system that fundamentally denies the right to a fair trial. That is why Ruben Vardanyan decided to continue his fight for justice through international legal mechanisms,” Sahakyan said.

Details of Vardanyan case

In her statement, Sahakyan disclosed further details of the case. She said the military court in Baku did not read out the full verdict. Now that Vardanyan’s family has passed the written judgment to his lawyers, it has become clear that he was convicted on 41 counts under 21 articles of Azerbaijan’s Criminal Code.

According to Sahakyan, the judgment does not substantiate Vardanyan’s personal criminal responsibility with facts or evidence.

“Instead, the court concluded that the ‘criminal organisation’ – the leadership of the self-proclaimed Republic of Artsakh – had been operating in Nagorno-Karabakh since 1988. It also found that Vardanyan joined this ‘organisation’ in December 2020, although he was living in Moscow at the time.”

She also said the court treated Vardanyan’s appointment to a civilian administrative post as a violent seizure of power. His commercial and charitable activities were classified as illegal entrepreneurship and financing terrorism, while his entry into Nagorno-Karabakh via the Lachin Corridor was deemed an illegal crossing of Azerbaijan‘s state border.

Sahakyan said Vardanyan had not appealed against the verdict because he regarded the trial as staged and pre-planned, and considered all domestic legal remedies ineffective.

Background

On 17 February, a military court in Baku sentenced Russian-Armenian businessman, billionaire and philanthropist Ruben Vardanyan to 20 years in prison. His case was heard separately from those of the former leadership of Nagorno-Karabakh.

A month after the verdict, Vardanyan’s family said he had tried to raise concerns with Azerbaijan’s Human Rights Commissioner, Sabina Aliyeva, during a phone call with relatives, but the call was cut off.

The family has repeatedly appealed to the international community, saying that neither Vardanyan nor the other Armenian detainees in Azerbaijan have access to institutional protection. They argue that the country lacks independent human rights protection mechanisms. They have also noted that the International Committee of the Red Cross, which had facilitated contact between detainees and their families, has ceased operations in Azerbaijan.

On 5 February, two weeks before Vardanyan’s sentence was announced, an Azerbaijani court handed life sentences to several other former Nagorno-Karabakh leaders, including former President Arayik Harutyunyan, former Defence Army commander Levon Mnatsakanyan, his deputy Davit Manukyan, former parliament speaker Davit Ishkhanyan and former Foreign Minister Davit Babayan. Former presidents Arkady Ghukasyan and Bako Sahakyan were sentenced to 20 years in prison.

All of the detainees faced a range of serious charges, including terrorism and genocide. Ghukasyan and Sahakyan received lighter sentences because they are over 65, and Azerbaijani law does not allow life imprisonment for people above that age.

Independent media and human rights observers were not allowed to attend the trials. Information about the proceedings was published by Azerbaijani state and pro-government media.

World.title: One minor killed, three injured in shooting in central Tbilisi
World.content:
Shooting in central Tbilisi

Late on July 22, four people, including two minors, were injured in a shooting on Vera, a central street in Tbilisi. All were taken to hospital. One of the minors died shortly after being admitted, Irakli Pirtskhalaishvili, a doctor at the clinic, told reporters.

Georgia’s Interior Ministry confirmed the incident, saying one person had been arrested in connection with it. The suspect has been charged with using a firearm and wounding four people.

He attempted to flee the scene but was detained after a police chase. According to the ministry, the suspect resisted arrest with a weapon and “sustained finger injuries during the arrest.”

The investigation is being conducted under Articles 19 and 109 of Georgia’s Criminal Code (attempted murder), which carry a penalty of up to 20 years in prison or life imprisonment.

Many witnesses to the shooting: what they say

The shooting took place in central Tbilisi, at the intersection of Akaki Shanidze and Akaki Khorava streets. The area was crowded at the time of the incident.

Eyewitness Elene Koridze wrote on social media that three young men sitting in a car “were shot simply because they were laughing.”

“About an hour ago, right outside my home, a man opened fire on three 17- and 18-year-old boys sitting in a car simply because they were laughing. He then also shot a woman who was nearby. He was quickly apprehended.

It was clear this was neither a premeditated attack nor an act of personal revenge. This is not just an isolated serious crime to which the police responded quickly, but a direct reflection of the reality we live in,” Koridze wrote.

Another eyewitness, Tiko Kvaliashvili, said:

“I was walking home when I saw a crowd on Shanidze Street and went over. Two patrol cars arrived, people started shouting, and someone was running. One boy was unconscious in the car, while two others were in shock. I gave them first aid as best I could. One had been shot in the arm, the other in the shoulder. I don’t know why they were shot.”

The son of journalist Eka Kvesitadze also witnessed the incident. She said it happened near their home while her son was out walking the dog.

“Someone had shot several minors. They were lying there covered in blood,” another witness wrote.

Witnesses also told reporters that a nearby parked red Alfa Romeo had around a dozen bullet holes.

As of now, Interior Ministry has not released any additional details.

World.title: Pro-EU protester Onise Okriashvili attacked in Tbilisi after disinformation campaign
World.content:
Georgia protester Onise Okriashvili beaten

Stand-up comedian Onise Okriashvili, an active participant in Georgia’s pro-European protests that have been ongoing for nearly two years, was brutally beaten by three people late on July 22 outside his home in Tbilisi’s Vake district.

Before the attack, Okriashvili had become the target of a disinformation campaign by pro-government media. Based on the context of the attack, this appears to have been the reason behind the assault.

A video of the attack, recorded by eyewitnesses, has spread on social media.

The footage shows three young men brutally beating Onise. “You insulted Nodar Dumbadze (a classic of Georgian literature), how dare you, bastard?” the attackers are heard saying to him.

Onise Okriashvili can be heard calling for help. Several people are nearby, but they do not dare approach him. The desperate screams of a woman trying to stop the attackers can also be heard.

Who is Onise Okriashvili and why did he become a target of propaganda?

Onise Okriashvili is known for his criticism of the ruling Georgian Dream party on social media. He also regularly organises solo protests aimed at drawing public attention — appearing with relevant posters in places where large numbers of people gather, including on public transport.

“Only their children study in Europe” — reads the sign held by Onise Okriashvili during one of his solo protests. Photo from the activist’s social media page

In recent days, the activist has become the target of a disinformation campaign by pro-government TV channels. They have repeatedly aired a fragment from a comedy show Punchline Therapy, in which he uses a vulgar expression while referring to Nodar Dumbadze, a classic of Georgian literature.

The fragment was shown without context, making it appear as if Okriashvili was directly insulting the writer.

On July 19, the comedian recorded a video in which he said:

“I apologise that in this video I am not talking about more important events in the country. Young people my age are dying every day because of drug use; there are political prisoners in the country; emigration is sharply increasing, and these emigrants have been deprived of the right to vote in elections, along with many other problems.

But for the third day now, Georgian Dream’s propaganda machine has been using all its resources to turn people against me. Here is an example of the video they are using to try to discredit me.“

The conversation in the video excerpt goes:

‘Is there someone you cannot stand?’ ‘What if I say Nodar Dumbadze? (vulgar expression) I will only name our government, no one else.’

“During a performance, we speak hypothetically and can say the most absurd thing that comes to mind at that moment.

This video clearly shows that I am, of course, not insulting (Nodar Dumbadze), but speaking only hypothetically, deliberately using the most absurd example that came to mind at that moment. Comedy often works exactly this way — it uses unexpected twists. That is why the audience laughs at that moment.”

“Just today we were discussing filing a lawsuit against the propaganda media for spreading defamatory claims, and today Onise was attacked,” his wife, Mariam Samushia, told journalists.

She said she heard shouting in the street in the evening. Since Onise had become a target of a propaganda campaign in recent days, she called him to warn him. Only later did she realise that her husband had been attacked.

“This is artificially created hatred,” she said.

The Interior Ministry said a criminal case had been opened over the attack on Onise Okriashvili under Article 126 of Georgia’s Criminal Code (violence). According to reports, one of the attackers has been taken to a police station and is being questioned.

News in Georgia

World.title: Chechnya’s recruitment machine: How Kadyrov sustains his forces by enlisting civilians
World.content:
Kadyrov’s Forces in Ukraine

An investigation by Novaya Gazeta Europe shows how the war has reshaped the system of power in Chechnya.

Ramzan Kadyrov has significantly expanded the number of armed units under his control. But his most loyal formations are largely kept away from the front lines.

Instead, combat losses are replenished with ordinary residents of the republic, who are often pressured into signing military contracts.

For the investigation, journalists interviewed 178 Chechen families who lost relatives in the war, as well as current and former servicemen. Their reporting examines how Chechnya’s recruitment system operates and reveals the true scale of its wartime losses.

Kadyrov’s forces

Over the course of the war, five new regiments and five battalions have been established in Chechnya. Formally, they are part of Russia’s Defense Ministry and the National Guard. In practice, however, Kadyrov determines key personnel appointments, where the units are deployed and how extensively they are involved in combat.

According to figures provided by Kadyrov, the number of security personnel in Chechnya has grown from 4,800 in 2003 to 36,243 today. At the start of 2022, before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, those forces numbered roughly 16,000 to 18,000. That means Chechnya’s security apparatus has approximately doubled in size over the course of the three-year war.

The human rights group Memorial argues that the expansion amounts to the strengthening of Kadyrov’s personal army. But a source in Chechnya’s regional office of the Federal Security Service offered a different explanation. According to the source, Kadyrov became trapped by the image of being “Putin’s chief foot soldier.” While he continued to create new units, he also sought to shield his most loyal security personnel from frontline combat.

At first, the authorities attracted recruits with high salaries. They then began actively recruiting people from other parts of Russia. Later, military service was opened to unemployed residents of Chechnya. As the flow of volunteers dwindled, the authorities increasingly turned to coercion.

The safe rear ended in the Kursk region

In 2023, Kadyrov secured the deployment of several Chechen units to the Russian border regions of Bryansk, Kursk and Belgorod. At the time, these areas were considered relatively safe rear positions, allowing Kadyrov’s forces to be pulled back from the most intense sections of the front.

That changed on Aug. 6, 2024, when Ukrainian troops crossed into the Kursk region. The Akhmat-Chechnya Regiment, which had been guarding the border, offered little visible resistance. Its personnel abandoned their positions, and some were surrounded and taken prisoner.

The border regions subsequently became the scene of heavy fighting involving the Akhmat special forces, the West Akhmat Battalion and the Akhmat-Chechnya Regiment. One Akhmat commander claimed that Apti Alaudinov’s unit alone suffered more than 1,500 killed and wounded.

Security forces are shielded, civilians sent to the front

After the fighting in the Kursk region, Kadyrov moved to reduce the involvement of key National Guard units in the war. Much of the burden was shifted instead to formations under Russia’s Defense Ministry.

Sources interviewed by the publication say the decision was driven by the need to preserve the foundations of Kadyrov’s rule. His grip on power depends on the loyalty of the republic’s security forces. A prolonged war depletes that resource faster than the Chechen leadership can replace it.

A telling example is the National Guard’s Baysangur Benoevsky Battalion. It is overseen by Adam Kadyrov, the 18-year-old son and presumed heir of the Chechen leader. The battalion has been equipped with modern weapons, its own training ground and a well-funded infrastructure. Its personnel signed contracts that предусматривают service in the war. Yet the unit has remained almost entirely in Chechnya, where it focuses on training.

Another National Guard unit, the Sheikh Mansur Battalion, was deployed to the front in December 2023 and has been engaged in combat ever since.

According to the investigation, the Baysangur Battalion is effectively financed with federal funds allocated for the war while serving as the Kadyrov family’s personal security reserve.

Coerced recruitment

Since the autumn of 2024, the Chechen authorities have carried out a large-scale campaign of forced recruitment. Kadyrov publicly proposed sending what he called “troubled youth” to the front. District police departments were then assigned monthly recruitment quotas of between 25 and 50 people.

Those detained are taken to collection centers in Sernovodsk and at the Khankala military base. According to testimonies from recruits and their relatives, they are held under guard, given inadequate food and receive little to no military training. Some are sent without proper uniforms or equipment, receiving weapons only after they reach the front.

People can be sent to the front for reasons as minor as a street fight, a traffic violation, driving without insurance, tinted car windows or unpaid utility bills. Others are detained for subscribing to opposition channels or for political posts found on their phones. In some cases, relatives are offered the chance to pay for a detainee’s release or to find other “volunteers” to take their place.

According to the journalists’ estimates, 67 such raids were carried out across Chechnya between October 2024 and May 2025.

Hidden casualties

The Chechen authorities prohibit the publication of information about those killed in the war. Families are often instructed to bury relatives at night and to forgo the traditional multi-day mourning rituals. As a result, publicly available casualty lists capture only a fraction of the true death toll.

Officially, around 500 residents of Chechnya have been confirmed killed. But a source in the republic’s government told the investigators that more than 2,300 deaths have been verified internally. Another roughly 1,000 people are listed as missing in action.

Of the 183 fatalities documented by the journalists, 113 were sent to the war after October 2024. Of those, 97 had signed military contracts under coercion. The average time between deployment and death was about two months. Only 84 of the 178 families interviewed were able to recover and bury the bodies of their relatives.

The investigation identifies a fundamental shift in Kadyrov’s approach. At the start of the war, he deployed members of the security forces while portraying those forcibly recruited as volunteers. Now, his most loyal units are kept inside Chechnya, while civilians are openly treated as expendable manpower.

The authors argue that this marks a troubling precedent. Repressive practices first tested in Chechnya have often, over time, spread to the rest of Russia.

World.title: History beckons as Stingers, Sharks surge into water polo semifinals
World.content:
It's been 26 years since Australia and the USA paved new ground for women's water polo, contesting the gold medal match at the Sydney Olympics.

Now, in the same pool used in those Games, the Stingers and the USA will meet once more, this time in a semifinal of the World Cup Finals.

"The moment's not lost on us," Australian skipper Bronte Halligan told ABC Sport.

"I hadn't made that connection yet, that the Aussie girls played the US in the final [at the Sydney 2000 Olympics], but now you've mentioned it, that is another thing.

"But no, it's not lost on us.

"Any game's an important game and a semi's a semi; you win, or you lose, and we're going to go in there and battle our little butts off and see what we can do, and then hopefully produce a really good result."

Australia's women's water polo team fought for the sport's inclusion in the Games, then won gold. (Getty Images: Martin Rose/Bongarts)

The Sydney Olympics water polo tournament was a groundbreaking one for the sport in so many ways.

For a start, it was the first to ever feature a women's competition, despite women competing at World Championships since 1986 and in World Cup competitions since 1979.

Australia's women were pivotal in getting water polo included, with player Liz Weekes threatening legal action if women weren't included and some 50 players protesting at Sydney Airport in 1997 when the president of World Aquatics, then known as FINA, arrived in the city.

Those players were vindicated and their dream realised, women finally permitted to play Olympic water polo — the oldest team sport at the Games.

Australia and the USA made it to the final of the six-team competition, playing out a thrilling final in front of 17,000 supporters at the Sydney Olympic Park Aquatic Centre.

And it was the Stingers who came out on top, winning 4-3 after a last-second goal to Yvette Higgins.

A four-year-old Halligan attended those Games, although the now 29-year-old was not among the thousands who were there for that historic final.

The Stingers are leading the way into the semifinal. (Getty Images: Andy Cheung)

But now she and her Stingers teammates have an opportunity to repeat history.

And not just history from a quarter of a century ago either — these two teams met in the semifinal of the Olympics in Paris too, the Aussies winning 14-13 after a heart-stopping penalty shootout.

The 'precious' bond driving the Stingers to success Australia's women's water polo team, the Stingers, were the most successful Australian team at the Paris Olympics, winning a stunning silver medal. This is the secret to their success.

That victory saw the Stingers progress to the final, where they fell agonisingly short of a gold medal against Spain.

The USA and Australia have continued to cross paths though — it was against the USA that the Stingers had a pre-tournament training camp last week in Brisbane.

"We know them as a team. We know them as a squad," Halligan said.

"They're a bunch of phenomenal athletes; they're really tough opponents.

"We're lucky to have trained against them last week; we can kind of foresee what we're coming up against, but it's not going to be an easy game, and we've got to just stay united."

Bronte Halligan played her 200th match for Australia in the quarterfinal victory over Italy. (Getty Images: Andy Cheung)

To Halligan, who spent most of the 5am training sessions from the age of 14 at the Sydney Olympic Park Aquatic Centre, this pool feels like home, which made the fact that she marked her 200th international appearance with a dramatic 15-14 win over Italy.

"It kind of all just fell into place," Halligan said.

"It became this really special moment here in Sydney, in a pool that I grew up training in and with my family and friends at a huge event in a World Cup quarterfinal.

"It just was kind of almost picture perfect.

"I just feel lucky that it all kind of fell into place and this is what happened."

Gabi Palm was named player of the match against Italy. (Getty Images: Andy Cheung)

Halligan noted how special it was to see some of her former teammates and trailblazers in the stands — and that is exactly what the USA felt too.

The USA powered into the semifinal with a dominant 14-8 against China on Wednesday after meeting with some of their silver medallists from those 2000 Games.

"We heard from some of the players last night, and that was so amazing. Just taking us back, and learning our history," said 20-year-old USA driver Emily Ausmus, who scored four goals in that game.

"It was so cool to see the women before you that paved the path, and that got women's water polo into the Olympics.

"It's so cool that we're in the same venue; it's still so beautiful."

Emily Ausmus scored four goals for the USA in their quarterfinal victory. (Getty Images: Andy Cheung)

Beautiful and set to be packed for another massive Australian-USA clash.

"It's so important to have all the friends and family here, and especially the Stingers alumni," Halligan said.

"They've paved the way for us and a bunch of them have played with us; I saw a bunch of my ex-teammates here in the stands, and they're so special because they all have touched our careers.

"We just feel fortunate to be able to play a big game like this and play it here in Sydney."

Sharks 'showed we belong', stun champions Spain

The Aussies are making a habit of shocking the world's best. (Supplied: World Aquatics)

On Thursday night, the Aussie Sharks also channelled the class of 2000, stunning reigning world champions Spain in a thrilling penalty shoot-out.

Australia were four goals down at one stage of the match, trailed 6-3 at quarter time, 16-13 at three-quarter time and 18-16 with 40 seconds to play.

However, the side fought back incredibly to level the scores late on at 18-18.

And, on a night of extraordinary drama at the Sydney Olympic pool, the Sharks had to equalise twice inside the final 10 seconds.

Marcus Berehulak, bandaged after being opened up by a stray Spanish fist in the first half, thought he had scored the leveller with six seconds to play, only for it to be taken off him by the referees for taking a free throw inside the six metres zone.

Marcus Berehulak scored what he thought was the equalising goal. (Supplied: World Aquatics)

As the parochial Sydney crowd booed the decision, the Aussies kept their heads as they were told to replay the final 7.9 seconds.

With the Sharks keeper up to create an extra man, Matthew Burns powered home the actual leveller at the near post with 1.1 seconds to play to set up penalties.

Substitute keeper Laurence Barker saved from Fran Valera in the shoot-out, while Australia slotted all five of their penalty shots to claim a 23-21 victory.

The victory was fitting for an Australian team that have embraced the underdog tag but, just as they did in Paris against Serbia, stunned the favourites with a never-say-die display of pure grit.

"Congratulations to Spain," player of the match Jacob Mercep, who led the Sharks with six goals, said.

"They had us in the first half, but we were able to come back.

"We were kind of manifesting this semifinal; we've been talking about it all winter.

"When it matters the most, we showed we belong."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Berehulak scored four, Matthew Byrnes — who slotted the final penalty — scored three, while veteran Blake Edwards added two.

"I got stitched up, and I'm glad I came back out there because that win was incredible … nothing like I've felt before," Berehulak said.

"Spain is a fantastic team, but I think we really stayed composed. We had a game plan that we stuck to, and we just kept chipping away.

"Having that crowd, and being able to deliver a performance against the current world champions — it tops my number one water polo memory of all time."

Captain Nathan Power, Charlie Negus and Nicolas Constantin Bicari all scored one each.

World.title: Breaking: US confirms new 12.5pc tariff for Australia
World.content:
The Trump administration has confirmed a 12.5 per cent tariff will be placed on Australian exports to the US from later today (AEST).

The tariff was proposed last month, after a US trade investigation into forced labour.

The Australian government and Business Council of Australia made formal submissions opposing the tariff during a consultation period, which ended earlier this month.

The US Trade Representative (USTR) has now announced the proposed tariff will take effect from 12:01am Friday, local time (2:01pm Friday AEST).

A temporary 10 per cent "global tariff" on the US's trading partners, including Australia, will expire at the same time.

Australia is not the only affected country. Tariffs between 10 and 12.5 per cent will be placed on imports from 59 other economies, which represent all of the US's major trading partners.

World.title: Why this is the most interesting Western Derby in a decade
World.content:
Fremantle is storming towards a historic AFL campaign.

Never has the club won more than 17 games during a regular season, and never has it finished a season with a higher percentage than it currently boasts.

Even in 2015, when Fremantle won those 17 games, drew one and finished top of the ladder, Ross Lyon's charges only had a percentage of 118.

The Dockers have won 16 games so far this season. (AAP: Richard Wainwright)

This season, Justin Longmuir's side sits on 142 per cent with five games to play.

In tonight's Western Derby against West Coast, the Dockers could match their best-ever return and set up a comfortable run into finals.

A victory would see them remain at least three games clear at the top of the ladder with four matches to play, meaning they would need to win just one of their remaining games to clinch top spot.

Ross Lyon's Fremantle has a better percentage than the club's 2015 version that won 17 games. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

It's an enviable position, but after a barnstorming run of 14 wins in a row, recent weeks have shown sides are starting to get a handle on the Dockers.

Fremantle has lost four of its past five first halves, though it has gone on to win all bar one of those matches.

Quality talls the key for Freo Fremantle has lost its 14-game winning streak with a loss to GWS, but what are the keys for the Dockers to keep going and set up a tilt at their first flag? Cody Atkinson and Sean Lawson investigate.

It's something Longmuir is acutely aware needs monitoring, but otherwise there's little reason to panic.

His side boasts the stingiest defence in the league while also being the third-highest scoring.

The three-headed dragon of Jye Amiss, Josh Treacy and Patrick Voss has kicked 120 goals up forward.

The midfield is humming with or without Hayden Young, who has become something of the cream on a pretty spectacular cake.

Patrick Voss is part of a three-headed dragon for the Dockers up forward. (AAP: Michael Errey)

The premiership window isn't just open for Fremantle. It's been blown off its hinges.

Eagles on the up

West Coast shouldn't, on paper at least, pose much of a problem for the Dockers.

The Eagles have won just four games this year, and not since defeating a hapless Essendon back in May.

But that doesn't tell the whole story of coach Andrew McQualter's side.

In round eight, the Eagles returned from Melbourne after a 101-point belting by St Kilda.

West Coast lost to Fremantle by 56 points in April. (AAP: Richard Wainwright)

In the three weeks prior, West Coast had been thrashed by Sydney, Geelong and the Dockers.

Things looked bleak for the long-suffering Eagles faithful who had entered the season hopeful their club's rebuild would start bearing fruit.

Indeed, the flowers are starting to bloom, and it seems the fruit isn't too far away.

West Coast has been improving in recent weeks, with results including a win against Essendon. (AAP: David Woodley)

West Coast may have only won two more games since that shellacking by the Saints, but it has been a lot more competitive.

In their opening eight rounds, the Eagles' average margin was minus 46 points, which included wins in rounds two and three.

Since then, that margin is just minus 11 points. They beat GWS and Essendon, lost to Port Adelaide by a goal and North Melbourne by a point.

They led at half-time against the Western Bulldogs and Brisbane.

Wins and losses don't tell the entire story of Andrew McQualter's Eagles this season. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

Harley Reid has not dropped below 20 disposals since that loss to Saint Kilda in a sign he's finding consistency in his game, while Jake Waterman has kicked three or more goals in eight of his past 11 games.

McQualter has stated his side is hunting a "scalp" to crystallise its improvement. Fremantle would be the ideal trophy.

At Perth Stadium tonight, both the Dockers and Eagles have something to gain, but only one has a lot to lose.

World.title: Divers map underwater caves that weave under city streets
World.content:
The patchwork of caves and sinkholes on South Australia's Limestone Coast is an underwater wonder most people will never fully experience.

But a project using cameras to create 3D maps of the region's major sites hopes to give the public a glimpse of the caves that weave below streets and houses in Mount Gambier.

Advanced cave diver Will Passos, with assistance from fellow members of the Soggy Wombats dive team, has used photogrammetry and computer software to recreate these dive sites.

Corey Auld, Will Passos and Chloe Reid after their final dive to map Engelbrecht Cave. (ABC South East SA: Josh Brine)

"With photography being an interest [of mine] … this idea came about using photogrammetry to try and map them," he said.

"There are old and good maps that people have been doing for the past 40 or 50 years, but it's been a while since anyone updated those maps.

"We did a trial at Allendale [East], just with a big camera and not enough lights, and it was a great result."

The divers start at a pool at the bottom of the dry section in the cave's east. (ABC South East SA: Josh Brine)

Since that first trial, the method has been refined and resulted in models of a number of sites, including Pines and Iddlebiddy caves.

Mr Passos now uses four action cameras, each taking a photo every second, and plenty of lights to ensure the model is as accurate as possible.

With a scan of the Engelbrecht Cave in the heart of Mount Gambier now complete, Mr Passos said he wanted to show people how the passages wove under the city's streets.

"I really want to be able to tell people what's under their houses and I think that's pretty cool," he said.

Mr Passos can overlay the model on street maps to show how the tunnels run under Mount Gambier. (ABC South East SA: Josh Brine)

From primitive to high-tech

In the early days of caving in the region, mapping was a difficult task.

Ian Lewis, who has been diving for about 50 years, said the mapping efforts were a response to tragic deaths in the region.

But he said early efforts were "primitive", using adapted surface mapping techniques underwater.

Mount Gambier hydrogeologist Ian Lewis has been cave diving for decades. (ABC South East SA: Josh Brine)

"We'd take [measuring] tapes underwater, we had underwater compasses on our wrist, we had little waterproof notes that you could write on with a pencil underwater," he said.

"You'd pull the whole lot out, clean the mud off and everything else, and start drawing things up afterwards.

Corey Auld has been among the divers assisting Will Passos in his mapping efforts. (ABC South East SA: Josh Brine)

"We drew them out on graph paper and measured the angles that we'd recorded from the compass and then started drawing in the edges of it.

"These are similar techniques that they use to map the dry caves at Naracoorte, where the fossils were found, but it's just a bit harder underwater."

Mr Passos attaches four cameras and lights to a rig to take the photos for the mapping. (ABC South East SA: Josh Brine)

Mr Passos said he was similarly adapting techniques from other applications.

"Photogrammetry is well known. The construction industry uses point clouds all the time … so it's not groundbreaking technology, it's been there for 100 years," he said.

"The application is a little bit different, and the fact that it's underwater makes it even a little bit more different.

"Not everyone is willing to take a bunch of cameras to go underwater instead of diving to record things.

"I would say there is a trend globally for divers that are involved in cave diving to do that because it's just not us that realise that there is a gap and that we need more information."

Greenfield for exploration

The maps the team has created are now being actively used by divers, with the information available on the Cave Divers Association of Australia website.

The map created using photogrammetry of the Pines Cave. (Supplied: Will Passos)

But Mr Passos said he also thought about how the modelling could be used to better inform the public, including animations or videos.

"The whole thing is where you host that," he said.

"The models are really heavy because they're very detailed, so it's always a question of finance."

The modelling has also already led to the discovery of an extension at Pines Cave, near Tantanoola, after investigating part of the model that did not close.

"The scans helped us try to identify where to look, which is a great thing," Mr Passos said.

"We didn't think that we could get that sort of insight from the scan."

Divers find undiscovered tunnel Curious divers on South Australia's Limestone Coast are hoping to one day be able to dive into one cave and come out another, after discovering an underground tunnel.

Mr Lewis said he was excited to see what the technology enabled.

"Will [Passos] and the others are really at the cutting edge of all of this," he said.

"I just look back and think about our torches and things like that, handling ropes and lines and so on.

"It's fantastic what they're doing."

An example of an older map of Engelbrecht Cave. (ABC South East SA: Josh Brine)

Mr Passos said he wanted to look further afield for how this technology could be used, including on unmapped caves across Asia.

"When you go look overseas, like Thailand, Laos, even Japan, there's nothing," he said.

World.title: Family 'devastated' after alleged indecent assault of disabled child at school
World.content:
A Northern Territory family has accused the Department of Education of failing in its duty of care for their 12-year-old girl, after she was allegedly indecently assaulted at a school that caters for children with disabilities.

Warning: This story contains descriptions of an alleged indecent assault on a child that some readers may find distressing.

In cases involving alleged sexual offences against children, there are strict rules preventing the publication of details that could identify the children or the school involved.

The girl's mother was contacted by the school in April and informed of an incident allegedly involving inappropriate touching by a male student in a school bathroom.

The girl's grandfather told the ABC the alleged incident and the following forensic assessments by police had been extremely confronting for the family.

He said the girl was now refusing to attend school, and there had been noticeable changes in her demeanour.

The girl's family says she has been refusing to go to school since the incident. (AAP: Joe Castro)

"She loves giving a high five and cuddling people … that doesn't happen no more unless mummy says it's okay," he said.

" It's heartbreaking. As time goes on, things are not getting better. "

The incident report

According to an incident report prepared by the school and obtained by the ABC, a teacher had noticed the girl and a boy from the same class had not returned to the classroom after being let out, separately, to go to the bathroom.

The school has small classes of around half-a-dozen students, given their complex needs.

It is not clear from the notes exactly how much time passed before the teacher went to the bathroom to check on them, thinking it was "odd" they had not yet returned.

The teacher then found the two students in the boys' bathroom, in the same cubical.

According to the written account, the teacher found them "with the door closed" and their feet "facing each other".

The girl had then stepped out of the cubical "pulling/adjusting her pants up", according to the document.

The students were then interviewed separately.

The girl told school staff the boy had told her to go with him into the boys' bathroom before pulling her pants down and touching her "on the butt".

The teachers also interviewed the boy, but he was silent in response to questions.

When they read out what the girl had told them and asked if it was correct, he nodded, according to the incident report.

Family says girl needs close supervision

Like many children with disability, the girl had an "education adjustment plan" in place at the school.

The plan, which has also been obtained by the ABC, outlines measures to deal with the girl's autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability.

Among them was a note that the girl "needs reminders to close the toilet door while in the toilet", but suggested this could be done through "visual" aids inside the toilet.

A separate 22-page cognitive assessment, shared by the family with the ABC, outlines the girl's extreme vulnerability in detail.

The assessment found the girl required "significant supervision in daily living environments". (ABC News: Keana Naughton)

Her level of "adaptive behaviour" was within the lowest 0.1 percent for her age, according to the assessment.

The girl's ability to "protect her physical wellbeing" was in the "extremely low range".

"The implication of these results are that [the girl] requires significant supervision in daily living environments, with limited independent safety awareness," the cognitive assessment found.

The girl's grandfather said it was unacceptable for the school to lose track of the girl when they well understood her cognitive capacity.

" Why did my granddaughter end up in the boys' toilets? And then why did it take so long … before they realised? "

"There should have been someone there with her at all times."

Family questions school's response

The girl's family is angry at the response from the school and the education department.

In the immediate aftermath of the incident, the girl's mother took her to hospital, where a case worker "advised [her] to call the police".

"The school, believe it or not, did not inform the police of what took place," the girl's grandfather said.

Child-on-child sex abuse in schools Child abuse prevention researchers say the "huge" problem of child-on-child sex abuse within Australian schools is growing. It's sparked urgent calls to overhaul the curriculum on porn and consent.

He also said it had taken the school "an hour" to notify the girl's mother, who works at a location only 10 minutes away from the school.

The ABC sent detailed questions about the handling of the complaint to the school and the Department of Education.

Marinda Watt, acting deputy chief executive for schools, said the department was "aware of the matter" and was working closely with authorities.

She said the department had "been in contact" with police, but did not specify when.

"The Department recognises the distress this matter has caused and will continue to work with the school, the family and the relevant authorities to support the safety and wellbeing of all students," Ms Watt said.

"The matter remains subject to ongoing investigation. For that reason, and to protect the privacy of the student, family and others involved, the Department cannot comment further on individual details, including school operations, notifications, support arrangements or risk-management steps."

The ABC contacted NT Minister for Education Jo Hersey about the case. She referred the broadcaster to the department's response.

Marinda Watt says the education department "recognises the distress this matter has caused" and will continue to work with authorities. (ABC News: Floss Adams)

The girl's grandfather said Northern Territory Police had been excellent throughout the process and had made things as "gentle as possible" for the young girl, who he said had the "mind of a five- or six-year-old".

"I cannot thank them enough for what they've done," he said.

But he said it had been "devastating" for the girl's mother to hand over the girl's clothes and underwear for forensic testing.

NT Police said it was "investigating allegations of indecent touching involving two children, both with known cognitive impairments".

"Investigations remain ongoing," the police spokesperson said.

Claims psychological support lacking

The girl's grandfather also questioned what he said was a lack of psychological support from the school in the aftermath of the alleged event.

"The school has sent down a psychologist, but the funny thing was, that was to talk to my daughter and son-in-law, not to my granddaughter," he said.

"I'm hearing that there is not a child psychologist [available in the NT to] assist my granddaughter.

"Surely there would be somewhere. I know we're behind on a lot of things, but not that far."

Child-on-child abuse on the rise Parents are demanding answers from centre operators after their children were allegedly sexually abused by other children while in child care.

He said the school had seemed more focused on the girl's attendance, rather than offering support.

"The thing what they're doing now is that they're trying to fix these mistakes by trying to push my granddaughter back to school without ever giving her any assistance," he said.

" Bad move. Don't work that way. "

The family said they understood the accused boy had been allowed to remain at school.

Meanwhile, the school has suggested options including distance education for the girl.

"I am not going to sit back and watch my grandchild miss out [on] all the good things in school that a child should have because of the sake of one person who's still allowed to attend that school," the girl's grandfather said.

World.title: Live: Gambling the focus at second day of Labor National Conference

The Trump administration has confirmed a 12.5 per cent tariff will be placed on Australian exports to the US from later today Australian time.

The tariff was proposed last month, after a US trade investigation into forced labour.

The Australian government and Business Council of Australia made formal submissions opposing the tariff during a consultation period, which ended earlier this month.

The US Trade Representative has now announced the proposed tariff will take effect from 12:01am Friday, local time (2:01pm Friday AEST).

A temporary 10 per cent "global tariff" on the US's trading partners will expire at the same time.

Australia is not the only affected country. Tariffs between 10 and 12.5 per cent will be placed on imports from 59 other economies, which represent all of the US's major trading partners.

World.title: New airport's neighbours feel overlooked in billion-dollar spend
World.content:
Luddenham is a five-minute drive from Western Sydney International Airport (WSI), but some residents say they are missing out on the benefits it should be bringing them.

The New South Wales and federal governments have invested $28 billion to deliver the airport, which will open for freight aircraft on Monday, as well as surrounding infrastructure and the foundation of the city of Bradfield.

Luddenham has a population of about 2,000 people. (702 ABC Sydney: Declan Bowring)

The Luddenham Progress Association's Wayne Wilmington says Bradfield has been getting the lion's share of investment and approvals for development while plans for his town have stalled.

He said about 500 homes were removed to make way for the airport and that they should be replaced.

"The community is shrinking," Mr Wilmington said.

" We've lost a lot of housing and a lot of people. So just so that Luddenham can survive as a community, we need some more housing. "

Luddenham Public School has 35 students, down from 74 in 2016, although the Catholic primary school has consistently had 250 students for the past 10 years.

Wayne Wilmington's family owned some of the land the airport is now on. (702 ABC Sydney: Declan Bowring)

Mr Wilmington, whose connection to Luddenham goes back to the 1850s, said the NSW government's plan for more housing in Luddenham had stalled since the 2023 state election.

"Bradfield is where the government owns the land — they're getting everything," he said.

"We don't want high-rise in Luddenham … we want it to remain a viable community. Not a city, but a community."

Luddenham village plans stall

A 2022 state government document outlines a scenario in which 1,200 homes could be added in Luddenham's north, away from expected aircraft noise.

According to the document, consultation with councils, the federal government, state agencies and the community was to start in 2022.

Mr Wilmington said there had not been any movement since then.

A NSW Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure spokesperson said the airport and federal government were involved in a working group to identify and respond to possible noise impacts on the village.

"Targeted consultation with state agencies and local councils is underway to determine next steps for the village," the spokesperson said.

"We look forward to progressing with the most sustainable strategy for the future of Luddenham."

A spokesperson for the planning department said Bradfield City had a housing target of 10,000 homes, 10 per cent of which were to be affordable dwellings.

Some people travelled from as far afield as Castle Hill and Zetland to watch the trial flights. (702 ABC Sydney: Declan Bowring)

The price of progress

Road and infrastructure construction has brought business to Luddenham, but residents, having seen the test flights overhead, wonder if that will last.

"When the airport opens, I think they'll [local businesses] struggle some more, because they're getting a lot of business at the moment from the people who are working over at the airport," Luddenham Progress Association member Glen Marsden said.

Road improvements have been welcomed by residents, but the changes have brought an end to John Cilpani's 34 years in Luddenham.

The Northern Road now cuts through his property, which sits at the south-western end of the runway, and he says runoff from the airport has filtered into his dams.

Qantas kangaroos were outnumbered by the real thing last week. (702 ABC Sydney: Declan Bowring)

"I bought knowing that I bought on the boundary of Badgerys Creek airport," Mr Cilpani said.

"I didn't think I'd live long enough to see it."

He said he had been offered noise insulation, but the noise of the traffic from the road was bad enough when he was outside.

"When you're in an open green area, you can't expect it to stay like that forever," Mr Cilpani said.

" It's progress and I accept that. "

Matt Vella is reserving his judgement about the impact on Luddenham. (702 ABC Sydney: Declan Bowring)

Matt Vella, who has run the Luddenham farmers market in the village for 10 years, says business is still good despite the loss of some customers due to the rerouting of the Northern Road.

He said he would wait and see whether or not the town was missing out on development.

"It's a good country town," he said.

"It's been good to us, so I can't complain there."

Norman Schuk, who made the 20-minute drive from Leppington to watch a freight plane landing, said the airport's opening would be a turning point for Western Sydney.

"You can already see the industry starting to come out here, freight terminals, things like that. This will just boom now," he said.

"It'll be easy for me to get to Bali."

World.title: Trump hikes tariffs on Australia to 12.5 per cent under guise of human rights
World.content:
Washington: The United States will increase tariffs on Australian products to 12.5 per cent under the guise of human rights, after the US trade office determined Australia and 59 other countries were not doing enough to eliminate forced labour.

The decision means tariffs on Australian goods will rise from 10 per cent, which was the rate set under a temporary measure after the Supreme Court ruled President Donald Trump’s “reciprocal tariffs” were unlawful.

President Donald Trump at the White House on Thursday. AP Photo/Alex Brandon

The Australian government made a submission arguing that Australia maintained a robust legal architecture against modern slavery, albeit in a different form to the US. It also pointed out that Australia and the US have a 20-year-old free trade agreement.

But in a notice issued on Thursday (Washington time), the US trade office said it had decided to impose the tariffs anyway, based on public comments, testimony, the advice of its own committee, “and in accordance with the specific direction of the President”.

World.title: Trump warns of ‘massive attack’ on Iran as oil hits $US100 a barrel again
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastMiddle East at war Trump warns of ‘massive attack’ on Iran as oil hits $US100 a barrel again Michael Koziol July 24, 2026 — 6:38am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Oil is trading above $US100 for the first time since the last phase of the Iran war after Houthi rebels fired at two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, prompting US President Donald Trump to warn of bigger strikes against the Iranian regime and its surrogates. The price of Brent crude rose more than 8 per cent on Thursday (US time), amid widespread fears that Houthi attacks in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait will disrupt shipping in another crucial waterway. President Donald Trump on Thursday. AP Photo/Alex Brandon Trump warned that if the Iran-backed militants in Yemen fired on another ship, he would inflict “major military punishment” on Iran and the Houthis themselves – “who I am very disappointed with in that they have, until now, acted very professionally and smart”. The president also told US news site Axios that he was considering a “massive attack, bigger than ever before” against Iran, and that the military was prepared to execute.



Iranian parliamentary speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf seized on the rapidly rising oil price to declare victory. “They wanted to punish Iran. Punished themselves with triple-digit oil instead,” he wrote on X. Despite the attacks, two supertankers carrying an estimated 4 million barrels of Saudi oil exited the Red Sea through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait on Thursday, shipping data showed, apparently escaping the Houthis’ announced blockade. The Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the mouth of the Red Sea is another crucial global shipping passage. Graphic: Nathan Perri The Singapore-flagged tanker Xin Long Yang, which made a U-turn and paused in the middle of the Red Sea on Tuesday, resumed its journey south, followed by the Chinese-flagged tanker Cosnew Lake. Both exited the Red Sea later on Thursday, the data showed. Gregory Brew, an Iran and oil analyst at the Eurasia Group consultancy, said some cargo vessels were turning around and heading north, with at least one large tanker offloading some of its load to cross the Suez Canal to the Mediterranean Sea.



It was “a reminder that the Houthis can ‘disrupt’ crude flows, but they can’t stop them, Hormuz-style, from reaching their destination”, Brew said on X. Meanwhile, the US House of Representatives again passed a resolution calling on the president to stop the war against Iran unless it was specifically authorised by Congress, after four Republicans crossed the floor. The resolution carries no practical effect, and it stalled in the Senate. The effective blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, on top of fresh attacks on shipping in the Red Sea, has raised concerns of a spike in oil prices. AP Democrats used the rising price of oil to sharpen their attacks on Trump ahead of the summer congressional recess. “The American people are against this war,” said Chuck Schumer, leader of the Democrats in the Senate, adding that it had “no direction or purpose”.



“They’re definitely against paying over four bucks for a gallon of gas.” Related Article Opinion

Middle East at war The real oil shock from the Iran war might be just beginning Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Speaking at an event spruiking data centres, Trump defended the ongoing war, noting it was far shorter and less deadly than American campaigns in Vietnam, Afghanistan and Iraq. “We want to get it over with, and we want to do it right, but we have to do what we came to do,” he said. Trump also attempted to impose a caveat on a deal signed with Saudi Arabia on Wednesday that provides US companies access to the kingdom’s civilian nuclear energy program – a controversial move worth billions of dollars for those American firms.



In a TruthSocial post, the president said the deal was conditional on Saudi Arabia joining the Abraham Accords, an initiative from Trump’s first term by which Arab nations normalise their relations with Israel. Related Article Middle East at war Houthis target Saudi ships as Trump repeats threat to hit Iran’s bridges, power plants Riyadh has long insisted that it must see meaningful progress towards a two-state solution for Palestine before it would consider joining the Accords. The deal announced on Wednesday made no mention of Saudi Arabian policy on Israel changing, and White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt provided no further information at a briefing. “If they don’t join the Abraham Accords, the deal is off,” she said of Trump’s position. “This agreement is still being worked out. It will eventually hopefully be finalised ... with the condition that the president spoke about this morning.”



With Reuters Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: ASX set to slump as oil surges over $US100, Tesla and Alphabet tumble
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slump as oil surges over $US100, Tesla and Alphabet tumble Stan Choe Updated July 24, 2026 — 6:31am ,first published 5:24am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Brent oil shot to its highest price since May after increased fighting in the Middle East on Thursday threatened to slow the global flow of crude. At the same time, sharp drops for two of Wall Street’s most influential companies, Alphabet and Tesla, yanked the US stock market to its worst loss in a month. The S&P 500 fell 1.2 per cent and is on track for its first back-to-back weekly loss since March. The Dow Jones dropped 506 points, or 1 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite sank 2.2 per cent. Rising oil prices and a slump for Alphabet and Tesla weighed down Wall Street. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to fall, with futures at 5am AEST pointing to a loss of 61 points, or 0.7 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.2 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was 0.5 per cent lower to US69.64¢. Stocks fell under the pressure of rising oil prices, which raise costs for businesses and erode their customers’ ability to spend. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil, the international standard, jumped 7 per cent to settle at $US100.69.



It touched $US102 during the day, the highest price since May for the most actively traded Brent contract in the market. The cause: attacks on two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea. That threatens another avenue that oil companies use to move their crude from the Middle East to customers worldwide, along with the Strait of Hormuz. Underscoring the importance of the sea route for the economy, President Donald Trump threatened “major military punishment” against the Houthi rebels in Yemen, who are backed by Iran, if they keep attacking ships. It was just a few weeks ago that Brent had dropped below $US72 per barrel, roughly back to where it was before the United States and Israel attacked Iran to begin their war, on hopes that a wind-down in the war would fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz. World.title: Trump hikes tariffs on Australia to 12.5 per cent under guise of human rights
World.content:
Washington: The United States will increase tariffs on Australian products to 12.5 per cent under the guise of human rights, after the US trade office determined Australia and 59 other countries were not doing enough to eliminate forced labour.

The decision means tariffs on Australian goods will rise from 10 per cent, which was the rate set under a temporary measure after the Supreme Court ruled President Donald Trump’s “reciprocal tariffs” were unlawful.

President Donald Trump at the White House on Thursday. AP Photo/Alex Brandon

The Australian government made a submission arguing that Australia maintained a robust legal architecture against modern slavery, albeit in a different form to the US. It also pointed out that Australia and the US have a 20-year-old free trade agreement.

But in a notice issued on Thursday (Washington time), the US trade office said it had decided to impose the tariffs anyway, based on public comments, testimony, the advice of its own committee, “and in accordance with the specific direction of the President”.

World.content:
WorldMiddle EastMiddle East at war Trump warns of ‘massive attack’ on Iran as oil hits $US100 a barrel again Michael Koziol July 24, 2026 — 6:38am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Oil is trading above $US100 for the first time since the last phase of the Iran war after Houthi rebels fired at two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, prompting US President Donald Trump to warn of bigger strikes against the Iranian regime and its surrogates. The price of Brent crude rose more than 8 per cent on Thursday (US time), amid widespread fears that Houthi attacks in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait will disrupt shipping in another crucial waterway. President Donald Trump on Thursday. AP Photo/Alex Brandon Trump warned that if the Iran-backed militants in Yemen fired on another ship, he would inflict “major military punishment” on Iran and the Houthis themselves – “who I am very disappointed with in that they have, until now, acted very professionally and smart”. The president also told US news site Axios that he was considering a “massive attack, bigger than ever before” against Iran, and that the military was prepared to execute.



Iranian parliamentary speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf seized on the rapidly rising oil price to declare victory. “They wanted to punish Iran. Punished themselves with triple-digit oil instead,” he wrote on X. Despite the attacks, two supertankers carrying an estimated 4 million barrels of Saudi oil exited the Red Sea through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait on Thursday, shipping data showed, apparently escaping the Houthis’ announced blockade. The Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the mouth of the Red Sea is another crucial global shipping passage. Graphic: Nathan Perri The Singapore-flagged tanker Xin Long Yang, which made a U-turn and paused in the middle of the Red Sea on Tuesday, resumed its journey south, followed by the Chinese-flagged tanker Cosnew Lake. Both exited the Red Sea later on Thursday, the data showed. Gregory Brew, an Iran and oil analyst at the Eurasia Group consultancy, said some cargo vessels were turning around and heading north, with at least one large tanker offloading some of its load to cross the Suez Canal to the Mediterranean Sea.



It was “a reminder that the Houthis can ‘disrupt’ crude flows, but they can’t stop them, Hormuz-style, from reaching their destination”, Brew said on X. Meanwhile, the US House of Representatives again passed a resolution calling on the president to stop the war against Iran unless it was specifically authorised by Congress, after four Republicans crossed the floor. The resolution carries no practical effect, and it stalled in the Senate. The effective blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, on top of fresh attacks on shipping in the Red Sea, has raised concerns of a spike in oil prices. AP Democrats used the rising price of oil to sharpen their attacks on Trump ahead of the summer congressional recess. “The American people are against this war,” said Chuck Schumer, leader of the Democrats in the Senate, adding that it had “no direction or purpose”.



“They’re definitely against paying over four bucks for a gallon of gas.” Related Article Opinion

Middle East at war The real oil shock from the Iran war might be just beginning Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Speaking at an event spruiking data centres, Trump defended the ongoing war, noting it was far shorter and less deadly than American campaigns in Vietnam, Afghanistan and Iraq. “We want to get it over with, and we want to do it right, but we have to do what we came to do,” he said. Trump also attempted to impose a caveat on a deal signed with Saudi Arabia on Wednesday that provides US companies access to the kingdom’s civilian nuclear energy program – a controversial move worth billions of dollars for those American firms.



In a TruthSocial post, the president said the deal was conditional on Saudi Arabia joining the Abraham Accords, an initiative from Trump’s first term by which Arab nations normalise their relations with Israel. Related Article Middle East at war Houthis target Saudi ships as Trump repeats threat to hit Iran’s bridges, power plants Riyadh has long insisted that it must see meaningful progress towards a two-state solution for Palestine before it would consider joining the Accords. The deal announced on Wednesday made no mention of Saudi Arabian policy on Israel changing, and White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt provided no further information at a briefing. “If they don’t join the Abraham Accords, the deal is off,” she said of Trump’s position. “This agreement is still being worked out. It will eventually hopefully be finalised ... with the condition that the president spoke about this morning.”
