World.title: Silver Ferns pair cleared for Commonwealth Games
World.content:
The Silver Ferns have received a timely boost on the eve of their Commonwealth Games campaign, with two previously injured stars declared fit.

Having both been under injury clouds, Catherine Hall and Kimiora Poi's availability was subject to a medical assessment when the squad for Glasgow was announced last month.

Hall underwent surgery on an injured foot in May which had forced the Mystics defender out of the ANZ Premiership.

The 22-year-old had been afforded as much time as possible by the national team to prove her fitness, with Parris Mason on standby as the sole travelling reserve.

Poi was also scrubbed from domestic duties for the Southern Steel due to an injured calf.

Speaking to reporters in Glasgow, Silver Ferns coach Dame Noeline Taurua confirmed both would be available to take to the court.

"Tick, tick. So really happy for both of them," she said.

Hall received the official all-clear only a few days ago and would be available for the team's Commonwealth Games opener on Saturday.

"[It's] been a massive job for Catherine and our support staff to make this happen for us."

Midcourt star Kimiora Poi said she felt the stars were aligning for her after being cleared to play at the Commonwealth Games. AAP / www.photosport.nz

Poi was feeling good having spent plenty of time during the Silver Ferns pre-games training camp.

"I've had a good progressive load and plan from the medical staff so back on court and feeling pretty good," she told RNZ in Glasgow.

Disappointed to be struck down as the Steel made a premiership finals push, the 26-cap mid-courter was also left to contemplate her Commonwealth Games prospects.

Now she and Hall both have a clean bill of health, Poi felt "the stars were aligning".

"We've both been following strict plans to get us here. Despite missing the backend of the ANZ, it's kind of cool that we've been rewarded by making the team and cleared to play this weekend."

World.title: How New Zealanders are cutting the cost of their insurances
World.content:
What if you don't want a slice of the AI hype? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 13m

Insurance costs have been a major pain point for many households in recent years, but data from insurers shows many of us are finding solutions.

It was reported mid last year that insurance had the largest increase of any item in the consumer price index since 2000, up 916 percent.

Insurance experts told RNZ that some health insurance policies lifted 50 percent last year.

But while there are signs that premium rises may be moderating, some policyholders are finding other ways to reduce their costs.

How households are saving on insurance costs Morning Report Download MP3 2m

Higher excesses

Generally, if your insurance policy has a higher excess, you may be able to pay lower premiums.

Excess is the amount that a policy-holder pays when they make a claim, before the insurer chips in the rest.

Vero said its research showed 57 percent of the 1172 insured homeowners it surveyed had home insurance excesses of more than $500, even though "standard" was $300 to $500.

Nichola Young, executive manager of pricing and underwriting, said Vero had noticed customers had been opting for higher excesses since mid-2022.

She said more people were choosing an excess of $1000 excess, while $400 excesses were becoming less popular.

She said a very high excess, for example of more than $5000, could reduce the cost of an average premium by about $300 a year, although other factors would affect it.

"We've seen more customers voluntarily increasing their excess, and we noticed that this shift coincided with broader cost-of-living pressures."

Vero's research found affordability was the main driver for the higher excesses, and 66 percent of homeowners who had increased their excesses said they did so to lower the cost of their insurance.

"It shows that our customers are making trade-offs to balance the cost of premiums with the level of risk they're willing to carry. The choice ultimately sits with the customer, but the important thing is understanding what that means if you ever need to make a claim."

Young said it would not help in every situation.

"It's important to understand that increasing your excess won't necessarily offset every driver of rising insurance costs. Premium increases in recent years have been influenced by factors such as the growing cost of natural hazards, and increased taxes and levies. If your premium is higher because your home faces greater flood or weather risk, increasing your excess is unlikely to significantly reduce your premium."

The research showed 9 percent of people who had a higher excess said it was a temporary measure.

Justin Lim, founder of insurance comparison website Quashed, said his site had recorded a 19 percent increase in excesses for house insurance year-on-year, a 14 percent increase for car insurance and 6 percent for contents cover.

Changing cover type

Lim said people were also looking for cheaper insurance options.

He said some vehicle owners were considering third-party covert rather than comprehensive insurance.

"While most consumers still ultimately purchase comprehensive car insurance, year-on-year growth in comparison activity for third-party was double that of comprehensive. Consumers are actively exploring cheaper, more basic options."

Dropping cover

Some people are dropping policies completely. Southern Cross reported a drop in membership numbers in the year to June 30, 2025, of 3493 members, bringing total membership to 951,808.

The Insurance Council said surveys showed New Zealanders still had relatively high levels of insurance cover overall, and the percentage of homes with house insurance was in the mid-90 percent range.

Shopping around

Lim said people could often save money by comparing their options.

He said people who looked at what else was on offer could find they could save up to $1500 a year.

He said the chances of finding a cheaper policy were eight out of 10 for car cover, seven in 10 for contents, and six in 10 for home insurance.

Reducing risk

You may sometimes be able to reduce your insurance costs by reducing the risk to the insurer.

For health or life cover, that could mean quitting smoking.

For vehicle insurance, you might be able to install an immobiliser or park in a garage rather than on the street.

The Insurance Council said home insurance rose only 0.4 percent in the year to March and vehicle insurance was down 2 percent.

World.title: Rescue jetskis parked by FENZ last year to be allowed back
World.content:
River rescue jetskis back after community campaign Morning Report Download MP3 4m

Waikato is getting back its rescue jetskis that were parked up by Fire and Emergency (FENZ) last year sparking a public outcry.

Locals warned someone would drown as a result of FENZ saying local volunteers were no longer allowed to use motorised boats because it was too risky.

A request by the Cambridge brigade over jetskis it wanted to deploy with local fundraising is understood to have triggered what became a national directive from Wellington fire commanders, that only trained firefighters in rafts were allowed to do water rescues.

RNZ revealed this last October prompting online comments such as, "Huntly ... had a really good water rescue unit until FENZ Numpties banned it."

But now a group separate from FENZ is being set up to run jetski rescues on the Waikato River covering volunteers from all three local brigades - Huntly, Ngārauwāhia and Cambridge.

"It's looking positive and we are hoping to get back on the river pretty soon," Huntly brigade chief Kerry Holland told RNZ on Thursday.

This looks like it would be finalised in a meeting next week.

FENZ chief executive Kerry Gregory had been grilled by MPs earlier this year about taking a hard line on motorised water rescues, which he defended by saying this fell outside what they were funded for, trained for or had set health and safety standards around.

This suggests the new move in Waikato depends on FENZ not being in charge. RNZ expects to get more details from FENZ later on Friday.

FENZ chief executive Kerry Gregory. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

The jetskis came up again at Parliament on Monday this week - when Gregory was able to deliver different news to a select committee inquiry looking into fire truck fleet problems.

National MP Tim Costley had asked if some local brigades felt they needed to "hide" trucks or jetskis they had bought themselves with local fundraising.

"Because when we had the annual review hearing [in January], I know there was a large discussion around jetskis, swift water rescue, but are brigades, where the brigade owns something, whether it's an appliance, a jet ski, a buggy, or whatever it might be, are they able to use it or are they going to have that taken off them?" asked Costley.

Gregory replied: "Yeah, so if I just start on the jetskis, and it's good to be in a position now where Ngārauwāhia and Huntly, which were the ones with the jet skis ... have decided to make up a separate entity - that's a local solution to a local issue."

Ngārauwāhia volunteer brigade chief Karl Lapwood said they really had no choice.

"We had one of two options - forget about the risk it poses to the community or we come up with a solution," he said.

On Friday FENZ said it supported the brigades' plans to set up a new entity to enable them to use their watercraft for search and rescue on the Waikato River, independently of it.

"We welcome the brigades' initiative and the progress they have made so far, and we will continue to provide support where we can," it said in a statement.

River rescue jetskis back after community campaign Morning Report Download MP3 4m

Lapwood told Morning Report they hoped to have jetskis back on the river by Christmas under an incorporated society.

"We will be back up and running on the water as we were - the response will be the same but we will be reporting directly to police."

World.title: Weather: 'Cloud burst' hits Grey District, flooding homes and causing a slip
World.content:
About half-a-dozen homes flooded in the South Island overnight.

Fire and Emergency (FENZ) crews responded to flooded homes in Greymouth, Cobden, Brunner and Runanga in the Grey District.

Southern shift manager Lyn Crosson said they also responded to a slip on the road in Cobden.

Crosson said they were gearing up for more heavy rain and possible flooding this afternoon.

A heavy rain watch had been in place for the Westland Ranges from 8pm on Thursday until 3am on Friday, with heavy rain forecast to move northwards over the North Island on Friday.

West Coast Emergency Management said on social media it was a "cloud burst style rain event".

"Please take care as first light arrives."

Images uploaded by Grey District Council showed surface flooding in Greymouth.

Surface flooding in Greymouth, July 2026. Grey District Council

Surface flooding in Greymouth, July 2026. Grey District Council

State Highway 7 was closed between Greymouth and Stillwater. The New Zealand Transport Agency advised road users to avoid the area or delay their journey if possible.

The council said parts of Wickes Street, Richmond Street, Bright Street, Barkley Place, Peel Street, and Sturge Street, all had high surface water, and there were reports of a tree down on Taylorville Road.

Heather Keats with details of this weekend’s cold snap Morning Report Download MP3 4m

MetService head of weather Heather Keats told Morning Report the heavy rain would head up the west of the country over the next couple of days.

"Sunday's okay, but today and tomorrow, very much looking messy," she explained.

"We've got a bunch of fast-moving features and fronts tied up and that will be thunderstorms, snow, heavy rain, maybe even some small tornadoes and water spouts. And that'll race up and over the country - the North Island - tomorrow, and then it kind of races away.

"But then we're left with a very cold southerly flow. So we've got every type of weather coming over the next sort of 48 hours."

Localised clean-up

Grey District Mayor Tania Gibson. Supplied / Frank Film

Grey District Mayor Tania Gibson said the rain had eased for the moment, but more showers were expected later in the day.

"Our crews have been out since two o'clock this morning, and now that we're in the light of day, there's a lot of assessment going on, there's a lot of debris to clear, there's still road closures in the area and we're trying to find out who's been affected the most.

"But... some of those outer-lying suburbs have been affected and we had a lot of rain come through on the catchment on the hills, which has brought a lot of rain down into town and to those areas and which has brought a lot of debris down as well."

She said there would be a reasonably significant clean-up ahead.

"I was at home, but I was up because we had some poor little lambs in the paddock outside that were crying their hearts out. So, but we do have rain events quite often, but it's hard to assess until you start getting the reports because sometimes, nothing happens, but when they happen in those isolated areas, it's very quick.

World.title: Long-time Wellington party flat shut down by council
World.content:
Walking into 13 Garrett Street in the Wellington CBD, you're welcomed by a wallpaper of gig posters over concrete walls, a display of the home's legacy.

But no more posters will be added, as a complaint to Wellington City Council has forced the cancellation of all events, and the tenants will be exiting to make way for redevelopment.

The home nearby Cuba Street shops has been the place for gigs, markets, poetry readings, movie nights, and more since as early as possibly the late 90s.

The three story building is set to be turned into offices on the upper floors, and a new venue space on the bottom.

The tenants of the home who will be leaving in November - all 16 of them - say the Capital is losing a space for community.

The Wellington City Council received a complaint alleging that the building had been hosting paid live events, which it did not have the permits for.

A pillar of music and arts scene

Flatmates Ollie Warren and Sarah Lee sit on their couch remembering their time hosting.

"It's become quite a pillar of what Wellington music and arts community can look like," Warren said.

A floor to ceiling shared wardrobe sits in the entrance hall, by the front room full of murals and speakers, along with mismatched vintage furniture.

A wooden stage stands at one end of the room, which while it looks peaceful in the daylight, comes alive at night.

In just the past four years, the flatmates said hundreds of people have performed.

In its history of performances, names like Mac Demarco pop up, Welly band Heavy Chest, and founder of music collective Eyegum, Joel Cosgrove who they say had his first gig there at 17.

"Garrett is a place for people to be prototyping and sharing things that aren't quite ready," Lee explained.

A wooden stage stands at one end of the Wellington flat's living room. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

The flatmates said they made no income from the events, and any money from ticket sales went to the artists and organisers.

They said they always tried to operate events with safety in mind, and they respect the council trying to keep everyone safe.

"Obviously the council were going to catch up on us at one point," Warren said.

The group has had to cancel over a dozen events planned for this year as a result of the complaint.

Wellington City Council said it had set out its vision and partnership with the creative sector on supporting groups and artists, and providing access to new and under-utilised spaces to host events.

However, it said this support still needs to comply with building and planning regulations, for safety reasons.

The front room is full of murals and speakers and mismatched vintage furniture. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Music journalist Martyn Pepperell remembered going to the flat as a teenager in the late 90s.

He said the music changed with each group of tenants - from techno, drum and bass, electro punk, new rave, to indie dance.

Pepperell said people would team up and do multi-level shows, even on the roof.

A floor to ceiling shared wardrobe sits in the entrance hall. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

He compared its closure to if the famous Cuba Street Bucket Fountain vanished.

"For some people this has just been part of the fabric of their life for decades."

Now, Pepperell said the building was at a crossroad moment, and Wellington would have to wait and see how the new venue fit into its history.

"In 10 years time, we may find that that's just another chapter in the bigger story of 13 Garrett Street."

Owners' plans

The owners of the property, Emily and William Broadmore, bought the building late last year with the plan to earthquake strengthen it for redevelopment.

They said the top half of the building will be turned into character offices, and the bottom half will be a venue.

The owners are working with DJ and promoter, Jack Parry, and architect and interior designer Allistar Cox, to develop the bottom floor of the building into an official venue.

The owners said they always knew the home was a party flat, but not that events were being ticketed and publicly advertised.

"This is not how we wanted the end of the era for them."

Flatmates Ollie Warren and Sarah Lee say the flat became a pillar of what the Wellington arts and music community can look like. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

While the owners said an end of the tenancy was always planned for earthquake strengthening and redevelopment, they said they had to begin this conversation sooner than anticipated because of the complaint.

"They always knew this day would come. It's just a real shame that it came as a result of a complaint from council."

With earthquake strengthening starting on the upper floors, the owners said it's possible that lower tenants - thrift shop Dirty Laundry and coffee spot Pour & Twist - could stay slightly longer.

Neighbours say the flat was never a problem

Speaking with neighbours, they say the party flat never bothered them.

Victoria Court Motor Lodge - a hotel next to the flat - said the noise was never an issue.

Owner Liam Wang said the noise didn't worry him, as the city was noisy regardless, and other music venues like The Rogue and Vagabond are close by.

However, he said if the home didn't have the right permits, it was fair for the council to shut it down.

Neighbour Dan Craig said he went to a gig at the flat 20 years ago, and felt it was a real shame it had been shut down.

"That's pretty rank bro."

He said it was part of the fabric of Wellington.

"It's like a little hidden secret, it's a shame."

Could the legacy continue?

While 13 Garrett Street itself is closing, the tenants hope the idea of it can continue at a new address.

The flatmates said they want to continue living in large numbers, and are looking for houses with six-plus bedrooms, where they could continue to host.

World.title: Doctors issue warning to treat scabies more seriously
World.content:
Warnings to take scabies seriously Morning Report Download MP3 2m

It is time to stop treating scabies as a minor skin condition and recognise it can lead to serious conditions like rheumatic fever and heart disease, warn experts.

A group of medical professionals want the government to increase funding for screening, diagnosis and treatment of the condition.

Highly infectious scabies is caused by a parasitic mite that burrows into human skin to lay its eggs.

Symptoms can include intense itching - that worsens at night - and a pimple-like or bumpy rash; and thin, raised, wavy burrows under the skin.

A Marlborough woman - who RNZ has agreed not to identify - said it had made life unbearable for her daughters.

"So they're just not sleeping at night. They wake up multiple times in the night, they cry, they think that the insects are in their room. My older daughter is just beside herself, she thinks the things are creeping in a biting her. Their skin's a mess."

This Whanganui mum, who had three boys, felt powerless.

"I'm frustrated, some days really overwhelmed and guilty that I can't really do anything for my boys especially when a couple of them are school age and they're a bit self-conscious now about wearing shorts or t-shirts or going swimming at school. It's frustrating."

She said getting a diagnosis was difficult in the North Island town which had been at the heart of an ongoing outbreak.

"Sometimes they say scabies, sometimes impetigo, sometimes it's hives, sometimes it's 'oh, that's really strange, we don't actually know'."

Dr Simon Thornley is a senior lecturer of epidemiology at Auckland University.

His research on scabies' prevalence in South Auckland found that about 50 percent of children in early childcare centres had clinical signs of the disease.

Dr Simon Thornley (back left) with others at a 2023 scabies symposium. Supplied

Dr Thornley said there was growing evidence it was linked to more serious conditions.

"You're looking at the relationship with scabies and rheumatic fever, scabies and skin infections, scabies and kidney disease. We've found an extraordinary strong link between having records of a diagnosis of scabies and coming into hospital with rheumatic heart disease."

Dr Thornley is one of a number of medical professionals who have penned an open letter calling for screening for scabies at at-risk early childhood centres and schools.

They also want administrative barriers to prescribing Ivermectin tablets removed and better funding for follow up care.

Dr Aidan Cabezas-Hayes has experience treating patients with scabies in South Auckland and was a signatory to the open letter.

"You just used to see it all the time and people would come in whole families affected and they had been trying to get rid of the infection for some time."

He said cost was a barrier to care.

"I think they find it very hard, very frustrating, stigmatising and it is obviously difficult to get into see a GP and a lot of people are struggling with the cost of living, and going to pay however much it is for to see an urgent care doctor is expensive."

Cabezas-Hayes said in some Pacific countries with a very high prevalence of scabies mass drug administration was used where everyone was treated.

"That could be a targeted option, but it's got to come from the communities that are affected, so that we're not reinforcing stigma."

A man receives treatment for a scabies rash on his arm. ANNA MARGUERITAT / AFP

National Public Health Service chief public health clinical officer, Maria Poynter, said scabies was not a notifiable disease, so Health NZ didn't have national case numbers, but it recognised it was a concern in some places.

"We are aware of emerging research on scabies and potential links with more serious conditions, including rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease. We will continue to monitor the evidence as it develops."

She said Health NZ's focus was on practical action, improving access to treatment and advice, as well as supporting consistent household treatment.

In the meantime, the Marlborough mother was at her wit's end.

"We've literally had all the medication we could possibly get in New Zealand and we've followed all the infectious disease procedures and we just can't get rid of it. They're just so uncomfortable."

World.title: Live: Glasgow Commonwealth Games opening ceremony
World.content:
NZ’s Chef De Mission speaks from Glasgow Morning Report Download MP3 4m

The Glasgow Commonwealth Games will officially begin on Friday morning (NZT), after four years of doubt over their survival.

Since it was first awarded to Birmingham, the 23rd edition of the event has become something of a hot potato, with several potential hosts bailing out on financial grounds.

Thank goodness for the brave Scots, who will stage the Games - albeit a trimmed-down version - at Glasgow for the second time in 12 years.

World.title: David Liti and Moira de Villiers to lead NZ team at opening ceremony
World.content:
Weekly Sports Panel: Lima Sopoaga and Dana Johannsen Morning Report Download MP3 9m

Weightlifter David Liti and Judo athlete Moira de Villiers will lead the New Zealand team out at this morning's Glasgow Commonwealth Games opening ceremony.

Liti has been chosen as Pou Hāpai - Tāne and will carry the New Zealand flag at the opening ceremony, while de Villiers has been named Pou Hāpai - Wahine and will carry Te Kaunoti, New Zealand's King's Baton, into the ceremony.

De Villiers said receiving the call from New Zealand team chef de mission Nigel Avery was a special moment.

"When I got the call it was unbelievable. This is a chance for me to represent not only my family and my club, but the entire nation and I think it's such a special thing to be a representative for judo as well," said de Villiers.

Moira de Villiers with the Glasgow Commonwealth Games King's Baton. supplied / NZOC

Liti said carrying the flag was a privilege and something he's super proud of.

"I think back to my first Commonwealth Games, when we went to the Opening Ceremony and I thought carrying the flag was a dream that would never come around. Fast forward two Commonwealth Games later and here I am with the same opportunity to represent everyone and uphold the standards of the athletes from the New Zealand team."

World.title: This footy club wants better for its women's team but is in a pinch
World.content:
Macedon Football Netball Club president Ron Rutledge says his club does things a bit like Ted Lasso.

The "Lasso Way", inspired by the popular TV show, is a leadership style centred on kindness, personal growth and human connection, often over winning.

"Our number one thing is 'thank you' and our number two thing is 'please'," Rutledge tells ABC Sport.

"We're a very easy club to get on with … But we are in a desperate pitch now for our female participants."

The club is in the heart of the Macedon Ranges in central Victoria, about 60 kilometres north-west of Melbourne.

Ron Rutledge says the club has worked hard to grow its women's and girls' teams. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

Founded in 1887 as an original member of the Riddell District Football League, its clubrooms contain cabinets filled with trophies won by generations of men's teams.

The latest additions are the two premiership trophies won by the senior women's side.

Six years ago, the club underwent a significant change when it established a women's team, followed by a girls' team.

"A lot of people before me worked very hard on getting a junior program going for females, particularly in the AFL sense. It's been a netball club for many years, and that has continued to grow and grow and grow," Rutledge says.

The senior women's team is again among the premiership favourites this season.

MFNC female participation keeps on growing. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

But, like many long-standing clubs across the country, Macedon encountered a significant problem as female participation grew: its facilities were neither large enough nor suitable for the new women's and girls' teams.

The Cats' home ground, Tony Clarke Reserve, is also used by the local bowling, cricket and tennis clubs.

The football teams also train around the corner at JD Clifford Reserve during the week.

On Thursday nights, the youth boys, youth girls, senior men's and senior women's sides all train across the two grounds.

'Made for men'

Reigning senior women's club best and fairest winner Ruby Watts has played football since 2017, the year AFLW started.

Now 21, she played Auskick as a child but stopped after a year because she "didn't like playing with the boys", which was then the only option available.

She returned to the sport as a teenager when her local club, Gisborne Football Netball Club, established a girls' team. But she was forced to leave in 2024 when the club could no longer field a women's side.

Ruby Watts won the best and fairest last year. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

She joined Macedon with about six other players from Gisborne. The difference between the clubs' facilities was immediately noticeable.

"At Gisborne it was fine. Like, the facilities are perfect, they're clean, they're nice, but the ones here are a bit… they're just old and they're mainly made for men," Watts says.

"It's open urinals and just open showers, and it's just disgusting. There's one toilet with a door, so it's a big struggle.

"We have to use it after the men's teams, and it's not their fault. Like, they clean it nicely, but it's still disgusting. It just smells gross and it's not right. In 2026 we should be doing better, I reckon."

Women's players say the toilet situation in the change rooms isn't good enough. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

Watts says the club does its best to make sure the women's side is included, but understands sometimes it is constrained by a lack of space.

At Thursday night selection dinners, for example, the women are encouraged to get their food first, while the men listen and cheer as the women's team is announced.

The club has also had several pride rounds this year for the women's competition, in which the shared space gets decorated with streamers and posters.

The away rooms for Macedon's home ground have just the one open showers room. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

But during training beforehand, the women have only a small section of the oval to use if one is rained out.

"There is quadruple the amount of them than there is of us. It would be nice to get half of the ground, but we don't need it in comparison," she says.

The same imbalance means the men fill the clubroom on shared nights, while the women leave their belongings on nearby benches. By dinner, the men have showered and changed, while the women remain in their wet training clothes.

"You can't walk on the ground without your socks getting wet, like we don't have a locker to put our stuff in. A girl, a few weeks ago, lost all of her clothes, because there's nowhere safe to put them," Watts says.

Women's players have to leave their belongings on benches while they train. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

"She literally lost her jumper, her pants, like everything. And she still hasn't gotten her clothes back, just because we have no locker or nothing to put them in, nowhere safe.

"We put our clothes on the chairs and just along the fence and it gets nice and wet and dewy … Then the boys shower after training, but all of us girls have to go fully kitted, fully in our wet socks and everything.

"The boys have comfy jumpers and pants on because they don't care, they'll shower around anybody. We don't have a shower to get changed in. It's different for us."

MFNC has a successful women's program. But the players still have nowhere to get changed. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

Eve Moait, 19, plays in the senior women's side and coaches the under-14 girls.

She loves the club and has embraced its Ted Lasso philosophy. A "Believe" sign hangs above the door to the home change rooms.

"My junior girls love it, they think it's hilarious … They think it's the thing that won them their first game because they all tapped it on the way out and truly believed it," Moait says.

Some of the younger players could not quite reach it.

"They were actually really good jumpers, but we had some really, really small girls and they'd lift each other up to tap it. They're so sweet."

There is a "BELIEVE" sign above the door at MFNC's change rooms. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

Before training, she gets changed in her car and then heads onto the ground.

She says the main club room is good, particularly since indoor artificial turf was installed, even if it's "terrible to clean as a coach".

"But then when we come to the toilet side, the girls just don't want to go in there," she says of her junior team.

"It's smelly because we come in on a Sunday after all the senior men have played the day before, and then all of the boys' teams have played the morning, so we come in during the afternoon at about one o'clock and it is disgusting.

" It smells, and there's grass, and there's underwear, and pee in the corner. It is so gross. "

The junior girls' team at Macedon Football Netball Club. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

Moait often takes the junior players to a public toilet block 200 metres away, but says that can be difficult when she is responsible for all 18 members of the team.

"It's also a very awkward age for these girls," Moait says.

"We've noticed when they first come to the team, when they're at the very bottom age, so 11 or 12, they're typically fine. They'll go to the toilet, or try and avoid it if it's dirty, but it won't bother them as much.

"But when they hit the upper end and they start going into that time [puberty], they just shut off when it comes to the toilet, be like, 'nah, don't want to', and it's like I can't provide them with much better, so it's frustrating.

"There's no sanitary bin, it's dirty, and there's only one toilet there. It's not working for them, that's the problem."

MFNC train on cold and foggy Thursday nights. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

The push for an upgrade

Rutledge has been lobbying the council and state government for help upgrading Tony Clarke Reserve, attracting visits from politicians across the political spectrum.

Macedon Ranges Shire Council has allocated $380,000 in its 2026–27 budget to upgrade the change rooms.

The away rooms at Macedon Football Netball Club. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

The council's assets and operations director, Dom Testoni, told the ABC: "The proposed project, valued at approximately $650,000, would bring the facilities up to current standards and better support the needs of the growing number of participants using the reserve.

"While Council's recent application to the Victorian Government's Country Football Netball Program was unsuccessful, a number of funding avenues remain available.

"Council will submit a new application through the Victorian Government's Local Sports Infrastructure Program, which is currently open, and will continue to pursue other state and federal grant opportunities as they become available."

Macedon Football Netball Club home rooms. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

But Macedon Ranges Shire Mayor Kate Kendall said that funding "falls a little bit short".

She described the facilities as "absolutely prehistoric" and in "such a dire state" that they deterred local girls and women from participating in sport.

"We look at inclusion and a lot of people talk about inclusion, but if we don't have the very basic needs met, where people can go to the toilet safely and privately, then it's just, you know, a poor tale," Kendall told ABC Sport.

MFNC president Ron Rutledge in the club's away rooms. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

Macedon MP Mary-Anne Thomas told the ABC she had visited the club and it was clear the facilities were past their use-by date. She said she had pressed the council to find a short-term solution while it pursued grant funding.

Rutledge hopes portable change rooms can be installed while the club identifies a long-term solution.

Victorian Animal Justice Party MP Georgie Purcell said the situation demonstrated the consequences of cutting the Office for Women in Sport and Recreation from last year's state budget.

Girls players getting changed on the benches outside the football field. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

Purcell said the office was not merely symbolic and had provided important support to sporting clubs, particularly those with relatively new women and girls' teams.

"It's not enough to just say women can play and think everything is going to magically resolve overnight. It requires commitment and work from the government," she told ABC Sport.

"I think the big problem with women in sport, and what we confront now, is women worked really hard and clubs worked really hard to let women into the spaces, but letting women into the spaces doesn't necessarily mean that they feel welcome or supported, or that the facilities and access are there for them to feel comfortable and like they're taken seriously.

" We say women are welcome in sport. We have women's sporting teams, but we just don't have the access or the facilities to allow those teams and club cultures to thrive. "

Macedon senior women's team are going for the three-peat this year. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

The Macedon way

Rutledge says he feels he is letting down the club's women's and girls' programs.

"I feel personally disappointed as president of the organisation. One of my commitments on the day that we had the election was that I want to make female participation one of our main goals," he says.

"We define outcomes not necessarily as premierships, but as participation and doing things for the community as well. We are a community club and we're very focused on letting the community judge us rather than us judging them.

"We've got a very powerful and energetic committee that works very closely with all parts of our operation… but we sit here tonight in a draconian position with our change rooms for our women."

Players say the culture at Macedon is different. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

The women want better facilities and are not quiet about it. But they are not going anywhere.

Even after Gisborne re-established its women's team, players such as Watts decided they would rather make the longer drive to keep doing things "the Macedon way".

World.title: Live: King Charles opens Glasgow 2026 after ceremony buoyed by Scottish pride
World.content:
(Getty)

It's literally my job, and I'm afraid to admit I cannot sum up the emotion and power of that performance in the Hydro.

If you've ever watched a pre-match show at the footy, you know they can tend to underwhelm as the noise dissipates in the open air and the performers are too far from the crowd, singing songs fans half remember from So Fresh CDs they bought with their first pay cheque from Maccas.

Inside this impressive circular arena, those pipers and drummers playing Flower of Scotland as the crowd sang unaided. Oooooof.

(Getty)

For those who don't know, Scotland's anthem is about Robert the Bruce's victory over King Edward II of England at the battle of Bannockburn, and the official lyrics go...

"And stood against them ..." And every good Scot knows to scream in that moment: "'GAINST WHO?!" "Proud Edward's army ..." "BASTARDS!" "And sent them homeward, to think again."

(Getty)

It is the epitome of rousing.

I, an Australian here trying to do a job, felt it in my bones (and tear ducts). I can't imagine what that must feel like to the thousands of Scots in here tonight.

Even the King applauded the song about one of his predecessor's being run out of the colonies.

How can they not top the medal tally after that?

World.title: Netball agents frustrated as pay talks roll into Glasgow 2026
World.content:
Has netball learned much since 2023? You be the judge.

The messy and drawn-out pay negotiations that dominated headlines during that World Cup year are once again overshadowing a major tournament for the sport.

The Diamonds are aiming to defend gold at the Commonwealth Games, and that mission starts on Saturday night in their opening match against Tonga at 8pm AEST. But the world number one team hit the court in Glasgow with uncertain futures.

The current Super Netball collective player agreement (CPA) expires on September 30, meaning all 88 players will be off contract. It is a chaotic way of doing things and leads to a mad scramble for everyone involved, with so many trying to secure opportunity at the same time.

Netball Australia surrenders, as players win long and bitter pay war Netball Australia has finally agreed to a modest revenue share partnership with its players, but how much have its brutal tactics throughout the pay negotiations damaged the game?

The 2027 signing window was supposed to open the Monday after the grand final on July 4. That has been delayed a month so the athletes can focus on their international duties while the terms of the next deal are worked through.

There are several sticking points that the national sporting organisation and the Australian Netball Players' Association (ANPA) cannot agree on. More on that later.

It is important to note that ANPA provided a detailed submission late last year to try and get the ball rolling. Netball Australia wanted to wait and sort out its new broadcast agreement with Nine, which underwrites the majority of the costs of the CPA first. That was done in April.

Although from the sport's point of view, discussions are more respectful and constructive this time, with greater transparency of information shared amongst parties, the players are incredibly frustrated. And so are their agents, who argue they are unable to make meaningful progress on behalf of their talent.

There is no prohibition to hold non-binding conversations with your own club or another right now, yet a request to allow non-binding written offers while CPA talks take place was denied. The agents believe this would've freed up the system and given players more certainty.

Kathryn Deiulioi is the founder of Behind Your Brand, which manages several Diamonds athletes, including the Australian captain. (Image Supplied)

Kathryn Deiulio, the founder of Behind Your Brand, said it was her understanding that the Diamonds players did not ask the sport to push back the contracting window and wanted discussions to continue. There are concerns this kind of assumption could create a divide amongst the group, positioning some as more important than others.

"This misunderstanding creates the impression that they didn't consider the impact it could have on the remaining 60-70 players not playing at the Games," Deiulio told ABC Sport.

"It is our role to continue contract negotiations on their behalf, and it would have created an additional layer of complexity, given the time difference and the need to carefully manage communication with players so as not to distract them from their performance.

"However, ultimately, that is part of our role as agents and something we are equipped to manage … These are professional athletes who dedicate their lives to their sport, and they deserve the same level of security around employment expected in any other profession."

Australia won gold at the Commonwealth Games in Birmingham. (Getty: Sue McKay)

Jace Bode is the chief executive of W Sports & Media, which works across a range of elite codes, such as cricket, Aussie Rules, football, golf and tennis.

"The fact that 80-plus athletes have once again been put in this position is incredibly disappointing and challenging to manage from our perspective," Bode told ABC Sport.

"We have the best netball competition in the world, and it is frustrating to watch these athletes continue to navigate uncertainty around their careers when it has so much potential."

This CPA will only be a 12-month deal, allowing Netball Australia to try and bring in more revenue from 2027 onwards with the free-to-air broadcast agreement and present a stronger offer. But both agents worry that without a longer CPA in place we may be right back here next year, ahead of a World Cup on home soil.

The Diamonds players have been in camp since Friday July 10. (Supplied: Netball Australia)

According to the new dates, contracts will open for clubs' own players from August 4-16. Non-binding written offers are permitted for all players during these 12 days. Then, from August 17-28, contracting officially opens for those looking to switch allegiances.

The agents argue this process favours those who intend to remain at their existing club, while placing players who may be looking elsewhere at a significant disadvantage. The time frame is also not ideal for those weighing up their options overseas, with the English Superleague contracting window already in full swing.

Complicating things further, in other sports it is normally the responsibility of the governing body to handle CPA talks with the players' association, but here the clubs appear to have taken greater control of the wheel.

All eight Super Netball franchises are likely to have competing ideas slowing progress further, and it is unclear if their vested interests will be prioritised over what is best for the sport as a whole.

Shimona Nelson represents Jamaica at the Birmingham Commonwealth Games. (Getty: Mark Kolbe)

The delay has wide-reaching implications beyond the Australian team at the Games.

In-form Melbourne Mavericks star Shimona Nelson had already flagged with Netball Jamaica that she would be unavailable for selection for Glasgow ahead of the Super Netball season. The goal shooter needs to get her tonsils removed and deal with a knee issue.

Although the Sunshine Girls did try and get her to change her mind, an appearance at the major tournament would be risky. Should she injure herself, with only one-year contracts being offered, where would that leave her?

It makes sense that Nelson has put herself first, considering the history of her career. After the Collingwood team disbanded, Nelson had to forge her way back into the league as a No.11 player with the Mavericks, working hard to return to a full-time contract the next season.

It is unfair that athletes are being forced to make these tricky decisions based on what is happening in Super Netball, and what is right for each of them is extremely individual.

Shimona Jok keeping an open mind as 11th player signing confirms she's eligible for Diamonds Super Netball import Shimona Jok was in the headlines after the Mavericks found a loophole to sign her as their 11th player. But now her eligibility for the Diamonds has been confirmed, would she ever go there?

There has been a rumour that Nelson isn't playing because she instead wants to represent the Diamonds at the next World Cup.

Nelson indeed plans to get her citizenship in September, purely to cement her status in a country she has lived in for almost 10 years and now classes as home.

At this point, there have been no discussions between the Australian camp or Shimona's about the possibility of her playing for the Diamonds.

So, what are some of the sticking points of the CPA talks?

Currently on the table is a 25 per cent pay increase for those on the minimum wage and a three per cent pay increase for everyone else.

This all sounds rosy until you do the numbers. Australia's consumer price index sits at four per cent. Once these changes are factored into the salary cap, with increased superannuation contributions and the rising cost of living, the take-home pay for many of the athletes could actually be worse off than they were this year. It may lead to a pay cut in real terms.

Former Thunderbird and Diamond Kathryn Harby-Williams is the chief executive of the players' association. (ABC News: Patrick Rocca)

Despite this, the sport will continue to restrict player opportunities to make extra cash in sponsorship deals. The cap for commercial arrangements with an existing team sponsor or partner is going to be raised to $50,000 but the agents want the cap removed entirely.

There are no monetary limits on a player's commercial agreements with third parties, but agents find the amount of compliance their talent must go through to get approval is unreasonable and leads to sponsors turning to athletes from other codes.

"When athletes are able to work with brands and authentically leverage their own platforms, they bring different eyeballs to the sport … This should be viewed as a positive, not a threat," Bode and Deiulio said.

"If netball does not evolve in this increasingly competitive female sports landscape, these limitations will have a broader impact on its growth and visibility."

World.title: Glasgow was asleep and the Games weren't open as Australia got its first win
World.content:
In a world where everything costs a bit too much and "free summer holiday activities" is high in your auto-complete drop-down, a spot of barefoot bowls remains a glorious tradition.

The sun shining, warming your carbonated beverage to a few degrees warmer than is pleasant, baffling yourself with how you can be so bad at a sport that on its face seems so simple, all while trying to stay alive to the prospect of your mates accidentally breaking your toe with wildly flung rock while misquoting half-remembered lines from Crackerjack.

That wasn't quite the case as the sport kicked off the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

How we got to Glasgow 2026 The bumpy road to Glasgow 2026 has produced a Commonwealth Games that will look a little different than the ones that came before.

The city of Glasgow was still waking up as athletes, officials and a handful of fans filed into the Scottish Event Campus (SEC) for a 9:30am start to Commonwealth competition on Thursday.

Not least of which because the event isn't on lawn of any sort; it's being played on carpeted greens indoors at the SEC Centre.

It serves as a reminder of organisers' decision to hold as many events in existing halls and venues, and gives the in-house DJ prime acoustics as he tries to pump up a crowd described as "small but mighty" by the MC team.

Already the only sport running on every day of the Games, organisers added an extra session on Day Zero before the opening ceremony due to "unprecedented demand" for the sport at a distinctly Scottish Games.

The sport has the royal seal of approval. (Getty Images: Aaron Chown/WPA Pool)

But making that widely known to punters may have fallen by the wayside for an organising committee feeling the pinch as their rapid 22-month planning period suddenly reached its end.

Along with bowls, the SEC will host more than half – boxing, judo, 3x3 basketball, netball, weightlifting and para powerlifting – of the cut-down list of sports in Glasgow.

Everything from Naughty By Nature to drum and pipes renditions of ABBA and Tina Turner echoed through Hall 3 as the countdown began and pyrotechnics welcomed the athletes to the rinks, with Australia's 2018 gold medallist Kelsey Cottrell the consensus "one to watch" as eight women's pairs rollers and four in the men's singles stepped onto the field of play.

But the first competitive moments of Glasgow 2026 arrived with a startling lack of fanfare, at least for the uninitiated.

There was fanfare welcoming the first Commonwealth Games athletes to the arena. (Bowls Australia: Aidan Davis)

The in-arena announcer made sure to point out their warm-up rolls had no bearing on the scores, but the only marker that Jackaroos Cottrell and Dawn Hayman were officially kicking us off came when the scoreboard clicked on at the far end of the Siti Zalina Ahmad Rink.

Cottrell and Hayman got it ticking over straight away with a 4-0 lead after the first end of the first set against Gertrude Siame and Foster Banda.

It was the sort of lead you see sometimes at these sorts of meets, where one team is simply outclassed.

That was certainly happening in the concurrent men's singles, where 39-year-old former world champion Shannon McIlroy was kicking the tar out of 17-year-old Tongan Liam Hill, and Northern Ireland's Gary Kelly was rolling Frederrick Tafatu of Niue.

The biggest cheers of the morning came from Botswana's crew whenever bucket-hatted Diza Mphotho won an end, a raucous reaction that cracked through the polite hum and mild applause accompanying some of the other victories.

Meanwhile, the Zambian pair fought back before Cottrell got the Aussie team rocking on the sidelines with a clutch final roll to secure the 6-4 win in the first set.

A vocal Zambian team gave the Aussies a scare. (Bowls Australia: Aidan Davis)

"Just breathe through the nerves a little bit when you feel that adrenaline pumping on the mat," Cottrell said.

"Take that extra second; time is precious [with a 30-second shot clock], but take that extra second and breathe through it."

The heavily favoured Aussies looked more like themselves in the second set as they romped to a 2-0 win against a team that had never played on carpet before.

Even as they were getting walloped 14-0 in the second set, Zambian skip Banda was vocally gassing up her partner – "Come on Gertrude, you are trying my darling" – and apologising for her own performances.

It was a welcome distraction for the Australians as they tried to keep their own adrenaline in check.

"They're always very chatty," Cottrell said.

"It's just that fine line, being able to walk away and focus when we need to, but also it's kind of good to engage in it because it keeps us cool, calm and collected as well. Really lovely girls."

Hayman and Cottrell will walk in the opening ceremony at the Hydro from 5am on Friday (AEST), but they have already truly opened the 2026 Commonwealth Games.

World.title: Penrith flyer breaks record in comeback Panthers win
World.content:
Penrith have survived a scare at the hands of rivals Parramatta, claiming a 24-18 win to strengthen their outright lead in the race for the NRL's minor premiership.

The Panthers moved four points clear of the second-placed Warriors, who face Canterbury on Saturday, with an unconvincing victory in which they were forced to play 20 minutes with just 12 men.

Tom Jenkins and Isaiah Papali'i were both sinbinned for professional fouls at Parramatta Stadium on Thursday but the Panthers, who didn't take the lead until the 57th minute, were able to prevail.

"That wasn't our best stuff but that was the first time this year when we've had to sort it out and come back," said Panthers coach Ivan Cleary.

"The sinbins … we had two good periods but the end was super disappointing.

"We got away with a win and there was some good resilience shown which we did last week (in a loss to Brisbane) … but it's just a game in a season and we'll have to do a lot better than that."

Jenkins scored his 26th try for the year to surpass Rhys Wesser as the most-prolific Panthers player across a single campaign and remains a chance of running down Dave Brown's 38-try season in 1935.

"His all-round game this year has been very consistent and that's why he's getting the tries," Cleary said.

"Rhys Wesser was a try machine and a bit of a legend in our club so it's pretty cool."

Parramatta, meanwhile, will remain in 15th spot and will feel this game was a valuable win they let slip from their grasp.

The Eels had the Panthers on the ropes early when Mitch Moses and Jack Williams put the home side 12-0 up.

Moses was in excellent touch for the battling Eels. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

Parramatta failed to score across either period while the Panthers were down to 12 men and then let their rivals off the hook in the second half with barge-over tries and pressure-relieving penalties.

"Unfortunately fight and effort only get you so far," said Eels coach Jason Ryles.

"It's a six-again on the last play a couple of times and penalties on play one out of yardage … they are things that are avoidable and are a little bit around our game awareness that we need to improve."

Jenkins was the catalyst for dragging the ladder-leaders back into the game, catching and offloading a Nathan Cleary kick for Casey McLean to touch down on the left.

Penrith flyer Jenkins was sinbinned on the stroke of halftime for pulling back Brian Kelly as the Eels winger chased after his own grubberkick.

Henry's try proved to be crucial for Penrith's comeback. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

The Panthers trailed 12-6 at the break but Parramatta were unable to use the one-man advantage to their benefit.

And just as Jenkins returned, Liam Henry crashed over under the sticks and Cleary tied the game up with a conversion from right in front.

Liam Martin was next over to push the Panthers six points ahead.

But any hope Parramatta had of getting back into the game was undone by their own ill-discipline as they failed to capitalise when Papali'i was sent to the bin.

Jenkins crossed for his obligatory try afterwards before Williams grabbed a consolation try for the Eels at the death.

World.title: 'Fascinating world': McRae questions booing directed at Quaynor
World.content:
Collingwood coach Craig McRae reckons it's "fascinating" why the Adelaide Oval crowd booed Isaac Quaynor.

And his Crows counterpart Matthew Nicks said it's "not ideal" that the Magpie defender was again jeered by spectators.

Quaynor was the target of a homophobic slur from Adelaide's Izak Rankine in an August 16 game last year that resulted in a four-game ban for the star Crow.

Yet the Magpie defender was booed by sections of the Adelaide Oval crowd during Collingwood's 34-point win on Thursday night.

"It's a fascinating narrative around why they would boo him," McRae said after his side's 16.12 (108) to 11.8 (74) triumph.

"My understanding is he was a victim of a homophobic slur — and he's getting booed for that.

"It's a fascinating world we live in."

McRae sought out Adelaide's Rankine after the final siren.

"I said: 'Mate, we've got great respect for you'," the coach said.

"People are allowed to make mistakes; they are, we're all human. I've got great respect for him. He's a sensational player.

"And I don't know him as a person, but the way he stood up … took it on the shoulders or whatever, however you want to put it, there's something to be said about that.

"That's life, isn't it: make a mistake, fix it, or get on with it and improve yourself."

McRae's 10-year-old daughter Charlie was in the Adelaide Oval media room as the coach commented.

"I teach her: we don't boo, that's all I can control," he said.

"People pay their money and they do what they like when they come to a game.

"I teach my children that we don't boo. We show respect to all people."

Crows boss Nicks, on the eve of the match, called for supporters to be respectful in what was Rankine's first game against the Magpies since his suspension.

"I mentioned it during the week about why we play footy, why people come to the footy," Nicks said post-match.

"It's about entertainment, it's about enjoyment, passion. The game is a passionate game and sometimes we lose our way in that a little.

"It's not ideal, the way it played out tonight."

Daicos masterclass shakes up finals picture

Another Nick Daicos masterclass propelled Collingwood to a comeback 34-point away victory over Adelaide.

Daicos (39 disposals, one goal) helped the Magpies overturn a 25-point second-quarter deficit.

Collingwood extended their winning streak to six games and climbed to seventh on the ladder.

Adelaide great Taylor Walker kicked his 700th career goal but the fifth-placed Crows blew a chance to rise to third spot.

Adelaide held a 25-point lead nine minutes into the second term, when Walker had already booted three majors.

But the Magpies climbed from the canvas in style, scoring 13 of the next 16 goals to stun the 50,109-strong Adelaide Oval crowd.

Daicos was instrumental, as were ruckman Darcy Cameron (23 disposals, six clearances, 37 hitouts) and veteran Scott Pendlebury (29 touches, one goal).

Magpies Dan McStay, Tim Membrey and Ed Allan kicked two goals each, and defender Isaac Quaynor (20 possessions) and 200-gamer Jordan De Goey (20, one goal) were also standouts.

Adelaide's Walker couldn't add to his early three goals while Riley Thilthorpe also finished with three.

Crow Sam Berry collected 30 disposals and 10 clearances, Izak Rankine — facing the Pies for the first time since his homophobic slur suspension — had 25 touches, and defenders Wayne Milera (24 possessions) and Josh Worrell (21, seven marks) were busy.

Look back how the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Bomber Caddy to face Hawks after heart scare
World.content:
Essendon interim coach Dean Solomon says Nate Caddy will play in Saturday's match against Hawthorn following his recovery from a heart scare.

Caddy was taken to hospital during last Sunday's three-point win over GWS due to an elevated heart rate.

Bombers star cleared for return Nate Caddy is expected to fully train and play next weekend despite experiencing an elevated heart rate during Essendon's win over GWS.

The 21-year-old was released from hospital after being given the all-clear.

The club's medical staff has since given its approval for Caddy to face the Hawks.

"He'll be good to go," Solomon said.

"They said there's no risk with what happened and he's fully good to go. I trust our medical staff, and Nate's in a good headspace as well.

"He spent a lot of time with the docs and medical staff, gone through it all and has a good understanding that there's no risk at play here, and he's really confident.

"So we've just got to trust our medical staff."

Essendon has lost Xavier Duursma (hamstring) for the rest of the season, while Kyle Langford will miss the Hawthorn match due to suspension.

McKay sits out Blues training

Star Carlton forward Harry McKay failed to participate during the Blues' main training session on Thursday.

McKay suffered a minor tear to his meniscus, as well as bone bruising to his knee, during Saturday night's 21-point defeat to Collingwood.

The 28-year-old was ruled out early in the match after his knee knocked into teammate Sam Walsh.

Harry McKay was forced from the field against the Magpies last weekend. (Getty Images: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

But speculation around McKay ran rampant, with Fox Footy commentator David King questioning the one-time Coleman medallist's injury.

The Blues were privately seething with McKay's character being criticised, before the severity of the injury was confirmed on Sunday.

Interim Blues coach Josh Fraser said he "didn't spend a lot of time thinking about" the commentary surrounding McKay.

"Whenever there's an injury, your mindset goes to the care and support for the player," Fraser said.

"We act on the information we're given from our medical team, the commentary around all of that, I probably push it to the side.

"I can only judge him on the way he's presented and he's presented his usual self.

"Great energy around the group, trying as hard as he can to play and leading internally around the club."

Carlton's wildcard hopes will go on the line on Saturday when it host out-of-form Gold Coast at Docklands.

AAP

World.title: Aussie captain relishes 'special' chance 'to take time to be a dad'
World.content:
Water polo is a brutal sport.

Relentless swimming. Incessant wrestling. Elbows and fists flying around as if the combatants were half-submerged within a flooded UFC cage.

To put it mildly, it is not a place for the faint of heart.

So it is somewhat incongruous, then, to see Australian Sharks captain Nathan Power sitting on the side of the Griffith University pool on the Gold Coast with his son, Sebastian in his arms, feeding him a bottle.

Power, 33, will lead the Australian men's water polo team at the World Aquatics Water Polo World Cup event in Sydney this week, with the Sharks taking on reigning world champions Spain on Thursday.

He is also on six months of parental leave from his role as a manager with KPMG, giving him valuable time to be a dad as well as skippering his nation.

Nathan Power will skipper the team in his home town of Sydney. (Supplied: Water Polo Australia)

"It's been fun to get to do this," Power told ABC Sport, with Sebastian still in his arms.

"To get an opportunity to take time to be a dad, it's really special."

It's created some changes within the team environment too.

"This is the first time in my time with the men's team that there's been a baby on tour — and there's actually two at the moment, Blake Edwards has his son Jude here as well," Power said.

"It makes for a bit of a shift; even at breakfast time now, the boys all roll in and it's a case of, who's gunna take hold of the baby and who wants to look after a baby.

"It's amazing to see how a large group of men have all very quickly clicked into dad mode to help out where they can."

Australian Sharks Water Polo coach Tim Hamill (left) says the addition of kids to camp has been great. (Supplied: Zac Hudson)

Head coach Tim Hamill, who has led the Sharks since taking the reins post-Tokyo in 2021, also made note of the positive changes to the dynamic young children can have.

"It's a first for us," the former international player told ABC Sport.

"One of our values as a team is around family, so we talk to that in having those families here.

The 'precious' bond driving the Stingers to success Australia's women's water polo team, the Stingers, were the most successful Australian team at the Paris Olympics, winning a stunning silver medal. This is the secret to their success.

"We're really fortunate to have a nice balance of the group, we've got the spectrum covered in terms of interests and ideas and for the first time, in this preparation, we've got two of our players who have children, which we've never had before.

"So that changed the dynamic of the group.

"A lot of people have spoken about Paris and how do we get those results [that we got] and I'm conscious to talk culture because it's that overused word in sport at the moment.

"But for me, culture as a word is derived from that care, there's real care in this team.

"We know that our culture needs to be the best in the world, we know that our team care needs to be the best in the world, otherwise we can't compete, so we invest time in all of that, and that's conversations with those 18s all the way through to 30 plus year olds and now fathers."

The topic of keeping mothers in sport has been a hot one in the Australian space for a while now.

In December, the Australian Olympic Committee created the Olympians Future Fund, with a key pillar of that designed to help support female Olympians return to high-performance sport after giving birth, making them eligible to receive $10,000.

Although Power's situation is different, he noted that the support that he has received from KPMG and Water Polo Australia was just as valuable to him in order to allow both he and his partner Maddy to continue their careers.

Water polo is not exactly a gentle sport, as Power shows while wrestling Spain on their way to the world championship title last year. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

"That's kind of the thing that can maybe get lost at times, but really it's support for the family," he said.

"With the support that I get through my work at KPMG, that then enables Maddy to get back into work; the support I get from Water Polo Australia, that enables us as a family to be here.

"We both get to keep on pursuing what we want to pursue, but also get to spend some really meaningful time with Sebastian too.

"It's been awesome to come home from training and the first thing I see is a silly smile from the window, him looking out at me.

"It's a new, fun way to come home from training when you're a bit cooked and tired and maybe a bit grumpy."

Power beamed with joy when recounting how much Sebastian was enjoying finding his feet in the water during his lessons, adding that fatherhood has "massively" changed his perspective.

Nathan Power has competing priorities now. (Supplied: Water Polo Australia)

"I think, obviously parenthood becomes that key identity that you have and you see yourself as," he said.

"It's also something which for me, at 33, I guess we can probably confidently say I'm closer to the end than the start of my career, so it means you also get to take some moments and really appreciate that this isn't normal to get to do this and to share this experience with your family.

"It gets you to appreciate these experiences you have with the team too, because they can be very fleeting."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

The World Cup Final is the first time Australia has hosted a major water polo championships since the 2007 World Championships in Melbourne, and the first time Sydney has hosted a combined event since the 2000 Olympics.

Power said the opportunity to compete in front of friends and family will never be undervalued by the squad.

"The importance of it and the rarity of it is not lost on us," Power said.

"I've had teammates who've started their career and gone through their career and finished their career and didn't get that opportunity to be able to play in an event at home like that.

"Obviously, as we move towards Brisbane, this is one of those good examples of something which can hopefully lead to more of these events occurring as well."

Tech.title: Alexa Plus is getting an AI update to handle more complicated instructions
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Amazon is launching an update to its Alexa Plus assistant that will allow it to connect to smart home devices in new ways. With the update, Alexa Plus can link up with tech from Bosch, Delta, Ecovacs, iRobot, Yale Home, Whirlpool, Tapo, Eufy, and others, while automatically routing requests to the correct device.

In an example shared by Amazon, a person with a supported washing machine can say, “Alexa, my kid’s soccer jersey could use a deep clean, but the tag says cold wash only.” From there, Alexa Plus would navigate the washer’s cycle options and choose the correct setting. The new integrations are powered by Amazon’s new AI developer toolkit, which is supposed to make it easier for device makers to connect to Alexa Plus, “including those with unique capabilities that weren’t supported before.”

Amazon widely launched its revamped AI assistant in February, which can handle multi-step requests and help you create routines using your voice. It currently only performs tasks in a limited number of third-party services, such as Ticketmaster, OpenTable, Uber, Thumbtack, Expedia, Yelp, Square, and Angi.

But Amazon is trying to change this by adopting the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open-source standard that allows AI models to connect to external systems and tools. This will give more brands the ability to interact with Alexa Plus, with Canva, Headspace, Priceline, Lyft, Cengage, Virgin Atlantic, Weekend, and other companies launching integrations later this year.

For example, Priceline will give customers the ability to browse hotel options and book a trip directly through Alexa Plus. Priceline, along with Atom Tickets, Cengage, Fandango, and Taskrabbit, will soon support payments through Amazon Wallet as well.

Amazon Echo Show 21 $ 320 $ 400 20 % off $ 320 The Echo Show 21 can act as the centerpiece of any burgeoning smart home.
